## 2026-07-30 — Rail geometry: one set of numbers, from the global sidebar

User report: the Tasks rail's pinned "Completed" had inconsistent padding and
margins next to the Documents rail's "Trash", which looked right.

They were right, and the cause was that I had tuned the Tasks foot by eye against
a screenshot instead of taking the numbers from the system. `NavItem` in
`app-shell.tsx` is the app's canonical nav row — **34px tall, 8px inset, radius 6,
4px between rows** — and the Documents rail already matched it. The Tasks rail
didn't:

| | global sidebar | Documents | Tasks (before) |
|---|---|---|---|
| row inset | 8px | 8px | **14px** |
| gap between rows | 4px | 4px | **2px** |
| foot | — | `p-2` + full-width `border-t` | **`pt-2` + a `mx-[-14px]` hairline + `mb-[7px]`** |

So an identical pill read as narrower and more crowded in Tasks than the same pill
two modules over, and the foot's separator was a negative margin dragged out to
fake a border.

Fixed by taking the geometry rather than guessing it: the 8px padding moved onto an
inner wrapper so the foot's `border-t` can span the rail on its own (no negative
margin), the row gap went to 4, and the foot became the same `p-2` + `border-t` box
Documents uses. The section dividers use `-mx-2` — the same trick `NavDivider` uses
against the sidebar's own padding — instead of a hardcoded `-14px`. The narrow
(horizontal) shape is now its own early return rather than `!narrow &&` sprinkled
through one tree.

**Measured, both rails, after:** row inset **8**, height **34**, foot padding
**8px**, foot border **1px**, radius **6px**, icon↔label gap **8px**, font **14px**
— identical. Hover was already the same token (`--hover` and
`--color-surface-hover` both resolve to `#ffffff0f`).

Two more inconsistencies closed while in there:

- **Rail width 232 → 230**, matching Documents. Nobody would notice 2px alone, but
  it meant the content pane started at a different x depending on the module.
- **Documents' SELECTED row was `bg-surface-hover`** — its own hover colour — so a
  selected row was pixel-identical to a merely hovered one. It's `surface-selected`
  + medium now, per the global sidebar's `NavItem`, which the Tasks rail already
  followed. This one goes the other way from the report: Documents was the outlier
  against the system, so it changed, not Tasks.

## 2026-07-31 — Deployed to production; dev-preview cut out of the build

**Live:** version `e836cf43-83f5-4ce7-9d7c-4c44bc1d3d2d` at
<https://zenboard-web.designdotrushil.workers.dev>. First deploy since the header
work, the Tasks rail, Habits v2, link-paste, and the Phase-1 consolidation.

### The deploy failed first, on size

Cloudflare rejected the upload: **worker 3.15 MiB gzipped against the free plan's
3 MiB limit** (`code: 10027`). The cause was not the app — it was the harnesses:

| | server output |
|---|---|
| `app/dev-preview` (34 harness routes) | **3.6 MB** |
| `app/(app)` — the actual product | 1.4 MB |

The harnesses were also *publicly reachable on the live worker*: 34 URLs of
half-built UI and fake numbers. They read no data (every one is `'use client'`
with hard-coded fixtures, zero touch Supabase), so nothing leaked, but they had
no business being served.

**Fix, in two layers:**
1. `app/dev-preview/layout.tsx` — `notFound()` unless `NODE_ENV === 'development'`.
   Hides them, but still ships every byte, so on its own it did NOT fix the size.
2. **The real fix:** every harness page renamed `page.tsx` → **`page.dev.tsx`**, and
   `next.config.ts` puts `dev.tsx` in `pageExtensions` **only** under `next dev`.
   A production build never sees them as routes, so their code is never compiled.

`pageExtensions` is the documented Next mechanism for this
(`node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/03-api-reference/05-config/01-next-config-js/pageExtensions.md`)
— no file shuffling in a build script, nothing to restore if a build crashes.

**Result:** routes 72 → 38 · server app output 5.8 MB → 2.2 MB · **gzip 3221 KiB →
2596 KiB**, ~475 KiB under the limit. Deploy succeeded, startup time 23 ms.

### `--keep-vars` is mandatory on this project

Deploy with **`wrangler deploy --keep-vars`**. `wrangler.jsonc` declares no `vars`,
and a plain `wrangler deploy` *deletes every var not in the config* — the runtime
secrets (`SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`, `GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID/SECRET`,
`GEMINI_API_KEY`, `RESEND_API_KEY`) were set through the dashboard per SETUP.md §4,
so an unguarded deploy would silently break form uploads, notifications, Calendar
sync, AI and email. Note `wrangler deploy` does **not** read `.env.local` (only
`wrangler dev` does) — the dry-run shows only the IMAGES and ASSETS bindings.

`NEXT_PUBLIC_*` are baked in at build time from `.env.local`, so those travel with
the bundle and are not affected either way.

`/login` 200 · `/` `/tasks` `/onboarding` 307 (auth redirect) · `/dev-preview/habits`
and `/dev-preview/design` **404** · `/f/does-not-exist` 200, which is the useful one:
the public form renderer went through the server-side Supabase client and rendered
its not-found page instead of a 500, so the runtime env survived the deploy.
Login page screenshot clean, zero console errors.

Dev harnesses re-checked after a **full dev-server restart** (not just an HMR pass):

## 2026-07-31 — Why switching pages was slow, and what actually fixed it

User report: "when i switched to one page to another page its takes time." It was
not rendering, not the bundle, and not the design — it was **round trips**.

**Measured:** steady-state latency from here to Supabase is **~220ms median**
(175–310ms over six requests on one connection). Every one of those is a wall.

### What one navigation to Home cost

The (app) layout and the page each opened with the same three questions, and
nobody remembered the answers:

| Asked | Times per navigation | Where |
|---|---|---|
| `auth.getUser()` | **3×** | layout · `loadTodayData` · `userTimezone` |
| `spaces` | **3×** | `activeSpaceId` in the layout · the layout's own switcher query · `activeSpaceId` in the page |
| `profiles` | **2×** | layout · `userTimezone` |

`auth.getUser()` is the expensive one and it does not look expensive: it is a
NETWORK call to `/auth/v1/user` that asks the Auth server to verify the JWT,
not a local cookie decode.

On top of that, `loadTodayData` awaited nine independent things one after
another — tasks, then subtasks, then projects, then events, then habits, then the
stage counters — none of which needed the one before it.

**Critical path ≈ 11 serial round trips, 17 requests.** At 220ms that is roughly
**2.4 seconds** of a navigation spent waiting, and — see below — with nothing on
screen to show for it.

### What changed

1. **Request-level memoisation** with React `cache()`. `createClient` is now
   `cache()`d, so a request shares one client; `auth.getUser()` is memoised on it
   (an explicit-JWT call still goes through). New `lib/profile.ts` `currentProfile()`
   and a `spaceList()` in `lib/active-space.ts` do the same for the two repeated
   queries. Call sites keep their signatures — the memo sits on zero-argument
   functions, because `cache()` keys on arguments and `activeSpaceId(supabase, …)`
   takes a client that is a new reference every time.
2. **`loadTodayData` fires its independent queries at once** — tasks ‖ events ‖
   habits ‖ stage counters in one wave, then subtasks ‖ project chips in a second.
3. **The layout stopped fetching `spaces` twice**: `spaceList()` selects the
   switcher's columns too, so `activeSpaceId` rides along on the same query.

**Critical path ≈ 4 waves, 9 requests** — derived as counted hops × measured RTT,
≈2.4s → ≈0.9s. Not measured end to end: that needs a signed-in session.

### The part that will be felt most: there was no loading state anywhere

**Zero `loading.tsx` files and zero `Suspense` boundaries in the whole app.** Click
"Tasks" and the Home screen sat there, frozen and still looking clicked, until the
last query returned. `app/(app)/loading.tsx` now renders a skeleton
(`components/shell/app-loading.tsx`) inside the layout, so the chrome never blinks
and only the content area swaps. It also makes `<Link>` prefetch meaningful —
prefetching a dynamic route with no loading boundary fetches nothing.

### Two traps, both worth remembering

**Never import the DS barrel from a server component.** `components/ds/ui/index.ts`
re-exports 63 things, and `field.tsx` / `toggle-group.tsx` call `createContext` at
module scope. Because `loading.tsx` is in every (app) route's module graph, one
barrel import there took down `/design`, `/automations` and `/library` with
`(0 , e.createContext) is not a function` — first at "Generating static pages",
then, after a failed workaround, even earlier at "Collecting page data". Import
`@/components/ds/ui/skeleton` directly. `skeleton.tsx` and `view-container.tsx`
have no `'use client'` and no hooks, so they render on the server fine.

**I chased the wrong cause first** — assumed `loading.tsx` was triggering a static
shell prerender these pages could not survive, and reached for `force-dynamic` on
`/design`. It "worked" only by moving the failure to the next page. Isolating by
removing `loading.tsx` and rebuilding proved the file was involved; the barrel was
the actual defect. The `force-dynamic` workaround has been reverted — no workaround
left behind for a bug that is gone. Also note Next 16 no longer lists `dynamic` in
the route-segment config table at all.

**Deployed:** `bff845d5-4544-44cc-a45d-4abf3d67a078`, gzip 2608 KiB. tsc exit 0 ·
239/239 vitest · `/login` 200 · `/f/does-not-exist` 200 · `/dev-preview/*` 404.
Skeleton verified in `/dev-preview/loading`: `aria-busy`, 14 shimmer elements,
48px header row, "Loading" for screen readers.

### Still on the table (not done)

The remaining gap to Linear is architectural, not incremental: Linear reads from a
local store and syncs in the background, so navigation costs nothing. The next real
step here would be caching read data client-side so a revisit paints from memory
while it revalidates. Worth doing only after the above is confirmed on real usage.

## 2026-07-31 — <PageView>: one opening system for every record

User spec: every openable thing — task, document, project, client, invoice, form,
habit, goal, calendar event, database row, meeting, finance entry, contact —
opens through ONE component. Only the content differs; the toolbar, transitions,
keyboard grammar and view modes are identical everywhere. **Never build a
module-specific detail panel again.**

### What shipped

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `components/ds/ui/page-view.tsx` | The primitive — 3 render modes + new-tab action, universal toolbar, breadcrumbs, keyboard grammar, resizable side peek |
| `lib/page-view-mode.ts` | The preference: per-content-type default + global override + remembered width, in `localStorage['zb:pageview:v1']` |
| `components/ds/ui/dropdown-menu.tsx` | `DropdownMenuItem` gained `description` (two-line rows) and `active` (trailing check) — the view-mode menu needs both |
| `components/ds/icons.ts` | `ModeSidePeek` · `ModeCenterPeek` · `ModeFullPage`, added as a set |
| `app/dev-preview/page-view/page.dev.tsx` | Harness — 4 records across 3 content types |

### Two things it deliberately does NOT do

**It does not navigate.** Eleven of the thirteen content types have no per-record
route to push to, and a primitive that invented one would lie about where you are.
Hosts keep owning addressing (`lib/use-record-param.ts`); `href` here powers
"Open in new tab" and middle-click, and full page renders in place.

**It does not fetch.** Content is `children`, always resolved by the host — which
is exactly what makes "switch record without closing the panel" fall out for free.

### Verified in the harness (not by reading the code)

- Toolbar renders exactly the spec's controls: Back · Forward · *module actions* ·
  Open in full page · View mode · Open in new tab · More · Close.
- Breadcrumbs render 4 levels (`Projects / Balluji / Packaging / Balluji brand portal`)
  via the **existing DS `<Breadcrumbs>`**, which already collapses >4 levels into a
  "…" menu. I had hand-rolled a second one; deleted it.
- **Switching records keeps the same DOM node.** Tagged the panel with a data
  attribute, clicked Forward, and the tag survived while title and breadcrumbs
  changed — the spec's "don't close the panel, replace the content".
- View-mode menu reads exactly as specified, descriptions and all.
- Side peek is non-modal (view behind stays interactive); center peek and full page
  are modal — confirmed via Radix's `aria-hidden` on body siblings.
- ⌘↵ switches to full page **without overwriting the saved default** — a session
  pick and a preference are separate on purpose.
- "Set as default for tasks" wrote `{"byType":{"task":"center-peek"}}`, and after a
  **full page reload** a task opened center-peek while a document — no override —
  still opened full page from its type default.

### Notes

`useSyncExternalStore`, not read-in-an-effect: localStorage IS an external store,
and this avoids the extra render (and the cascading-render lint). Both snapshots
return a **string or a number, never an object** — React compares with `Object.is`,
so a getter building a fresh object would re-render forever. The server snapshot is
mandatory or SSR throws. The session-mode reset likewise adjusts state during
render (React's documented prop-change pattern) rather than in an effect, which
would flash the previous mode for one frame on every reopen.

tsc exit 0 · 239/239 vitest · eslint clean on all new files · build clean.

### NOT done — the migration

The primitive exists and nothing uses it yet. Every module still has its own panel,
and `components/task-detail/task-detail-drawer.tsx` is the worst of them: a
hand-rolled panel of inline styles that never even reached the DS `<Drawer>`.
Migration order, easiest seam first: **task → database row (already on DS Drawer) →
invoice → client → project → document**. Each one is a real UI change to a working
screen, so they want doing deliberately, not in a batch.

## 2026-07-31 — Tasks are the first module on <PageView>

Deployed `e7bc6157-3d04-49be-8ed0-d484301aa61a`, gzip 2609 KiB.

`components/task-detail/task-detail-drawer.tsx` was the worst panel in the app —
a hand-rolled scrim + `<aside>` + breadcrumb strip in inline styles that never even
reached the DS `<Drawer>`. All of that shell is gone; only the task's own content
remains, inside `<PageView contentType="task">`.

**What tasks gained by inheriting the system, none of it written for tasks:**

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Modes | side drawer only | side peek · center peek · full page · new tab |
| Width | fixed `min(600px, 94vw)` | resizable, remembered across sessions |
| Behind the panel | scrim, list blocked | visible and scrollable |
| Toolbar | a close button | back · forward · full page · view mode · new tab · close |
| Breadcrumbs | hand-rolled strip | DS `<Breadcrumbs>`, with >4-level "…" collapse |
| Shortcuts | none | ⌘↵ · ⌥↵ · ⌘⇧↵ · ctrl+\ · ← → · Esc |

Two things the migration needed from the primitive, both added there rather than
worked around: **`footer`** (the comment composer must not scroll away) and the
knowledge that `href` can be a *search param* — `?task=<id>` is already this
record's address, so "Open in new tab" is a real link, not a simulation.

**Back/forward now means something for tasks.** The panel walks an infinite-depth
subtask tree, so ← / → move through the nodes you actually visited, with a fresh
trail per task (`hist`/`histIdx`, truncating the forward branch on a new pick, the
way a browser does). Breadcrumb clicks and subtask-row clicks both go through
`select()` so the trail stays honest.

### Corrected against the spec

## 2026-08-01 — Selection-aware statistics (user priority #1)

The user's roadmap named this first: "the counter should become contextual." The doc
footer printed the same five document numbers forever — including a "Spaces" count
nobody asked for — and said nothing about what you had selected.

- **`lib/text-stats.ts` (new, 12 tests)** — ONE counting rule for the app:
  `textStats()` (characters excluding line breaks · words · sentences · paragraphs),
  `readingSeconds` (200 wpm) / `speakingSeconds` (130 wpm), and `formatDuration`
  ("23 sec" · "3 min" · "1 hr 5 min"). Sentences count a trailing run with no full
  stop, so typing a line never reads "0 sentences" — that's a guarded test.
- **`DocStats` is now contextual** — nothing selected: `559 characters · 89 words ·
  7 sentences · 9 paragraphs` (the stray "Spaces" is gone, casing is consistent).
  Text selected: `**Selection** · 247 characters · 39 words · 2 sentences ·
  1 paragraphs · 12 sec read · 18 sec aloud`. The `aria-label` flips
  Document↔Selection and the region is `aria-live="polite"`, so it is announced.
- Selection is scoped to the doc scroller — selecting in the sidebar or a popover
  must not repaint the doc footer.

**Gotcha worth keeping:** the component reads the selection's RANGES, not
`sel.toString()`. The browser pane runs with `document.visibilityState === "hidden"`
and `hasFocus() === false`, where `sel.toString()` returns `""` while the ranges
still hold the text (measured: range 247 chars, toString 0). Reading ranges is
equally correct, more robust for a background tab, and it is what made this
verifiable at all.

Verified live on `/dev-preview/documents`: no-selection → document stats; select a
paragraph → Selection + reading/speaking time; clear it → back to document stats.

## 2026-08-01 — Optimistic creation is now TRUSTWORTHY (user priority #2)

Audited every creation path first. Finding: creation was **already optimistic**
everywhere (`newPage`, `createFolder`, `DbStore.addRow` all insert a `tmp-` row and
reconcile) — so the roadmap's "instant UI updates" was largely done. The real defect
was the other half: **every one of those paths rolled back in SILENCE.** On a flaky
connection a page/row/folder appeared and then vanished with no explanation, which
reads as the app eating your work. That is a straight §2.5 violation ("never silent
on failure") and the thing that actually destroys trust in optimistic UI.

- **`lib/db-store.ts`** — new `rollbackRow(id, message)` replaces bare `dropRow` on
  the failure paths of `addRow` (both the `else` and the `.catch`) and of the
  delete-UNDO restore, which could also fail silently and lose a row the user had
  just chosen to bring back. Imports `toast` directly from its module (a singleton
  store dispatch, not rendering — the file's "no JSX" doctrine is intact).
- **`documents-view.tsx`** — `newPage` and `createFolder` now toast on failure, and
  `newPage` also clears `selectedId` so a failed create can't strand the editor on a
  page that no longer exists.
- **`expandCollection` made optimistic** — the one genuinely non-optimistic path: it
  awaited TWO serial round trips (create page → attach collection) before anything
  appeared, so "turn into page" felt broken on a slow link. Now it opens the page
  instantly and reconciles, with rollback + a message on either failure.

Verified on `/dev-preview/db-row`: database renders (the lib→toast import introduces
no cycle) and `New` inserts a row instantly, 3 → 4, no round trip. tsc 0 · 251 tests.

## 2026-08-01 — Filter groups: AND / OR (user priority #5, first slice)

The user's list said "Filter groups — AND, OR, nested conditions." Audited before
building and found the interesting half was already done: **`db-engine.matchesFilter`
has always recursed into nested groups and honoured `logic: 'or'`.** The types
(`FilterGroup`) supported it too. Only the CHIP UI was flat-AND-only — and worse, it
actively *destroyed* structure: it read `rules.filter(r => !isFilterGroup(r))` and
then wrote `{ logic: 'and', rules: <flat list> }` back, so any nested group in a
view was silently deleted on the next filter edit, and `or` could never be set.

- **The join between chips IS the control.** Chips after the first are preceded by a
  small `and`/`or` button; clicking it flips the whole group (Notion's model — the
  join belongs to the group, since "A and B or C" has no unambiguous reading).
  Labelled for screen readers ("Match all filters — click to switch to any").
- **Sub-groups are now carried through untouched** (`writeFilter` re-appends
  `subGroups`), so a nested group survives chip edits instead of being dropped.
- **`lib/db-engine.test.ts` (new, 4 tests)** — the engine had NO tests at all. Covers
  and/or/nested/empty, including the nested case "done AND (5h OR 1h)".

Verified live on `/dev-preview/db-row` with two real rules (`Status is Done`,
`Tags has Design`): **AND → 0 rows** (nothing is both) · **OR → 3 rows**. The toggle
round-trips through the store (and → or → and). tsc 0 · **255 tests**.

### Still open in #5 ("database settings 30% complete")

A nested-group BUILDER (add a sub-group in the UI — the engine and persistence
already handle them), saved filters, view permissions (private/shared/locked),
database templates, advanced sorting (manual/natural/random). Conditional colour
already exists (`colorRules` + the Conditional colour panel).

Finishes the "nested conditions" item. The engine and persistence were already
ready (previous entry), so this is the UI that can finally CREATE a group.

  properties, so `Group on Tags` creates `{ logic: 'or', rules: [<that rule>] }`.

editor auto-opens, adding a condition updates it to "2 conditions", and toggling
Match all/any round-trips through the store (chip label or → and). **2 more engine

## 2026-08-01 — Phosphor is the ONE icon family (user directive)

Answering the Phase 0 audit's question 1: **keep the existing B&G system, no rebrand,
Phosphor only.** The app had THREE icon libraries installed and the seam
(`components/ds/icons.ts`) was a deliberate hybrid — Phosphor for screens that had
taken the Figma pass, Tabler for the ~160 that hadn't — so two drawing styles could
meet inside a single row.

- **~160 Tabler glyphs re-pointed to Phosphor equivalents** in one pass (Activity →
  Pulse, Filter → FunnelSimple, Mail → Envelope, History → ClockCounterClockwise,
  Bold → TextB, ExternalLink → ArrowSquareOut, …). Every export now goes through the
  existing `phosphor()` adapter, so the Tabler-shaped call-site API (`size`,
  `strokeWidth`, `className`) is unchanged and **no call site needed editing**.
- **4 direct `lucide-react` imports removed** — `command.tsx`, `dialog.tsx`,
  `menu.tsx`, `context-menu.tsx` were bypassing the seam entirely. They now import
  from `@/lib/icons` (the shim over the seam) with local aliases, so the mirrored DS
  components keep their names.
- **`@tabler/icons-react` and `lucide-react` removed from package.json.** Phosphor is
  the only icon dependency left. (`@tanstack/react-table` is also installed and
  imported nowhere — flagged in the audit, not touched.)
- Seam header rewritten: the rule is now "never import an icon library directly in a
  component — this file is the only place that may."

**Verified by measurement, not eyeballing:** Phosphor draws on a `0 0 256 256`
viewBox, Tabler and lucide on `0 0 24 24`. On `/dev-preview/db-row` all **22** SVGs
report 256, and on `/dev-preview/shell` all **9** do — with **zero** empty SVGs
(an unmapped name would render an empty `<svg>`). tsc 0 · 264 tests.

**Why tsc was the safety net:** `Ph` is a typed namespace, so a wrong Phosphor name
is a compile error, not a silent blank icon. All 176 names resolved first try.

### Phase 0 decisions the user delegated ("just make it like Notion")

- **Row = page → option (b), incremental.** End state is Notion's exactly (every row
  is a real page with body/icon/cover/comments/history), reached by additive schema +

- **Scale → ~2,000 rows client-side**, not 10,000. Single-user app with hundreds of
  rows; virtualization + server-side pushdown is a phase of work that would not be
  felt today. Nothing in the design may BLOCK adding it later.

## 2026-08-01 — Version history, wired at last (roadmap #4 / Phase 10)

**All 27 migrations are live** (user confirmed) — the Phase 0 audit's drift question
is closed. And the audit's best find pays off here: **`page_versions` has existed
since 0001, with correct RLS, and had ZERO code referencing it.** So document
version history needed no migration at all.

- **`lib/version-policy.ts` (new, 9 tests)** — the rule, pure and testable. A
  **coalescing window**: while you keep editing, one entry; stop for 10 minutes and
  the next edit starts a new one. Snapshotting every autosave would give 400 entries
  an afternoon, each a keystroke apart — a log, not a history. Also `versionsToPrune`
  (keep newest 50, order-independent) and `versionBucket` (Today/Yesterday/Earlier).
  The unchanged-check runs FIRST so an idle doc can never accrue entries just because
  time passed.
- **`lib/actions/versions.ts` (new)** — list / get / save / restore. **Restore
  snapshots the CURRENT content before overwriting**, so restoring is itself
  undoable; a history feature whose restore is destructive is worse than none.
  Pruning is best-effort — 51 versions is not worth failing a save over.
- **`components/documents/version-history.tsx` (new)** — opens through `<PageView>`
  (§2.11), so it inherits peek/center/full, Escape and the toolbar instead of
  inventing a panel. Grouped list, body preview, confirm-before-restore.
- **Wired**: "Version history" in the doc ⋮ menu (optional prop — a grid card has no
  body loaded, so it doesn't offer it), and `saveVersion` fires after each autosave.
- **`types/database.ts`** gained `page_versions` (hand-authored file) and `pages`
  gained a writable `updated_at`.

### A real bug the browser check caught

The panel hung on "Loading history…" forever. Cause: the server actions' `requireUser()`
**throws**, so `await listVersions(...)` REJECTED — neither the success nor the
`'error' in res` branch ran, and `versions` stayed `null`. Not a harness artifact: any
transient auth or network failure in production would have wedged it identically, and
`restore` would have left its button disabled on "Restoring…" permanently. All three
awaits are now guarded; verified it settles into the empty state. This is why the
"never silent on failure" rule needs a `catch`, not just an `if (error)`.

tsc 0 · **273 tests**. Verified on `/dev-preview/documents`: the menu item renders in
order, the panel opens as a side peek titled "Version history", and it settles.

## 2026-08-01 — Phase 1 step 1: "every row is a page" (migration DRAFTED, not applied)

The structural fork from the Phase 0 audit. Decided **incremental** (the user
delegated the call): same end state as Notion, reached without a big-bang rewrite.

**`0028_rows_are_pages.sql` — additive only, nothing dropped, idempotent.**
- `pages` gains `database_id` (non-null ⇒ this page IS a database row),
  `properties` jsonb (keyed by PROPERTY ID so renames never touch row data), and
  `row_order` text (fractional index — text not float, because a double runs out
  of precision after ~50 midpoint inserts).
- `collection_rows` gains `page_id` — the **bridge**. This is what makes the
  migration incremental: both tables coexist, each row knows its twin, readers
  move one at a time, and a half-migrated app is still a working app.
- Backfill creates one page per row: `data - '__content'` → `properties`, and
  `data->'__content'` (the body that was smuggled into the property bag) → the
  page's own `content`. Only touches rows with `page_id is null`, so re-running is
  safe. Rows where BOTH `r.space_id` and `c.space_id` are null are skipped rather
  than guessed at — `pages.space_id` is NOT NULL — and the report query surfaces them.
- `row_order` seeded as a fixed-width hex string in the current float order, so the
  first drag has something to bisect between.
- GIN on `properties` (filters are per-property and ad hoc, so a btree per property
  isn't knowable up front); partial btrees on `database_id` and `(database_id, row_order)`.

**`0028_rows_are_pages_rollback.sql` — total, with a guard.** 0028 modifies no
pre-existing data, so the rollback returns the DB byte-for-byte. It **refuses to
run** if any generated page has been edited since the backfill (`updated_at >
created_at + 1s`) — that is the signal application code has started writing to
these pages, and deleting them then would destroy real edits.

`types/database.ts` updated for the three new `pages` columns (hand-authored file).
tsc 0 · 273 tests. **NOT APPLIED — the user pastes SQL; I cannot run DDL.**

### Next, once 0028 is applied
Repoint readers one at a time (database-view's row list → pages where database_id),
then writers, then retire `collection_rows` in a later migration. Rows inherit
icon/cover/archive/history/backlinks the moment they become pages.

## 2026-08-01 — 0028 APPLIED, and the regression it caused (caught + fixed)

The user applied 0028. First thing after any structural migration: find what it
broke. It broke two things, both real and both user-visible.

**Every database row is now a `pages` row** — that is the point of 0028 — but two
queries list pages WITHOUT qualifying which kind, so they silently absorbed the
backfill:

1. **`app/(app)/documents/page.tsx`** — the Docs hub selected every page in the
   space. After the backfill it would list **every row of every database as a
   loose document**. Fixed with `.is('database_id', null)`: a row belongs to its
   database and is reached through it, never through the docs hub. The pre-0028
   fallback query is deliberately left unfiltered — on that path the column does
   not exist and there is nothing to exclude.
2. **`lib/search.ts`** — global search matched titles and bodies across all pages,
   so searching "invoice" returned every row of a tracker mixed in with documents:
   the same string meaning two different things in one list. Same fix on both the
   title and the jsonb-body query.

**Checked and deliberately NOT changed** — `lib/connected.ts` (client docs, child
pages), `lib/projects-data.ts`, `lib/portal.ts`. All three scope by `client_id`,
`parent_id` or `project_id`, and the 0028 backfill sets none of those on generated
rows, so they cannot leak. Stated here so the omission reads as a decision.

tsc 0 (in app code — `.next/dev/types/validator.ts` noise is Next's own generated
file, cleared by `rm -rf .next`) · 273 tests.

**The general lesson:** a migration that widens what a table MEANS silently changes
every unqualified query against it. `select * from pages` was unambiguous before
0028 and ambiguous after. Grep every reader before declaring such a migration done.

## 2026-08-01 — §5.21 property type conversion (coercion + data-loss report)

The spec's §5.21 in full, as pure logic. The audit found `RETYPEABLE` existed but
there was no coercion and no loss warning — so retyping a column silently emptied
it, which is the most destructive thing a database can do to you *because it looks
like it worked*.

**`lib/prop-convert.ts` (new, 14 tests)** — `planConversion(prop, to, rows)` returns
new values, any options to create, kept/lost counts, and plain-English warnings.
Nothing is written: the caller shows the warnings and only applies on confirm.

Every rule from §5.21, and the judgement calls inside them:
- **Text → Select** invents one option per DISTINCT value, case-insensitively
  ("Design"/"design" share an option). At the 100-option cap it **clears** the
  overflow rather than collapsing it into a wrong option — a wrong value is worse
  than an empty one.
- **Multi-select → Select** keeps the first value, and counts as lost **only the
  rows that actually had more than one**. Warning on a count nobody lost is noise.
- **Anything → Formula/Rollup** clears everything (the type computes its own
  value) — but warns about *nothing* when the column was already empty.
- **→ Number** parses through the READABLE form, so a select whose option is named
  "42" converts to 42, and strips thousands separators.
- **→ Checkbox** only checks on explicit yes/true/1/checked/done.
- **→ Text is the universal sink** — always lossless, but a **date** gets its own
  warning: it becomes a string, so it leaves the calendar and stops sorting as a
  date. Lossless is not the same as harmless.

`valueToText` resolves an option **id → its name**, which is what makes every
"through text" conversion correct rather than writing raw ids into cells.

tsc 0 in app code · **287 tests** (was 273).

**Not yet wired** — this is the engine; the confirm modal in `database-view`'s
property editor is the next step, and it should render `plan.warnings` verbatim
with the affected row count.

## 2026-08-03 — Phase 1 unit #1: the readers are repointed — and 0028 was never applied

Two things happened here. The unit is done; the more important finding is why it
could not be verified the way it was supposed to be.

### The finding: 0028 is not on the database

`MASTER_PRODUCT_PLAN` §v2.1 states "all 28 migrations are live" and the
2026-08-01 entry above records "0028 APPLIED". A column-by-column PostgREST
probe against the running project says otherwise:

| column | live? |
|---|---|
| `pages.database_id` | **missing** |
| `pages.properties` | **missing** |
| `pages.row_order` | **missing** |
| `collection_rows.page_id` | **missing** |
| `pages.content` / `sort_index` / `archived_at` | ok |
| `collection_rows.id` / `data` / `sort_index` | ok |

Paired with a must-fail control (`select=nope` → the same `42703`), so the
probe is measuring the schema and not the connection.

**Why nobody noticed:** `types/database.ts` is hand-authored (it always has
been), and someone added the 0028 columns to it when the migration was
*written*. So `tsc` has been happily typechecking code against columns that do
not exist. A hand-written schema type cannot fail the way a generated one does —
it only ever describes intent.

**The house rule this earns:** a migration is applied when the database says so,
not when the plan does. Probe before building on one.

### The unit, shipped behind a gate

Rows now come from `pages where database_id`, with `collection_rows` as the
fallback — the same fetch-time capability pattern as `mentionsSupported` (0027)
and `goalsV2Supported` (0026). Without the columns the app behaves exactly as it
does today; with them, a row is a page. A half-migrated app is still a working
app, which is 0028's own stated strategy.

- **`lib/row-order.ts` (new, 16 tests)** — text fractional index. Ordering had to
  move regardless: `collection_rows.sort_index` is a `double` holding
  `Date.now()` (~1.75e12) and `pages.sort_index` is an `int`, so the value does
  not fit. **0028's own backfill has this bug** — `round(r.sort_index)::int`
  would raise `integer out of range` on any row created through `addDbRow`. It
  has not bitten because the migration never ran. Fix it before applying, or use
  the corrected copy noted below.
- **`DbRow` reshaped** — `sort_index: number` → `order: string`, plus a real
  `content` field. The row body used to be smuggled into `data.__content`, a key
  *inside the property bag*, which is why a row's prose was invisible to search,
  version history, the outline and backlinks. It is the page's own content now,
  and writing prose can no longer clobber an in-flight cell edit.
- **`lib/actions/collections.ts`** — the one place that knows the mapping, both
  eras, plus `legacyToRow`. Row writes are narrowed with
  `.not('database_id','is',null)` so they cannot touch a standalone document now
  that the two share a table.
- **`lib/db-store.ts`** — subscribes to *both* tables (the client has no cheap
  way to ask which era is live; a filter on a missing column simply never
  matches), and the conflict rules are stated once in `applyRemote`.
- **`lib/db-store.test.ts` (new, 10 tests)** — the store had none. Covers append
  ordering, undo/redo key distinctness, and that a body edit and a cell edit no
  longer overwrite each other.

## 2026-08-03 — Phase 1 unit #4: the @-mention write path (the fabric fills)

0027 shipped the `mentions` table and `lib/connected.ts` has read it ever since. Nothing
ever wrote a row — so every backlink section in the app has been rendering an empty list
against a table that could not fill. Probed first this time: **0027 IS applied** (unlike
0028), so this was the highest-value unblocked gap the plan named, and it needed no
migration.

**The design decision: a mention IS an internal link.** Zenboard already has one
canonical address per record (`recordHref`), so a span whose href resolves to a record is
a reference to it — whether it arrived from a picker, a pasted "Copy link" URL, or a
dragged breadcrumb. That is why this needed no new inline node type, no ProseMirror
schema change and no migration; the edges were already being typed into documents and
nobody was collecting them. Links already sitting in existing docs become real edges the
next time those docs save.

- **`parseRecordHref`** (in `lib/connected.ts`, deliberately beside `recordHref`) — the
  inverse mapping. Kept adjacent because a route changed in one and not the other stops
  producing backlinks with no error and no visible symptom.
- **`lib/mentions.ts` (22 tests)** — extract edges from a block document (anchor = block
  id, context = the line, truncated at 180) and diff against what is stored. Two rules
  worth keeping: a doc's links to itself are navigation, not references; and `context` is
  NOT part of the identity, or editing the sentence around a link would rewrite the row
  on every keystroke.
- **`lib/actions/mentions.ts`** — reconcile one source, gated on `mentionsSupported`,
  entirely best-effort. Deletes run before inserts so a link moved between blocks never
  collides with 0027's unique index. No `onConflict`: that index is an EXPRESSION index
  (`coalesce(anchor,'')`) which PostgREST cannot name, and a rejected duplicate leaves
  exactly the row we wanted.
- **Wired into the document autosave**, never awaited into it. Deleting a doc forgets
  what it POINTED AT and keeps what pointed AT it — §7H wants a deleted target to leave a
  tombstone, not a list that silently shrinks.
- `types/database.ts` gained `mentions` (it was missing entirely, which is why the insert
  typed as `never[]`).

376 tests · tsc 0 · lint 0 on every file touched.

**Owed:** the `@` typeahead in the editor. The spine works today via paste/link; the
picker mirrors the existing slash-menu machinery in `block-editor.tsx`.

## 2026-08-03 — Phase 1 unit #4 finished: the `@` typeahead (and one record search)

The write path shipped earlier today could only be fed by pasting a record URL. This is the
picker that makes it a keystroke — and it deliberately produces the *same span* a pasted link
produces, so the fabric still has exactly one kind of mention in it.

**The decision that mattered: record search became one function, not two.** The obvious build
was a second set of "find things by name" queries inside the editor. But the ⌘K palette already
had that set written out longhand, and two copies is how a new entity type ends up findable in
one place and invisible in the other. So `searchRecords` (lib/search.ts) is now the ONE record
projection and both callers use it; what stays at each call site is presentation — the palette's
group headings and drawer-over-page routing, the picker's glyph rows and link insertion.

- **`lib/editor-trigger.ts`** — `triggerAt(text, caret, char, {maxQuery})`, now the single rule
  for *both* menus. `/`'s trigger detection was an inline regex clump in `setRich`; adding `@`
  beside it would have made two, which is precisely how the two menus drift apart in what counts
  as a query. Word-anchoring is what keeps `sarah@example.com` and `and/or` out of the menus with
  no special case for either. `@` allows spaces (titles have them), capped at 32 chars so a stray
  `@` can't hold a menu open across a paragraph. Only the LAST occurrence is considered — typing
  an address inside an open query closes the menu rather than re-targeting an older `@`.
- **`lib/search.ts`** — `searchRecords` + `rankRecordHits` (exact → title prefix → word-start →
  contains → body-only, recency breaking every tie). An empty term is not an error: it means
  "most recently touched", which is what a bare `@` shows. That recent list is a SERVER answer,
  unlike the slash menu's localStorage one — block types are a fixed set of twenty, but a
  remembered *record* can be renamed or deleted, and offering a record that no longer exists is
  worse than offering nothing. `MENTIONABLE_TYPES` is exactly the set `recordHref` can address,
  with a test that fails if the two ever disagree.
- **`lib/mentions.ts`** — `insertMention` does the text surgery, beside the function that reads
  those links back out as edges. Round-trip test: what the picker writes, `mentionsInBlocks`
  reads. The trailing space isn't cosmetic — it's what makes "@Acme is late" come out as prose.
- **`components/documents/mention-menu.tsx`** — the panel + a cancel-safe, 150ms-debounced,
  30s-cached search hook. While a longer query is in flight the previous results stay up, but
  ONLY when the old query is a prefix of the new one: a row you can press Enter on must never
  belong to a search unrelated to what you typed.
- **`CaretLayer`** (block-editor) — the menu anchors to the caret, portalled and fixed, because
  an absolute popover is clipped by the first scrolling ancestor and every host of this editor
  scrolls. Flips above when it would run off the bottom, clamps horizontally, follows scroll, and
  dismisses when its caret leaves the viewport. `SurfaceHandle.caretRect` is the new seam.

**Benchmark vs Notion.** Trigger, space-tolerant query, recent-on-bare-`@`, caret anchoring:
matched. Two deliberate differences. (1) Notion inserts an atomic chip carrying the page icon;
ours is a normal linked span, so a mention survives plain-text export, paste into another app and
⌘F, and needed no ProseMirror schema change. The cost is no inline glyph — the type is named on
the picker row instead, where it actually helps you choose. (2) Notion's `@` also searches page
bodies; ours matches names only (`deep: false`), because the picker writes the record's NAME into
your sentence and matching on anything else makes the inserted text unpredictable. Body search
stays in ⌘K, where you're looking for content.

**Edge cases handled:** `@` mid-word (no menu) · `@ ` (dismisses, keeps the character) · Escape
(dismisses, keeps the character) · **Enter with no results is NOT swallowed** — a slash query
resolves once you finish a known word, but a name may simply not exist yet, and a menu that eats
your Enter until you notice is a trap · trigger moved between click and handler (refuses, rather
than cutting the wrong range) · a query change re-ranks, so the highlight can never point past the
results · arrow keys clamp rather than wrap, which is right for a ranked list.

**Verified.** 404 tests (+28), `tsc` clean, zero new lint findings. In the browser at
`/dev-preview/editor`: menu opens on `@` after whitespace, portals to `<body>`, anchors to the
`@` glyph's left edge with a 6px gap under the caret; `sarah@example.com` opens nothing; `@ ` and
Escape both dismiss and keep the character; Enter with no matches creates a block (44→45) instead
of being eaten; at a 300px viewport it flips above with the same 6px gap and stays on screen; it
follows a scroll and closes when its caret leaves. Panel geometry measured against the DS: 36px
rows, #262626 raised surface, 12/8px radii, 14/12px type, `surface-hover` active row. The live
region announces "Acme rebrand, Project. 1 of 6." New harness `/dev-preview/mention` covers the
populated panel's four states.

**Owed:** the picker's *populated* list can't be exercised in the browser — the dev-preview
harnesses have no session, so RLS returns nothing and the live editor can only reach the empty
state. Ranking, insertion and the round-trip are covered by unit tests instead.

**Also this session (docs):** §9's migration ledger renumbered. It had reserved 0016–0023 for work
that other features then took, so every "gated on 00XX" line in the roadmap pointed at the wrong
file. Now: 0029 memories · 0030 task_events · 0031 reminders · 0032 milestones+task_links ·

## 2026-08-03 — Phase 1 unit #3: the two property systems are one vocabulary

The last Phase 1 unit. Zenboard had two property systems — `doc-properties.tsx` (page
properties, 22 types) and `lib/collections.ts` (database columns, 16) — sharing no code,
no types and no editors.

**The decision that mattered: they stay two SHAPES, and become one VOCABULARY.** The
tempting merge is a single `Property` type. That would be wrong: a page has exactly one
value per property, so its definition and value live together; a database property is a
column whose values live on the rows. That difference is real and load-bearing. What was
never real was two type lists, two option models, two icon maps and three copies of "is
this type computed".

`lib/properties.ts` is now the vocabulary — deliberately pure (no icons, no React) so it
stays importable from a server component. `components/documents/property-icons.ts` holds
the glyphs as `Record<PropType, IconType>`, so adding a type without a glyph is a type
error rather than a silent fallback.

**What the compiler found the moment there was one union** — every place the two had
drifted, none of which was written down anywhere:

- **`updated_time` vs `last_edited_time`**: the same concept, spelled differently in each
  system. Canonical is Notion's `last_edited_time` (it comes with a matching
  `last_edited_by`); `updated_time` is now a normalized alias.
- **The option model**: `{ id, label, color }` on a page vs `{ id, name, color }` in a
  database. Canonical is `name`.
- **FOUR copies of the nine-colour palette.** `lib/palette.ts` is the real one;
  `collections.ts` declared an identical list as `OptionColor` plus its own copy of the
  token lookup, and `prop-convert.ts` had a third that was only eight long and in a
  different order — so options a text→select conversion INVENTED were coloured from a
  different sequence than options you added by hand, in the same column. Fixed, with a
  test.
- **Icons disagreed for four types**, so the same property wore a different face
  depending on where you met it: text (`TextAlignLeft` vs `TextT`), multi-select (`List`
  vs `Tag`), status (`CircleDashed` vs `CircleHalf`), email (`At` vs `Envelope`). Each
  resolved on the merits and the reason recorded at the map.
- **The page registry gave `created_time` and `last_edited_time` the SAME clock**, so its
  own Advanced list showed two indistinguishable rows. Created is now
  `ClockCounterClockwise`, last-edited a plain `Clock`.
- **`prop-convert`'s COMPUTED list was missing every page-only computed type**
  (`created_by`, `last_edited_by`, `id`), so converting to one wasn't treated as
  discarding data.

**Persisted-data migration.** Property types and options are stored as JSON
(`pages.content`, `collections.props`), so retiring a spelling cannot be done by editing a
union — anything already saved keeps the old string. `normalizePropType` /
`normalizeOption` / `normalizeProps` run at every read boundary (`readMeta` in
documents-view, `normalizeCollection` in actions/collections), and the next save writes the
canonical form back, so each page and collection migrates itself once. Same shape as
`liftText` in lib/blocks.ts.

**Also.** `surfaces` on each registry entry records which surface has an editor for that
type — page 22, database 12. That difference used to be invisible drift across two files;
it is now one column, with a test that pins both counts so a change has to be acknowledged.
Dead code removed: `Cell`'s unused `isTitle` prop, ~30 now-unused icon imports.

**Verified.** 425 tests (+21), `tsc` clean, zero new lint findings (documents-view's five
are pre-existing: a `Date.now()` in `newPage`, an unused `BlockType`, three old effects).
In the browser: the database picker lists 12 types from the registry and now says "Last
edited time", not "Updated time"; the page picker lists all 22. The proof the merge
actually landed — for text, multi-select, status, email and date, the SVG path data
rendered on the two surfaces is now byte-identical, and created-time and last-edited-time
no longer render the same glyph. The documents harness gained a deliberately
legacy-shaped page (an option stored as `{ label }`, a property typed `updated_time`):
both render correctly, the option chip reads "Shipped" and the row's type reads "Last
edited time".

**Written down, not started:** `lib/db-engine.ts` contains three LITERAL NUL bytes used as
a filter separator. They work, but they make `file` report the source as binary and
`grep` silently return nothing for that file — which cost a detour when searching for
`RETYPEABLE` found nothing despite it being defined on line 130. One-character fix
(`'\0'`), own task.

## 2026-08-03 — Phase 3: the timebox twin (migration 0030, gated)

The plan's own cancelled-subscription test names this as what stands between Zenboard and
cancelling Sunsama/Akiflow. §7D states the contract exactly: *"a timeboxed task is one
object with two projections — completing either side completes both; moving the event moves
the task's scheduled time; deleting the event un-timeboxes (never deletes) the task."*

**The decision that mattered: the event has no `done` column.** The obvious build is a
completion flag on `calendar_events` kept in step with the task's. That is two mirrors of
one fact, and two mirrors eventually disagree — a failed write, a stale cache, a
concurrent edit. Instead the twin block renders the **task's** `done` and its checkbox
calls the same `toggleTask` a list row calls. "Completing either side completes both" is
then not a sync rule that could drift; there is only ever one flag with two views. The
migration is smaller for it, and there is no reconciliation code to get wrong.

- **`0030_task_events.sql`** — `tasks.event_id` ⇄ `calendar_events.task_id`, both
  `ON DELETE SET NULL`, which is §7D's "never deletes the task" encoded in the schema
  rather than trusted to the application. Two partial unique indexes make the 1:1 real
  where it cannot be forgotten. Two columns, not a join table: the relationship is 1:1 and
  both sides are read on their own hot path, so a join table would add a query to both.
- **`lib/timebox.ts`** — the rules, pure. `timeboxMinutes` clamps (a 6000-minute estimate
  is a project someone hasn't broken up, not a block that should paint over a week);
  default 30 min, deliberately not an hour, because an hour-shaped default makes five
  small tasks look like a full day and then the capacity line lies. `timeboxDay` is the
  seam where an absolute instant becomes a calendar `scheduled_date` — it goes through
  `isoDateIn`, never `toISOString().slice(0,10)`, which would have scheduled an evening
  block in Kolkata for the day before.
- **Twins never reach Google.** A timebox is a private planning artefact; pushing "Write
  the brief · 30m" to a shared work calendar broadcasts your to-do list to your colleagues.
  `syncsToGoogle()` is the one place that decides, so create/update/delete cannot disagree.
- **`lib/actions/timebox.ts`** — `timeboxTask` is idempotent (an already-timeboxed task
  gets its block *moved*, not a second one created) and orders its writes so the only
  reachable failure state is a plain calendar event, never a task pointing at a row that
  was never created; it rolls back rather than leaving one. `untimeboxTask` deliberately
  keeps `scheduled_date` — the block said "2pm Thursday", and removing it should retract
  the time, not the day.
- **`lib/actions/events.ts`** — moving a twin now writes the task's `scheduled_date`;
  deleting one clears the link *before* the delete, so a concurrent read never sees a task
  pointing at a row on its way out.
- **The calendar** renders twins with the task's checkbox and strikes them through when
  done. The loader's hardcoded two-step column fallback was replaced with a loop over the
  optional columns (`color` 0012, `task_id` 0030) — it could not have survived a second
  optional column. The task's `done` comes from a follow-up query rather than a PostgREST
  embed: since 0030 the two tables reference each other from *both* sides, so an embed
  would be ambiguous and need the constraint name, exactly the kind of string that rots.
- **The task drawer** gains a Timebox chip beside Estimate, reusing the existing
  chip/`Pop` idiom. Slots run 07:00–21:00 in half hours — the window a working day falls
  in; a full 24h list is 96 rows of mostly-3am, and the chip exists to be faster than
  opening the calendar. The day is the task's own `scheduled_date` when it has one, so
  picking a time never silently moves a task to a different day.

**Gated.** `taskEventsSupported()` probes the *column*, not the table — both tables already
exist, so a table probe would report the feature available on an unmigrated database.
Without 0030 the chip is absent, the calendar renders every event as an ordinary event, and
every action returns a clean "needs migration 0030". Exactly as before this sprint.

**This was two sprints, and I finished the first.** §7D's flow is "drag a task from the
rail onto a slot" — but the calendar has no task rail, and building one (an unscheduled/
Today list docked beside the grid, with drag-to-slot and a keyboard equivalent) is a
sprint's worth of surface on its own. What shipped is the twin itself plus one creation
path; the drag rail is next and is written up as its own unit.

**Edge cases handled:** already-timeboxed (moves, never duplicates) · junk estimate
(clamped) · midnight crossing · unparseable instant (refused, no Invalid Date) · timezone
day boundary (the test pins Kolkata and New York, both directions) · a stray `task_done` on
a non-twin cannot strike an ordinary event through · checkbox click does not open the event
composer.

**Verified.** 438 tests (+13), `tsc` clean, zero new lint findings. In the browser at
`/dev-preview/calendar` with staged twins in both states: ARIA reads "Mark “Write the
client brief” done" / "Mark “Send the invoice” not done" with matching `aria-checked`; the
done block renders `line-through` at 0.6 opacity and the open one does not; clicking the
checkbox flips both the state and the label, strikes the block through, and — the detail
that would otherwise be infuriating — does **not** open the event composer.

**Owed:** one line from you — paste `supabase/migrations/0030_task_events.sql`. Until then
the feature is dormant and the app behaves exactly as it did before.

## Reminders — §7B's one `remind_at`, delivered (2026-08-03, gated on 0031)

**First: 0028 and 0030 are applied.** Probed column-by-column before starting, each probe
paired with a must-fail control: `pages.database_id`, `pages.row_order`, `tasks.event_id`
and `calendar_events.task_id` all answer. That closes Phase 1 and lights up the timebox
twin. `tasks.remind_at` was the next thing absent, so it was the next sprint.

### What shipped

A task can carry **one** reminder, and Zenboard tells you when it arrives.

- **`supabase/migrations/0031_reminders.sql`** — `tasks.remind_at` (when to speak) +
  `tasks.reminded_at` (when we did), and a partial index over exactly the scheduler's
  query. One reminder is a column; a second would be a table, and §7B froze the anatomy
  at one on purpose.
- **`lib/reminders.ts`** — THE reminder vocabulary. The offered times, the chip's label,
  the status, and the delivery loop's arithmetic. Pure, so the picker, the scheduler and
  the server action all read one set of rules.
- **`lib/actions/reminders.ts`** — `setReminder` / `claimReminder`, gated behind
  `remindersSupported()`.
- **`components/reminders/reminder-chip.tsx`** — the Remind chip and its panel.
- **`components/reminders/reminder-scheduler.tsx`** — mounted once in the shell, renders
  nothing, and is the only thing that decides a reminder has arrived.

### The decision that mattered: delivery is a CLAIM

The app can be open in three tabs on two machines, each running its own scheduler, each
seeing the same reminder come due in the same second. The arbiter is one conditional
UPDATE:

```sql
update tasks set reminded_at = now() where id = $1 and reminded_at is null
```

Postgres runs that under a row lock, so exactly one caller gets a row back and everyone
else gets nothing and stays quiet. No lock table, no leader election, no dedupe window
that could be wrong. The notification row is written only by the winner, which is what
makes "one reminder → one entry in the bell" true rather than hopeful.

It is also why the predicate is `reminded_at is null` and **not**
`reminded_at < remind_at` — a two-column comparison PostgREST cannot express. It does not
need to: `setReminder` always clears `reminded_at` in the same write, so "delivered" is
always about the reminder currently set. Moving a reminder makes it pending again, which
is also what a person expects.

The same claim is what a push/email worker will run. It can deliver through another
channel later **without a schema change**, and the two cannot double-send.

### Benchmark (rule 7)

Linear's "Remind me" is elapsed time only — In 30 minutes / In 1 hour / In 3 hours /
Tomorrow / Next week / Custom — because a Linear issue has no hour of its own. Notion
attaches reminders to a date property, so its menu is relative offsets and needs a date
to exist first. Todoist allows several reminders per task and therefore needs a modal.

Ours matches Linear's speed and keyboard grammar, and **exceeds** it on the one thing
Linear cannot do: when the task already has an hour — a timebox block (0030) or a
scheduled day — those anchors come first under a "This task" heading. "Ten minutes before
the thing" is the reminder people actually want, and every one of the three makes you
compute it yourself.

We **deliberately differ** on count: one reminder, never a list (§7B). That is why this
is a chip and not a section.

Custom times are a natural-language field — "friday 9am", "in 2 hours" — parsed with the
same Chrono the DS date-picker already bets on, with `forwardDate` so "8am" typed at 9am
means tomorrow. Two nested Radix popovers inside a 252px panel would have been worse in
every way.

### Delivery, and what it deliberately is not

In-app: while Zenboard is open anywhere, a reminder toasts (with **Open**) and lands in
the bell. **Not** a push/email worker — that needs a cron runner and VAPID/Resend
credentials and is its own sprint; the seam is cut for it.

- **One timer, not a poll.** It sleeps until the next reminder, capped at a 5-minute
  heartbeat, and re-plans on four signals: tab visible (a closed laptop's timers do not
  fire), a `tasks` row changing anywhere, this tab setting a reminder, and the network
  returning. A once-a-second poll would be a query per second per tab forever for an
  event that happens a few times a day.
- **Stale reminders do not interrupt.** Come back after a weekend and every undelivered
  reminder is still claimed and still written to the bell — nothing is dropped — but only
  ones from the last hour raise a toast. §7O's whole argument is that notifications are
  how calm products become anxious ones.
- One chime per batch, gated on the app's existing sound switch. Three reminders arriving
  together should not play three chimes over each other, and a reminder is not a reason to
  invent a second preference.

### One realtime seam, not a second subscription

`RealtimeSync` now dispatches `zb:realtime` with `{ table }` alongside its
`router.refresh()`. Its own reaction re-runs server components, which is no use to a
client-side loop holding its own state — the alternative was a second subscription to
`tasks`. One socket, one subscription, many listeners.

### Defects found and fixed inside the sprint's area

- **`Pop` panels overflowed the viewport.** Measured at 375px: a chip at x=221 pushed its
  panel's right edge to 473 and made the whole **document** scroll sideways. Every chip in
  the task drawer had this. `place()` now pulls the panel back inside the window and
  clamps it against both edges, re-running on resize. Re-measured: 115→367 inside 375, no
  horizontal page scroll.
- **`Pop` had no keyboard grammar at all** — no focus in, no focus back, no Escape, no
  arrows, no `aria-expanded`. Extracted to `components/task-detail/chip-ui.tsx` (so the
  new chip reuses the six existing ones rather than forking a seventh look) and given the
  whole grammar. Focus *returning* is the part that mattered: without it, dismissing a
  panel drops focus on `<body>` and the next Tab restarts from the top of the drawer.
- **`touch-row`**, a new DS utility: 32px menu rows are right for a mouse and unusable for
  a thumb, so a coarse pointer gets WCAG's 44px. Verified the rule compiled *and* that it
  sits inside `@media (pointer: coarse)` — the z-index registry once compiled to nothing.
- **FOUR hand-rolled copies of "format a clock time", all hardcoded to `en-US`.**
  `fmtTime`, `fmtMinTime`, a private `fmtNow` in `week-grid.tsx`, and the hour rail's own
  label. `formatClock` / `formatHour` are the vocabulary's entries now and all four
  delegate. On an `en-GB` browser the calendar showed a 24-hour grid with a 12-hour "now"
  chip; it is one format everywhere, in the user's own locale.

  **The verification was wrong before it was right.** The first sweep looked for
  `/\d{1,2}:\d{2}\s?(AM|PM)/` and reported zero — but the hour rail renders "1 AM" with
  no minutes, so the regex could not see the copy that was still there. Re-swept with
  `/\d{1,2}(:\d{2})?\s?(AM|PM)/i`, found it, fixed it, re-swept: zero. **A negative
  result from a pattern is only as good as the pattern** — when sweeping for "no instances
  of X", first prove the sweep can *find* one.
- **`formatRelativeDay` measured against the real clock** while taking a `now` it ignored.
  `DateOpts.now` added — a formatter whose output depends on an unstated global cannot be
  asserted about, and "Tomorrow" is exactly the kind of answer that needs asserting.

### Verified

459 tests (+21 in `lib/reminders.test.ts`), `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every file
touched. Browser: `/dev-preview/reminder` — all four chip states; the panel's grouping
("This task" appears only with an anchor); presets dropping out as the day wears on
("Later today" gone after 18:00); the natural-language field's three outcomes (parsed /
unreadable / already passed); Escape closing and returning focus with `aria-expanded`
flipping; ↓↑ moving between rows; a pick round-tripping to the chip; and the 375px
overflow before and after the fix.

**Not verified in the browser:** delivery itself — the claim, the toast, the bell entry.
It needs real rows, a real clock and a session the harness has no way to mint. The logic
under it is unit-tested and the claim is one conditional UPDATE.

### Deliberately out of scope, with the reason

**A reminder indicator on task list rows.** It would put the gated `remind_at` column into
six hot-path list queries for a glyph that Things, Todoist and Linear all decline to show
(Todoist shows a clock only for reminders due today; Linear shows nothing on the row). The
reminder is visible where it is set, where it fires, and in the bell.

**Owed:** one line from you — paste `supabase/migrations/0031_reminders.sql`. Until then
`remindersSupported()` reports false, the chip is hidden, the scheduler never runs a
query, and the app behaves exactly as it did before.

## The drag-to-calendar rail — §7D's missing gesture (2026-08-03, no migration)

The timebox twin shipped in the previous sprint but could only be created from the task
drawer's Timebox chip. Planning a day one drawer at a time is not planning a day. §7D
names the gesture exactly: *"Drag task from the rail (Today list docked right) onto a slot
→ twin created with estimate as duration."* This is that.

**No migration.** 0030 is applied and the twin already works; this is entirely ergonomics.

### What shipped

- **`components/calendar/task-rail.tsx`** — open, top-level, un-timeboxed tasks docked
  right of the grid, in the two buckets the app already thinks in: the day's **Scheduled**
  work and the **Inbox**.
- **`WeekGrid` accepts an external drag** (`taskDrag` / `onTaskDrop` / `onTaskDragEnd`).
- **`TIMEBOX_SLOTS` moved to `lib/timebox.ts`** — two surfaces offer the same half-hours
  now, and a menu that disagreed with itself about which half-hours exist would be its own
  small madness.

### The decisions that mattered

**The grid owns the drop, not the rail.** The rail starts the gesture; the grid finishes
it. Only the grid knows which column a pointer is over and what minute a Y coordinate is.
The alternative — exporting column rects to the rail — is the same coupling pointing the
wrong way.

**Two ways in, always.** Dragging is a pointer gesture: it does not exist for a keyboard
and barely exists for a thumb. Every row also carries a slot menu that does exactly the
same thing. That menu is the keyboard path **and** the mobile "schedule at…" affordance
§7C asks for — not a lesser fallback.

**The ghost is the real block.** An incoming task paints the same ghost an internal drag
does, at its own length and under its own name. A highlighted row that then becomes
something else is a small lie about what you are about to get.

### Benchmark (rule 7)

Akiflow and Sunsama both sell almost entirely on this gesture — list beside calendar,
drag, done — and both use the task's estimate as the block length, which we match
(`timeboxMinutes`, 30 minutes when there is no estimate). Where we **deliberately differ**:
neither offers a keyboard equivalent, so planning a day in either is mouse-only. Ours is
five keystrokes per task and focus stays in the rail. Google Calendar's task drag has no
duration concept at all.

### Edge cases handled

- **A quick flick used to do nothing.** The drag-threshold listener was on the row, so a
  pointer that left the row's box between two move events was never seen to travel. It is
  on the *window* now. Pointer capture would also fix it, but capture redirects the
  following `click`, which would break opening a task by clicking its title.
- **Escape cancels** a drag in flight; releasing over nothing cancels rather than dropping
  at a nearest guess.
- **The grid does not start its own create-drag** while a task drag is running.
- **The slot menu's day was wrong.** It took `days[0]`, which in a week view is Sunday —
  so on a Monday the menu offered to schedule into *yesterday*. The rule is now: today
  when today is on screen, otherwise the first day on screen, and the menu header prints
  it either way so it is never a guess.
- **Focus was lost after scheduling** — the row the menu returns focus to no longer
  exists, so focus fell to `<body>` and the next Tab restarted from the top of the page.
  Planning a day is scheduling several tasks in a row, so that is the *second* thing that
  happens, not a rare edge. Focus now moves to whatever occupies that position.
- **Month view has no rail** — a month cell is a day, not a time, so there is no slot to
  drop onto and the gesture would have to mean something else. That is how one consistent
  interaction becomes two.
- **Below `xl` the rail is hidden** (drag is desktop-first, §7C); the drawer's Timebox
  chip remains the small-screen path.
- **Without 0030** there are no twins at all, so the `event_id` filter is dropped and the
  rail still works — it just cannot hide blocks that cannot exist.

### Also fixed: a FOURTH `en-US` clock formatter, and a wrong verification

The previous sprint's entry claimed the calendar was one clock format. It was not — the
hour rail rendered "1 AM" with **no minutes**, so the regex that swept for
`/\d{1,2}:\d{2}\s?(AM|PM)/` could not see it. Added `formatHour` to the date vocabulary,
repointed the rail through `fmtHourLabel`, re-swept with a pattern that can match both
shapes: zero. **A negative result from a pattern is only as good as the pattern** — when
sweeping for "no instances of X", first prove the sweep can find one. That entry has been
corrected in place rather than left standing.

### Verified

459 tests, `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every file touched. Browser, on
`/dev-preview/calendar` (seeded with `demoTasks`): a real drag from the rail onto Wednesday
produced a twin block at 18:15–19:45 — 90 minutes, the task's own estimate — 118px tall
(1.5h × 80px/h − 2) and carrying a working twin checkbox; the keyboard path (open menu,
↓×5, Enter) put a 30-minute default block at 8:00 and a 45-minute one at 9:00; focus
landed on the *next* task's schedule button; Escape cleared a live drag and left the task
in the rail; the rail is absent in Month view and `display: none` at 1100px with no
horizontal page scroll.

**Not verified in the browser:** the real `timeboxTask` write — the harness is auth-free,
so the demo path builds the twin locally. That action shipped and was verified in the 0030
sprint; what is new here is the gesture that calls it.


## 2026-08-03 — 0028 and 0030 applied; verified by probe, not by claim

The user applied both. Confirmed against the live database rather than taken on trust —
this document and the master plan have each previously asserted a migration was live while
the database disagreed, which is why `SPRINT_STATUS.md` exists at all.

- **Schema.** All four 0028 markers (`pages.database_id` · `properties` · `row_order` ·
  `collection_rows.page_id`) and both 0030 markers (`tasks.event_id` ·
  `calendar_events.task_id`) return HTTP 200. The must-fail control
  (`pages.zz_must_fail`) returns 42703, so a 200 means the column exists and not that the
  probe is broken.
- **0028's backfill is intact**, which mattered because its `round(sort_index)::int`
  overflow would have failed mid-run: 39/39 legacy rows carry a `page_id` (no partial run,
  no orphans), zero migrated rows have a null `row_order`, bodies moved out of
  `data.__content` into `pages.content`, and `properties` carried.
- **Manual row order survived exactly.** In every database, ascending `sort_index` maps
  onto ascending `row_order`. The keys are per-collection and gap-spaced (0x3e8, 0x7d0,
  0xbb8 …), which is why a global sort makes 17 rows look like they share one key — they
  are each their collection's *first* row.
- One cosmetic difference: the backfill wrote `NULL` where legacy rows held `''` for a
  title. `toRow` already normalizes with `p.title ?? ''`, so nothing downstream sees it.

**Phase 1 is complete.** 0028 was the oldest open structural item in the product.

**Operational gotcha worth knowing:** `rowsArePagesSupported()` is memoized for the life of
the server process ("a migration cannot appear mid-request"). A dev server started before
the migration therefore keeps serving the legacy `collection_rows` path until it is
restarted. Correct behaviour, surprising once.

**0031 (reminders) is written but NOT applied** — `tasks.remind_at` and `tasks.reminded_at`
both probe as 42703.

## 2026-08-03 — Attachments: the file spine (migration 0033, gated)

Phase 4's largest remaining gap. Zenboard could **link** a file (paste a URL into a
file/pdf block) but never **hold** one, and the only bytes it stored were images base64'd
into `pages.content` as data-URLs.

**Measured before building, not assumed:** the live database has **zero** data-URLs and
33 KB of content total, so the data-URL approach is not currently hurting anything. It
still does not scale — that column is re-read on every page open, re-written on every
autosave, and snapshotted into `page_versions` on every save — but the honest statement is
that this sprint adds a capability rather than fixing a live problem. Image blocks are
therefore **deliberately left on data-URLs**; moving them is its own sprint.

**The decision that mattered: the owner is a real foreign key, not a polymorphic pair.**
`mentions` (0027) is polymorphic with no FK, and that is right there — an edge to a deleted
record should leave a tombstone. A file is the opposite. An attachment whose parent is gone
is not a tombstone, it is bytes you keep paying for and can no longer find. Three nullable
FKs (`page_id` / `task_id` / `project_id`) with a CHECK that exactly one is set gives
cascade cleanup for free, an indexed lookup for the only query anyone runs, and a database
that can still answer "what is orphaned". A fourth owner type costs one column and one line.

**The app never stores a URL — only a `path`.** A private object's URL is a short-lived
signature, so a stored one is already expired by the time anybody reads it. Every read
mints a fresh signature through an action that has proven ownership first. Same spine as
the form-upload path (0022), which is why `safeFilename` was **extracted from
`lib/actions/forms.ts`** rather than copied — two copies of "what characters may reach
storage" is the kind of duplication that ends with one of them being wrong.

- `0033_attachments.sql` — table + owner-only RLS + a private `attachments` bucket with
  **no `storage.objects` policies**, identical reasoning to 0022: every path in and out
  runs through the service role inside an action that already proved ownership, and an RLS
  policy there would only add a second, weaker door to the same bytes.
- `lib/attachments.ts` — pure rules. `safeFilename` strips any directory part, so a crafted
  `../../secrets.pdf` cannot walk out of the per-user prefix the whole ownership model
  rests on. `attachmentKind` reads MIME first and extension second (real uploads arrive as
  `application/octet-stream`).
- **A unit mismatch caught by its own test:** the cap was 25 MiB while `formatBytes` is
  decimal, so an oversized file was refused with "the limit is 26 MB" — a number appearing
  nowhere else. Constant and bucket are both 25,000,000 now.
- `lib/actions/attachments.ts` — ticket → PUT direct to storage → record. The bytes never
  pass through the server, so the server-action body limit never applies and a 25 MB file
  costs us no memory. `recordAttachment` re-derives the prefix from the caller's own id
  rather than trusting the path, or one user could register another's object.
- `deleteAttachment` removes the row **first**: if the storage delete then fails the user
  sees the file gone rather than a row pointing at bytes we failed to remove.
- `lib/use-attachment.ts` — the browser half. `useAttachmentUrl` keys its state by the id
  it belongs to, so pointing a component at a new attachment never flashes the previous
  one's URL.
- The block editor's **file and pdf** blocks gain Upload beside the paste-a-link field —
  beside, not instead: linking a file you host elsewhere is still legitimate. Only those
  two types offer it; video/audio/embed/bookmark are about linking something already on the
  web. A page still unsaved (`tmp-…`) passes no owner, so the affordance is correctly
  absent rather than failing an FK.

**Verified.** 477 tests (+22), `tsc` clean, zero new lint findings (documents-view's five
are pre-existing). In the browser at `/dev-preview/documents` with staged empty file and
pdf blocks: both render "Upload" beside their link field, each with its own hidden file
input, and the paste-a-link path is untouched.

**Owed:** paste `supabase/migrations/0033_attachments.sql`. Until then
`attachmentsSupported()` is false, the Upload button's actions return "needs migration
0033", and file blocks behave exactly as they did. **Next:** attachments on tasks and
projects (the table already supports both), then moving image blocks off data-URLs.

## 2026-08-03 — 0033 applied; attachments reach projects

**Migration verified, not assumed.** `attachments.id/page_id/task_id/project_id/path` all
probe present, control `zz_must_fail` returns 42703, and the bucket reports
`public=false, file_size_limit=25000000` — the decimal figure, matching
`ATTACHMENT_MAX_BYTES` and the refusal copy.

**The integrity claim was tested rather than asserted.** Three inserts through the service
role: no owner → `23514`, two owners → `23514`, exactly one → `201`. The probe row was
removed afterwards. "Exactly one owner, enforced where it cannot be forgotten" is now a
checked fact.

**`<AttachmentsPanel>` — the one attachments surface.** Owner-agnostic: it takes an
`AttachmentOwner` and nothing else, so a project's Files tab, a task drawer and a document
render the same list with the same affordances. §7H says "files everywhere"; the way that
stays true is one component rather than three that drift.

- Uploads run **sequentially**, not in parallel: each holds a one-shot ticket, and ten at
  once would race for the same connection budget behind a spinner that means nothing. One
  at a time, each row appearing as it lands.
- A signed URL is fetched **at the moment of the click** and used immediately — never
  stored, never placed in an `href` that sits in the DOM going stale.
- Delete is the one action here that earns a dialog (INTERACTION_STANDARDS §2.2 triages by
  reversibility — bytes do not come back), and is optimistic with a restore on failure.
- The `owner` prop is an object literal at every call site, so the loader depends on its
  **value**, not its identity, or it would refetch on every parent render.

**Projects gets a Files tab**, sixth in the underline row. Named "Files" rather than
"Attachments" — one plain word per concept — and placed beside Docs because that is the
pair people think of together: Docs is what you wrote, Files is what you were sent.

**Verified.** 477 tests, `tsc` clean, **zero lint findings in the new panel** (the
projects-workspace findings are all pre-existing). In the browser at
`/dev-preview/projects`: the tab row reads Overview · Tasks · Docs · Files · Money ·
Portal, and Files renders its empty line, Add file button and hidden input.

**Owed:** the task-drawer surface (the table already supports `task_id`; the drawer is
being edited by a concurrent session, so it is deliberately not touched here), and moving
image blocks off data-URLs.
