## 2026-08-05 — `requireUser()` / `requireSession()`: a layout is not a gate

**Also found in the dev log**, one line below the hydration error:

```
⨯ TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'id')
    at TodayPage (app/(app)/today/page.tsx:16:71)   .eq('id', user!.id)
```

**The false premise, again in a comment.** Every page under `(app)` opened with *"Auth is
enforced by the (app) layout"* and then wrote `user!.id`. The layout does call
`redirect('/login')` — but **a layout cannot gate a page**: in the App Router a layout and
its page render *concurrently*, so the page body runs before the redirect can stop it.
Signed out, `user` is null and the `!` becomes an unhandled server error. **Seventeen call
sites** across ten pages and three loaders made that assumption.

A non-null assertion is a claim the type system is told not to check. This one was false.
`requireUser()` makes it true instead — it returns `User`, never null, because the only
other way out is the redirect.

**Then the same duplication story as the last two sprints.** Server actions already had a
`requireUser()` — **twenty-two private copies of it**, twenty-one byte-identical. They
`throw` rather than redirect, which is *correct* for an action (a Server Action answers the
caller; redirecting a POST is not the same as failing it). So the new page-side helper would
have been a third meaning for a name that already meant two things — worse than the bug it
fixed. Both shapes now live in `lib/auth.ts` and are named apart:

- `requireUser()` → `User`, redirects to `/login`. Pages and loaders.
- `requireSession()` → `{ supabase, user }`, throws. Server actions.

`forms.ts` keeps a three-line local wrapper because it alone wants the client under its own
`DB` alias — the cast stays at the one call site that needs it, not in the shared helper.

**The round trips come free.** `currentUser()` is `cache()`d and **zero-argument**, which is
the only shape `cache()` memoises usefully — the same reason `spaceList()` exists in that
form and `activeSpaceId(supabase, id)` could not be wrapped. The layout, the page and the
page's loader each used to issue their own `getUser()` (~220ms apiece); they now share one.
`currentProfile()` was routed through it too.

**Verified.** 708 tests, `tsc` clean, `next build` passes, **0 lint errors** in every touched
file (10 files had a now-unused `createClient` import; all removed). On a freshly restarted
server, all **17** `(app)` routes answer `307 → /login` with **no session and zero server
errors** — `/today` previously threw. Dev-preview routes still render 200.

**One test-only change, called out because it touches a guard:** `lib/auth.ts` carries
`import 'server-only'`, and a client store legitimately imports a `'use server'` action that
now reaches it. Next replaces that module with an RPC stub on the client so it never ships —
`next build` proves it — but vitest runs plain Node and followed the import literally.
`server-only` is aliased to a stub in `vitest.config.ts` only; the production guard is
untouched.

# 2026-08-05 — The capacity line (§7C, P0 Phase 3): one rule for "does the day fit?"

**No migration.** `preferences.dayStart` / `dayEnd`, both jsonb.

## What the sprint turned out to be

§7C's P0 line is "Shutdown→tomorrow picker + capacity line". The picker shipped long ago;
the capacity line existed only as a promise in two comments (`lib/actions/profile.ts:25`
and `lib/timebox.ts:23`, both saying the capacity line "reads this later").

The audit found something worse than a missing feature — **three capacity rules already
shipped, and they disagreed**:

| where | a day is | on overload |
|---|---|---|
| `today-view.tsx:100` | `DAY_BUDGET = 8 * 60` | warning prose |
| `week-view.tsx:44` | `DAY_CAP = 360` (6h) | the bar turns **red** |
| `ritual-flow.tsx` | *nothing* | "4h 30m committed" — against what? |

So the same Tuesday read "a manageable day" on Home and drew red on the Week board two
clicks away. And **onboarding asks, in as many words, "When does your day end?"**, storing
the answer in `preferences.dayEnd` — which **nothing read**, and which could never be
changed again after the onboarding flow.

The app collected the one number that settles the argument and then hardcoded two different
guesses instead. The sprint is that number, applied once.

## `lib/capacity.ts` — THE rule

Pure, timezone-free, exhaustively tested (33 tests). Everything is
**minutes-from-local-midnight**: work hours are stored as wall-clock strings, and all three
consumers are `'use client'` — server-rendered first, where `getHours()` answers UTC. Callers
convert once at the edge with the new `minutesOfDayIn(iso, tz)`.

Four decisions worth keeping:

- **Meetings are MERGED, not summed.** Two meetings at 10:00–11:00 cost one hour between
  them. You can only be in one. Summing reports two hours of load for one hour of
  double-booking — wrong exactly when a person most needs the number to be right. (Google
  Calendar's time insights merges; this is where the rule comes from.)
- **Meetings are CLIPPED to the working day.** A 07:00–10:00 appointment costs one hour of a
  9–5 day, not three. Charging someone for hours they said they don't work is how "your day
  is impossible" gets shown to someone whose day is fine.
- **Timebox twins are excluded.** A twin (0030) *is* the task's estimate placed on the
  clock. Home has been counting both since twins shipped, charging a timeboxed day twice.
- **Unestimated tasks are COUNTED, never invented.** Motion's mistake is guessing a duration
  and then judging your day against its own guess. An unestimated task is a fact about the
  plan ("you have not decided how long this takes"), and it is reported as one.

**Measured against the WHOLE working day, not the part left.** A line that shrinks all
afternoon is a countdown clock; by 16:00 it reports every ordinary day as a catastrophe. A
plan is a claim about the whole day. "How much time is left right now" is a different
question and belongs to Focus. Nothing in `capacity()`'s input can express "now" — the
guarantee is expressed as a type, and asserted.

### `deferSuggestion` — and the tier boundary

§7C: an overloaded day "suggests moving lowest-priority — **never auto-moves**". The rule is
one sentence: *the lowest priority tier that has anything movable, longest first, until the
overage is covered — and it never crosses into a higher tier.*

That last clause came out of a failing test I had written to describe good advice. A plain
greedy ("keep taking until it fits") reached past three low-priority tasks to offer a
five-hour **high-priority** one because the arithmetic was twenty minutes short. Stopping at
the tier boundary can leave the day still over, and that is the honest outcome: the
suggestion is a place to start, not a solved equation. **The highlight is never offered** —
it is by definition the one thing that makes today a win, and suggesting it would be the tool
arguing with the answer it asked for two steps earlier.

## The morning-plan step

A real step ("Does it fit?"), placed **after** the highlight and before the rhythm. That
order is the design: you decide what matters first, and only then find out whether the rest
fits — so the thing under pressure is the filler, never the win condition.

Each task carries a Tomorrow / Keep toggle; suggested ones are *labelled*, never pre-ticked.
Nothing is written until "Start the day" — the same `rescheduleTask` mechanism as shutdown's
carry-forward, pointed the other way, so Back is a real undo for the whole step. The defaults
are deliberately opposite: at night everything unfinished follows you unless you say
otherwise; in the morning nothing leaves your plan unless you say so.

The flow's step list is now **computed** rather than `total = hasHabits ? 4 : 3` plus a
matching `readyIdx` — two places to update and one to forget, and this sprint added a step
whose presence is conditional too.

Copy defect caught in the browser: the step said **"It fits."** with nothing estimated. That
is a claim the data cannot support — a day of five unmeasured tasks was being declared
comfortable. The empty case now asks ("How long will these take?") instead of answering.

## Home and Week repointed

Both read `lib/capacity.ts`. Home's number moved from **8h 45m → "runs past a typical day"**
to **7h 30m in an 8h day → full, but it fits** — and that one number is both new rules
visible at once: the twin's 15m dropped, and a 16:00–18:00 review clipped to 1h at the 17:00
day end. Week's per-day bars now use the user's real day and turned **amber, not red**: an
overloaded day is a planning signal (§7O), not an error, and a full Wednesday is not wrong.

Week deliberately does **not** count meetings — the board only loads tasks, and fetching
seven days of events to colour seven 4px bars is not a trade worth making. Its bar reads
"committed to tasks", which is what a task board is about; the full load lives on Home, where
the events are already loaded.

## Found in the sprint's area, so fixed in it

**SEVEN copies of "format a minutes duration"** — `tasks/task-row` (exported, 3 importers),
`calendar/task-rail`, `week/week-view`, `task-detail/task-detail-drawer`, `money/money-view`
(also exported), `rituals/ritual-flow`, and `forms/responses-view`. They disagreed: three
rendered a negative estimate as **"-30m"**, and the drawer's returned null. A duration in
minutes is a number a person *reads*, so it belongs to `lib/date.ts` exactly as a date does;
it simply had no entry there, which is why everyone wrote their own. `formatMinutes` is now
that entry, and `date-vocabulary.test.ts` fails on any component doing hour arithmetic. The
seventh copy was found *by the new test*, not by the grep that preceded it.

`toISOString().slice(0, 10)` in the rituals harness — **third** time in a dev-preview fixture.

## Design system

`SegmentedProgress` gained an optional `total` and two uncoloured weights. Without `total` it
is a *breakdown* (parts of a whole, always filling the track); with it, a *load against a
limit* whose segments may exceed the limit — the track scales to whichever is larger, a
marker is drawn at the capacity, and the overrun is washed in warning. That distinction is
why the prop exists rather than the caller passing a "free space" segment: normalising by the
sum rescales an over-capacity plan to exactly full, so the one state the bar exists to show
would be the one state it could not draw. `ink`/`neutral` keep the bar out of the
one-filled-accent budget a `berry` fill would spend.

## Verified

754 tests (+31 this sprint), `tsc` clean, lint **97 → 96** with no file worse.

Browser, all against the running app:

| case | result |
|---|---|
| fits (90 + 15 tasks, 1h meeting, 9–5) | "2h 45m planned in an 8h day — 5h 15m still free" |
| over (10h tasks + 2h meetings) | "12h planned in an 8h day — 4h more than the day holds"; only the two **low**-priority tasks marked Suggested |
| move both suggested | live → 9h, over 1h, suggestion re-derives to the next tier, still never the highlight |
| nothing estimated | "How long will these take?" + "2 tasks have no estimate" |
| meetings only, 10–16 day, 11:00–13:00 event | "2h planned in a 6h day" (clipping proven) |
| Home, twin + a review crossing 17:00 | 7h 30m, not 8h 45m |
| Settings, 08:30 → 18:30 | helper recomputes to "A 10h day", Save enables |
| 375px | no horizontal overflow; rows go two-line so titles stop wrapping three ways |
| keyboard | Tab reaches every control, `:focus-visible` matches, 2px outline renders |

Article selection is by SOUND, not letter — "an 8h day", "a 7h day" — because every duration
starts with a digit and the vowel test that works for words is wrong on 8, 11 and 18 and
wrongly passes on 1 and 7. Asserted.

## 2026-08-05 — `useServerState`: the app's optimistic contract, in one line

**The sprint:** the React-Hooks lint backlog. 96 source errors, dominated by
`react-hooks/set-state-in-effect` (57). These are React Compiler correctness rules, so the
count is also the distance to being able to turn the compiler on.

Classifying all 57 by their *enclosing effect* rather than the flagged line found one
pattern accounting for **21 of them**, written identically in eleven views:

```ts
const [rows, setRows] = useState(initialRows);
useEffect(() => { setRows(initialRows); }, [initialRows]);
```

**That is the app's whole optimistic-update contract** — hold rows locally so an edit paints
immediately, call `router.refresh()`, then let the refreshed server props win.

**Why it is a defect and not a style preference.** An effect runs *after* paint. So every
server refresh rendered the stale rows, committed them to the DOM, ran the effect, set state
and rendered again — two passes and a frame of stale data. React's own guidance (*You Might
Not Need an Effect* → adjusting state when a prop changes) is to compare during render
instead, which restarts the render before anything is committed. Setting state during render
is legal precisely because it is this component's own state.

**One hook, not twenty-one copies** — `lib/use-server-state.ts`:

```ts
const [rows, setRows] = useServerState(initialRows);
```

It is deliberately *not* for state the user owns. A filter, an open panel, a half-typed
draft must not snap back mid-edit; those stay `useState`. That distinction is the reason it
has a name rather than being a lint autofix.

**Verified.** 757 tests (+3), `tsc` clean, `next build` compiles, lint **96 → 75** with no
new findings (6 files' `useEffect` imports became unused and were removed). In the browser:
all eight affected dev-preview routes render 200; Clients renders all four of its
`useServerState` values and its Pipeline tab; an optimistic checkbox toggle paints `false →
true` immediately and holds. Specifically checked for the failure mode this pattern *can*
have — a render loop from an unstable prop identity: no `Too many re-renders`, `setTimeout`
lag 0ms, DOM stable. (The rAF counter reads 1/sec in the Browser pane because it is
`visibilityState: hidden`, not because the thread is busy — `setTimeout` latency is the
honest probe there.)

`lib/use-server-state.test.ts` keeps the effect form from returning, and asserts the hook
still compares during render — otherwise someone "fixing" the lint warning *inside* the hook
would silently restore two render passes at every call site while the scan kept passing. Its
first two failures were **comments** (one in `projects-workspace.tsx` explaining the
migration, one in the hook's own docstring), so the scan strips comments before matching: a
codebase has to be able to describe its own history.

**Not done, and honestly a separate sprint:** the remaining **75**. They are heterogeneous —
35 `set-state-in-effect` that are mount-only initialisation from `window`/`localStorage` (8),
dialog-open resets (7) and one-off shapes (20); plus 24 `react-hooks/refs`, 10 `purity`.
Each needs individual judgement rather than one pattern, and `triage.tsx` alone holds 15.

## 2026-08-05 — One temp id, one week start, and three lint rules to zero

Continuing the React-Hooks backlog. Started at 96 source errors, now **62**, with
**`purity`, `use-memo` and `no-unescaped-entities` eliminated entirely**. But the lint
count is the least interesting part — chasing it surfaced two conventions the app had
never actually agreed on.

### `lib/temp-id.ts` — the optimistic placeholder

`'tmp-' + Date.now()` appeared at **24 call sites**, and `id.startsWith('tmp-')` at **12
more**. The prefix is load-bearing: it is how the app knows not to hand the server an id it
has never seen. Both are now named — `tempId()` and `isTempId()`.

**The bug the old form hid:** `Date.now()` is unique only per millisecond, and these ids
are React keys. Two optimistic rows created in the same tick — a loop, a fast double-click,
two composers submitted together — got the **same id**, so React reconciled one row onto
the other's DOM node and the server's reply replaced the wrong one. `tempId()` is unique by
construction. A test mints a thousand in one millisecond and asserts a thousand distinct
ids.

The scan also caught a 25th site written `'tmp' + Date.now()` — **no dash** — so
`isTempId()` would have returned *false* for it: a temporary id that did not look temporary.

### One week start, after finding six

The app had **six independent answers** to "which day does a week begin on":

| where | was |
|---|---|
| `getWeekDays` (Tasks → Week) | Monday |
| `monthGrid` default | Monday |
| `lib/calendar.ts` `weekDays` / `monthCells` | **Sunday**, hardcoded |
| DS `date-picker` | whatever `navigator.language` said |
| `mini-month` labels | Sunday-indexed constant |
| `week-view`'s own month grid | Sunday |

The visible symptom: **Tasks → Week started on Monday while Calendar → Week started on
Sunday**, in the same app, for the same week. The DS picker's version was worse than
inconsistent — `navigator` is undefined on the server, so it rendered Monday there and
Sunday in a US browser: a hydration mismatch on top of the split.

`WEEK_STARTS_ON` and `startOfWeek()` in `lib/date.ts` are now the single answer, and all six
go through them.

**I broke it before I fixed it, and only the screenshot caught it.** Changing `monthCells`
to Monday-first left the mini-month's header row still printing a Sunday-indexed constant —
so every column was labelled with the wrong day, and 1 Aug 2026 (a Saturday) sat under
"Fr". The DOM assertions I had written all still passed; the picture did not look right.
The same bug was in its `col` variable, which decides which end of a selected range gets a
rounded cap: with a Monday grid, Sunday is column 6 but `getDay()` returns 0.

**One behavioural change, called out because it is not cosmetic:** `weekTally` in
`lib/habits-data.ts` — the tally an "N times a week" habit is judged by — counted a week
that began on Sunday. So on a Sunday the heat map drew the day in the old week while the
tally counted it in a new one. It now uses the app's week. `weekdayOf` in
`habit-schedule.ts` is deliberately untouched: it is weekday *identity* (an index into a
stored day set), not a week boundary.

### The DS pickers were formatting outside the vocabulary

`date-picker.tsx` held **four** `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(undefined, …)` formatters — the
same ambient-locale defect the date vocabulary exists to stop, spelled with `Intl` instead
of `toLocaleDateString`, **which is exactly how it hid from the guard I wrote this
morning**. A date typed into the picker read "Sep 4" while the same date in a task row read
"4 Sep". `time-picker.tsx` asked the ambient locale whether to show 12-hour, contradicting
the pinned 24-hour house clock.

`lib/date-vocabulary.test.ts` now also catches `Intl.DateTimeFormat` used to *format*,
while still allowing `…resolvedOptions().timeZone`, which is how a browser legitimately
reports where it is. Its `findOffences` strips comments first — for the second time this
session, a guard's first failure was the comment explaining the rule.

**Verified.** 769 tests (+12), `tsc` clean, `next build` passes, 0 lint errors in touched
files. Browser: Calendar week now runs **Mon 3 → Sun 9** (was Sun 2 → Sat 8) with every
time 24-hour and zero AM/PM anywhere; mini-month headers checked column-by-column against
real weekdays (all seven correct); habits journal renders with its weekly tally intact.

## 2026-08-05 — Triage's state model, and two more hooks the app was writing by hand

Lint **96 → 32** across the day. `react-hooks/refs` is effectively closed (24 → 1). The
count still isn't the point — each cluster was one idea the codebase had copied instead of
naming.

### `triage.tsx` — 15 errors, all one architectural mistake

The worst file in the backlog kept its **queue and undo history in refs**, then read both
during render: the queue to find the current card and print "3 of 12", the history to decide
whether Undo appears.

The tell was already in the file: a `bump` counter whose entire job was to force a re-render
after `undoLast` rewrote a queue slot. **That counter was the bug wearing a name** — React
cannot see a ref change, so the code had built its own change notification. Both are state
now and `bump` is gone.

Two things needed care:

- **`history.pop()` was the whole re-entrancy story.** It removed and returned an entry in
  one uninterruptible step, so holding Z could not undo the same action twice. Reading state
  cannot be atomic that way — `undoLast` awaits the server and a second press lands before
  the re-render — so the guard is now explicit, in a ref that nothing renders from.
- **`actBtn` was a function returning JSX that took a `key`** — a component written as a
  call. That is why reading `dateRef` inside one of its handlers was reported as a ref
  access *during render*: the compiler cannot see that the arrow it is handed only ever runs
  on click. It is a real `<ActBtn>` now, and the last error went with it.

**Verified in the browser**, because this was a state-model rewrite and tests cover none of
it: opened triage (1 of 9, no Undo — history empty), pressed **E** → advanced to 2 of 9,
inbox count dropped to 8, Undo appeared; pressed **Z** → back to 1 of 9, count restored to
9, Undo hidden, and the card showing the exact item that had been completed.

### `useLatest` — 7 copies

`const xRef = useRef(v); xRef.current = v;` in seven components. A render can be **thrown
away**, and a render-phase write has already mutated the ref by then — so it can hold a
value from a render that never committed. The hook writes in an effect, which runs only for
the render that did.

`week-view`'s `orderRef` deliberately does **not** use it: a drag reads it back several
times inside one gesture, before React re-renders, so it needs a synchronous write. What it
did have was a real seam — an effect set `order` without telling the ref, and the
render-phase line existed to paper over that. `applyOrder` is now the only writer, so the
two cannot disagree.

### `useChanged` — 7 dialog resets, and a visible flash

`useEffect(() => { if (open) { setQuery(''); … } }, [open])` ran **after paint**, so
reopening ⌘K painted the previous search for a frame before clearing it. Comparing during
render restarts the render before anything is committed, so the stale frame never exists.

The two app-level modals were **split** rather than converted: clearing a form is state the
component owns and happens during render; fetching clients and focusing an input are real
side effects and stay in effects (the fetch also gained the `alive` guard it was missing).

**Verified.** 772 tests (+3), `tsc` clean, `next build` passes. In the browser: typed
"invoice" into ⌘K, closed, reopened — input empty, no render loop, no stale frame. All three
hooks are guarded by tests that were each proved to fail first.

**Remaining: 32**, of which 29 are `set-state-in-effect` spread thin — mount-only
initialisation from `window`/`localStorage` (8) and one-offs (21). No cluster left bigger
than three in a file.

## 2026-08-05 — Deriving instead of syncing: lint 96 → 20

The last mechanical pass over `set-state-in-effect`. Twelve more effects removed, and the
remainder is now genuinely a different kind of thing.

**Eight were `useChanged` in disguise** — "reset a derived index when its inputs change"
(`combobox`, `command-menu`, `drawer`, `command-palette`) and "follow a prop that can change
while mounted" (`projects-workspace` ×2, `app-shell`, `mini-month`).

One trap worth recording: **`useChanged(a) || useChanged(b)` short-circuits and skips a hook
call.** Both have to be evaluated first —

```ts
const queryChanged = useChanged(query);
const openChanged = useChanged(open);
if (queryChanged || openChanged) setActive(0);
```

`mini-month` needed a different key again: `selected` is a fresh `Date` on every render, so
comparing the object would have reset the view continuously. It compares the **month**.

**Four were better derived than synced**, which is a stronger fix than moving the write:

- `projects-workspace` kept an effect writing `activeId` back whenever it fell out of the
  list. The rendered value was *already* derived (`projects.find(...) ?? projects[0]`); the
  effect existed only so `patchActive` matched the right row. Pointing `patchActive` at the
  derived id means the stored value can never be stale in the first place.
- `form-renderer` clamps `step` during render. Not redundant with the existing `safeStep`,
  which I checked before touching it: `safeStep` fixes what is *shown*, but the stored step
  must come down too, or re-widening a branch later jumps the reader forward to where they
  used to be.
- `tasks-view` clamps `focusIdx` in range and resets it on a composite view key.

**Verified in the browser**, since all of this is interactive and none of it is unit-tested:
mini-month navigates Aug → Jul → Jun and *stays* (the real risk with a render-phase sync
was an immediate snap-back); the projects tab switches to Docs and does not revert; the
tasks keyboard grammar walks `j` down, clamps at the last row, walks `k` back up
(Chase → Draft → Review) and clears on Escape. No render loop anywhere — checked with
`setTimeout` lag rather than rAF, which is throttled in the hidden pane.

**A measurement note, because it nearly misled me twice.** Sampling right after an edit
showed six readings of 0 ms then two of ~1000 ms, and an empty DOM. That is the HMR
recompile signature, not a render loop: **a loop produces *sustained* lag, a rebuild
produces spike-then-recover.** Re-measuring on a settled page gave a 5 ms maximum. The
collapsed mini-month in one screenshot was likewise a persisted sidebar state, not a
regression — worth confirming before believing either.

**Remaining: 20**, and they are no longer a backlog of the same mistake. Seventeen are
`set-state-in-effect` where the effect is *correct*: fetching (`version-history`,
`notifications-bell`, `portal-document`, `command-palette` search, `task-detail-drawer`,
`documents-view`, `focus-timer`) and client-only reads that cannot run on the server
(`localStorage` in `app-shell` / `emoji-picker` / `focus-timer`, `URLSearchParams` in
`settings-view` and four dev-preview harnesses). Contorting those to satisfy the rule would
make them worse, not better; the honest options are `useSyncExternalStore` for the storage
reads and leaving the fetches alone. The other three are one ref-in-render in
`block-editor`, one `pump()` ordering in `file-upload`, and one memo the compiler declines
to preserve in `database-view`.

## 2026-08-05 — The sidebar reflowed on every page load

Chasing the last of the lint list turned up a real defect rather than a lint nit.

**The saved sidebar mode lived only in `localStorage`, which a server render cannot see.**
So every page load rendered the *expanded* sidebar, painted it, and an effect corrected it
one frame later. For anyone whose saved mode is `collapsed` or `hover` that is not a
flicker — `hover` renders a structurally different tree (a positioned panel over a reserved
rail) and `collapsed` changes the sidebar's width, so **the whole page reflowed after
paint, on every navigation.**

I confirmed the shape by reading the render path before touching anything: the two branches
at `app-shell.tsx` differ structurally, and `collapsed` feeds the width. This is a layout
shift, not a repaint.

**The fix is the app's own existing answer to "server and client must agree": a cookie.**
`SPACE_COOKIE` in `lib/active-space.ts` exists for exactly that reason, with that rationale
in its comment. `lib/sidebar-mode.ts` now owns the vocabulary — the mode type, the cookie
name, the older `localStorage` key, and the parse — and `app/(app)/layout.tsx` reads it and
hands `initialSidebarMode` to the shell. The first paint is right; there is nothing to
correct.

**What the effect still does**, because these are the two things a server genuinely cannot
know: a temporary switch made in *this tab* (`sessionStorage` is per-tab, and a cookie is
shared across them — so it stays), and a `localStorage` default from before the cookie
existed, which it adopts *and mirrors forward* so the next render is server-correct too.

**Verified.** 778 tests (+6), `tsc` clean, `next build` passes, lint **96 → 19** (with
`react-hooks/immutability` now at zero — see below). In the browser: setting "Collapsed" as
the default writes `zb-sidebar=collapsed` and `localStorage` agrees; and the migration path
works — an install with only `localStorage` gets the cookie written on first load
(`zb-sidebar=hover`). Probe state was cleared afterwards.

**Owed, stated plainly:** I could not verify the *first paint itself*. The layout only runs
for a signed-in user, and every `(app)` route answers `307 → /login` without a session, so
the one thing I cannot demonstrate is the absence of the shift on a real load. The parse is
unit-tested, the write path is browser-verified, and the read is a single line the compiler
checked — but the end-to-end result needs a session.

**Also in this pass:**
- **`file-upload`'s `pump`** recursed into the `const` binding it was being assigned to —
  harmless at call time, since `.finally` runs later, but the compiler refuses to optimize a
  component that reads a variable inside its own initializer. A **named function
  expression** gives the recursive call its own binding and the error goes away.
- **`database-view` passed a literal `1`** for the week start — a seventh copy of that
  decision, agreeing by luck. It now takes the shared default.
- **`block-editor`'s remaining `refs` error is correct as written** and I left it: every ref
  access in that map is inside an event-handler prop (`onRowMouseDown` reads `selRef`,
  `copyText` reads `blocksRef`, `inputRef` is a commit-time callback). None run during
  render; the rule cannot prove it. Contorting a 200-line JSX map to satisfy it would make
  the code worse.

## 2026-08-05 — The NUL bytes that made a file invisible to grep

Two items cleared off the "written down, not started" list.

### `lib/db-engine.ts` was binary as far as the tools were concerned

Three **literal NUL bytes** sat in the source, used as a separator. They worked — and they
made `file(1)` report the source as binary and **`grep` silently return nothing for the
whole file.** Not "no matches printed": no matches *found*, ever, for anything. Searching
it for `RETYPEABLE` returned zero hits with the definition sitting on line 140. That is a
file the codebase cannot search, in a session where searching is most of the work.

The separator is not a mistake, though, and the fix had to keep it. `is` on a
select/status compares against the option **id and its name**, both joined into one
haystack so `contains` can match a substring while `is` splits it back for an exact match.
The separator must be a character no option name can contain — and the existing test
fixture already had one named **"To do"**. With a space, `is: "do"` would match it.

So: the byte became the escape `'\0'`, behind a named `SEP` with the reasoning written
down. Same value at runtime, ASCII on disk.

**Verified.** `file` now says "Unicode text, UTF-8 text"; `grep RETYPEABLE` finds lines
139–140 that were previously unfindable. 784 tests, `tsc` and `eslint` clean, `next build`
passes.

**And the reason got a test.** Nothing covered the filter path — the six existing
`db-engine` tests are the formula engine. Six new ones lock in the behaviour the NUL
exists for: `is` matches an option by name *or* id, `is: "do"` does **not** match "To do",
`is_not` is the exact inverse, and `contains` still finds the fragment. Proved by setting
`SEP` to a space: three fail, including exactly the one written for it.

### `staticItems(pathname)` ignored its parameter

The tempting fix is to use it — drop "Go to Tasks" while you are on Tasks. I deliberately
did not: a keyboard palette earns its speed from muscle memory, and a list that reorders
itself by location means the third row is a different command depending on where you came
from. Linear keeps the current page listed for the same reason. So the dead parameter is
gone, with that reasoning recorded where the next person will look — and `pathname` came
out of the memo's dependencies with it, where it had been rebuilding every row on every
navigation for nothing.

**Verified in the browser:** the palette still opens with all 12 nav rows plus Actions,
Rituals and Create; typing "final" filters them all out and offers `New task "final"`.

## 2026-08-06 — A mention you can actually click

`SPRINT_STATUS` carried this as "an internal link doesn't navigate on a plain click —
Notion solves it with a hover preview card; that is its own sprint". Reading the code first
changed the answer.

**What was actually happening.** A mention is a link mark on ordinary text — the design
that let mentions exist with no new ProseMirror node type and no migration. An idle block
renders its spans as static HTML and swaps to the live editor when clicked, so
`staticSpans` `preventDefault`ed every unmodified click to keep the caret placeable. The
result: a mention could only be opened with **⌘-click**, and `target="_blank"` meant even
that went to a new tab. The one thing a mention exists for had no cheap way to happen.

**The benchmark, stated precisely.** In Notion a page mention is an *atomic inline node*: a
plain click navigates and there is no caret to place inside it. Ours is a link mark on
editable text, so that is not available for free — but the part that matters is that **a
plain click follows the link**, and that we can match. The cost is the one Notion pays too:
to edit the words of a link you put the caret beside it and arrow in rather than clicking
its middle. ⌘-click still does the browser's thing, so "open in a new tab" is never taken
away.

**So the hover card was not the fix — it was a way of avoiding the fix.** A preview card
would have added a fetch, a positioning layer and a hover delay on top of a link that still
didn't work when clicked. It remains worth building later, on top of a link that does.

**Two changes, one decision.** `lib/use-follow-link.ts` owns where a link goes, split so
the decision is testable without a router: `resolveLink(href, origin)` returns
`internal` / `external` / `null`, and the hook performs it. Internal links are re-derived
through `recordHref` rather than followed literally, which normalises an absolute URL from
the clipboard (`https://app…/documents?page=…`) into a client-side navigation instead of a
full page load. `null` matters too: a record type that parses but has no page yet (goal,
meeting, feedback) does **nothing**, rather than falling through to `window.open` on a URL
we know is not a page.

The second change is in `StaticRich`: a mouseup that lands on a link with a **collapsed**
selection no longer activates the block. Without that, mouseup swaps the static render for
the editor and the anchor's own click never reaches a live element. Keying it on the
selection is what keeps drag intact — dragging *across* a mention still selects it.

**Verified in the browser, all three paths.** Plain click on an internal link performs an
in-app navigation — the dev server logged `GET /projects/9f8b1c2d-… 200`, and the `/login`
that follows is `requireUser()` doing its job without a session, not a failure. Plain click
on an external link calls `window.open(…, '_blank', 'noopener,noreferrer')` and the page
stays put (captured by stubbing `window.open` rather than actually leaving). Dragging
across a link activates the block for editing and does not navigate. Enter on a focused
anchor takes the same path, because Enter on an anchor fires `click`.

7 unit tests on `resolveLink` cover every record type, the absolute-URL normalisation, a
look-alike foreign origin, and the hrefs that must resolve to nothing. 791 tests total,
`tsc` and `eslint` clean, `next build` passes.

**One harness addition, deliberately kept:** the editor dev-preview now stages a paragraph
containing one internal and one external link. That state had no fixture, which is why the
defect survived this long — a block with a mention in it was not something anyone could
look at.

## 2026-08-06 — One answer to "what is this id", and a stale plan corrected

### The plan was telling the next session to build things that exist

`SPRINT_STATUS` Part 4 closed with *"proposals/contracts and attachments are larger and
later — the two places where the product is furthest from the plan's own description of
itself."* Both shipped. Attachments are `0033` + `lib/attachments.ts`; proposals are the
`lineitems` and `accept` block types with `0034_acceptances` and `0035_acceptance_invoice`,
all three migrations present.

That line would have sent the next session to build them a second time. **It is the third
time this document has been caught asserting something the code contradicts** — which is
the exact failure it was created to prevent. Corrected, with the real remaining order
written in its place, and a standing instruction to check the code before trusting any
"next" in there.

### `resolveSummaries` — the projection the preview card needs

A mention now follows on a plain click; a hover preview is the other half. It needs the one
thing the codebase could not answer: **given an arbitrary `type:id`, what is it?**

`resolveRefs` answered only "what is it called". The second line — a status, a date, an
amount — was computed **inline, per relationship, in nine separate places** inside each
loader, always with the row already in hand. Correct there, and useless for a card that has
nothing but an href.

So rather than add a third projection, `resolveRefs`' private `SOURCES` grew into a per-type
descriptor (table · label column · extra columns · how to build `meta`), `resolveSummaries`
returns the whole `RecordSummary`, and **`resolveRefs` is now a one-line projection of it**.
Existing callers are untouched; the app does not get a second answer to the same question.

**Every extra column was copied from a select that already ships**, never guessed — because
a column that does not exist fails the whole query, `safe()` swallows it, and the symptom
would be *every reference of that type rendering as a tombstone*. Silent and total. The
retry makes that degrade instead: if the enriched select fails, it re-asks for the label
alone and the caller sees exactly today's behaviour. A test asserts both queries by name.

**It has a real consumer, not a hypothetical one.** `mentionEdges` now resolves summaries,
so a mentioned task shows "Done" like the structurally-linked one beside it. Before, the
same row was described two different ways depending on how it reached the panel — and the
fix costs nothing, being the same query with more columns.

**Verified.** 798 tests (+7), `tsc` and `eslint` clean, `next build` passes. Seven new tests
cover label+meta per type, one-query-per-type with de-duplicated ids, the tombstone, the
untitled fallback, an unknown type, and the enriched-select retry. The Connected panel
renders unchanged in the browser — though that harness is demo-fed, so the DB path itself is
covered by the tests rather than by a page.

**Known cost, small and deliberate:** a batch in which *every* ref is deleted now costs two
queries instead of one, because an empty result is indistinguishable from a failed select
without inspecting the error. Two cheap queries for a fully-tombstoned batch is the right
side of that trade.

**Next:** the card itself — a hover trigger with a delay, portal positioning, and a keyboard
path. The data it needs now exists.

## 2026-08-06 — Memory M1: the spine (§7X, migration 0029)

The first module built on the premise that **a memory is a fact with a time validity, not a
saved thing.** Everything below follows from that one sentence, and the sentence is why this
is not a second Documents with a worse editor.

### What shipped

- **`supabase/migrations/0029_memories.sql`** — written, **NOT applied** (one line, below).
  The temporal spine (`valid_from` / `invalid_from` / `superseded_by`), six fixed kinds, four
  origins, a polymorphic subject, the receipt columns, and a **partial unique index** that
  makes remembering the same thing twice about the same subject impossible.
- **`lib/memory.ts`** — the rules, no React and no runtime Supabase import: the vocabulary,
  `normalizeBody`, `isCurrent` / `asOf`, `sortMemories`, `supersedePatch`, `factKey`, and the
  one subject-scoped read. 26 tests.
- **`lib/actions/memory.ts`** — `remember` · `supersedeMemory` · `updateMemoryBody` ·
  `setMemoryPinned` · `archiveMemory` · `forgetMemory`, all gated on `memoriesSupported()`.
- **`components/memory/memory-panel.tsx`** — facts on the record they are about, plus the
  inline capture affordance. Hosted on the client page (with capture) and the document
  properties area (read-only).
- **"Remember this"** in the document selection toolbar, plumbed host → editor → rich text
  as an opaque `RememberHook`. The editor still does not know what a memory is.
- **`app/dev-preview/memory`** — the harness, because the feature is correctly invisible in
  the real app until 0029 is applied.

### The decision that mattered: a sibling panel, not a Connected group

The plan put memories "in the Connected panel". They are next to it instead, and the reason
is typographic rather than architectural: **Connected renders references — a label, a status,
a chevron — and a fact is a sentence.** Putting facts in that panel meant either truncating
them to four words (a fact you cannot read is not a fact) or teaching one row component two
typographies. One heading rung, one hairline, no fill, so the two read as one band.

The corollary is that `EntityType` did **not** gain `'memory'`. Nothing at M1 can produce a
memory→record mention edge — bodies are plain text at this milestone — so adding the type
would have forced entries in two exhaustive `Record<EntityType, …>` maps for a group that
could never be rendered. The `mentions` reuse the plan describes stays true and arrives with
the milestone that gives memory bodies links.

### Never record a fact somewhere it cannot be read

A memory captured from a document takes the doc's **client** as its subject — "they pay on
the 1st" is true of Meridian Studio wherever you read it — and only a client-less doc is its
own subject. A **project** would be a fine subject and is deliberately not offered: the
project overview hosts no memory panel, so a fact filed there would be invisible. The
toolbar action hides itself rather than guessing, which is what keeps the module's own
"zero surprise" measure at zero.

The same rule moved one item out of M1: **the Memory type in quick capture is deferred to
M2.** A fact typed into the global capture box has no subject, and a subject-less fact has
nowhere to live until `/memory` exists — shipping it now would have created write-only rows,
which is a partial feature (rule 2). It is small once the home page exists.

### The four open questions, answered as defaults

Recorded in `MEMORY_MODULE_PLAN.md` §10 so they can be overturned:
1. **Derivation scope** — M3; clients and projects first, self-facts behind an explicit opt-in.
2. **Space scoping** — `space_id` set = that space, **null = everywhere**, and self-facts are
   null. A fact about you must not vanish when you switch spaces.
3. **Retention** — the system never hard-deletes. `forgetMemory` is user-initiated only, and
   the sole place it runs unprompted is Undo on a row seconds old.
4. **Razorpay** — unaffected; the payment-rhythm detector reads invoice history.

### Two real defects, found and fixed before they shipped

- **A rejected server action wedged the field.** `setBusy(false)` sat after an `await` with no
  `try/finally`, so an expired session or a dropped connection left the input disabled with
  the user's sentence trapped in it — in the toolbar's case inside a floating bar with no way
  out but Esc. Both fields now use `finally`, and the catch shows a human sentence rather
  than the thrown `Not authenticated`, which is engineering vocabulary, not UI copy.
- **A pinned row indented its own sentence.** The star was rendered only on pinned rows, so
  one starred fact pushed its text 19px right of its neighbours'. The slot is now reserved on
  every row whenever anything in the list is pinned — and it was the screenshot that caught
  it, not any assertion.

### Verified

824 tests (+26), `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every file touched — the two errors remaining
in `documents-view.tsx` and `block-editor.tsx` predate this sprint and are recorded, not
fixed here. In the browser: the panel's five states, sort order (pinned → confidence →
recency), the 274-character fact wrapping rather than truncating, the row menu, "Show 2 more",
the empty state at one line, a read-only empty panel rendering nothing at all, and the full
selection gesture — select → toolbar → Remember → field pre-filled and naming its subject →
Enter saves. The refusal path was exercised for real: the server action rejected, the message
rendered in place, and the field came back.

Verification needed its own dev server: another session held port 3000 and Next 16 refuses a
second instance in one directory, so the app was run from a scratch copy with a hard-linked
`node_modules` (a symlinked one makes Turbopack panic — it rejects a link out of the project
root). Cleaned up afterwards.

**Owed, one line:** paste `supabase/migrations/0029_memories.sql`. Until then
`memoriesSupported()` reports false, every action returns "Memory needs migration 0029", the
panel renders nothing and the toolbar action is hidden — the app is correct before and after.

## 2026-08-06 — Memory M2: recall (§7X)

M1 could record a fact and show it on the record it was about. That is half a memory
system: everything you captured was only findable if you already knew where to look. M2 is
the other half — the page, the index and the two capture paths that had nowhere to land.

### What shipped

- **`/memory`** — the home, in the Horizon nav group beside Goals and Habits. Facts grouped
  by what they are ABOUT, "About you" leading, with the archive as a disclosure at the foot.
- **⌘K Recall** — memories in the command palette under a `Recall` heading.
- **`lib/search.ts`** — memories joined the ONE index as a `memory` source.
- **Quick capture's Memory type**, the item M1 deferred.
- **`groupBySubject` / `selfFirst`** in `lib/memory.ts`, and `components/memory/memory-row.tsx`
  extracted so the home and the panel render the identical row.

### `EntityType` gained `'memory'` — and the criterion was already written down

M1 deliberately kept it out: with no `/memory` page, `recordHref('memory', …)` could only
have returned undefined, and the type would have been dead weight in three total maps. The
rule `lib/search.ts` states — *"a type joins this list the moment it gets a record route"* —
is exactly what changed. So `recordHref` gained one line, `parseRecordHref` its inverse, and
**TypeScript then demanded the other three entries**, which is precisely why those maps are
exhaustive `Record<EntityType, …>` rather than partials.

`memory` is deliberately **absent from `GROUP_ORDER`**, which is also the Connected panel's
filter — so a fact still never renders as a Connected row. `<MemoryPanel>` owns how facts
read, and it sits directly above Connected on every surface that hosts both.

### ⌘K Recall is one line, and that is the point

The plan asked for "a Recall section in the command palette". Because `searchRecords` is the
one index and the palette derives its headings from a per-type map, the whole integration is
`memory: { group: 'Recall', icon: Brain, hub: '/memory' }`. The never-list says "no second
search box"; this is what honouring it looks like when the architecture is right.

Recall shows only what is **currently true** — `invalid_from is null`. A superseded fact
surfacing beside its replacement is how a memory system starts contradicting itself.

### Quick capture: two commits, one field, no mode

No Task/Memory toggle. A toggle taxes every ordinary capture — nearly all of them — to serve
the rare one. The choice is made at COMMIT time instead: **Enter** saves a task, **⌥Enter**
(or the Remember button) commits the same words as a fact. That is the moment you actually
know which of the two you typed.

It takes the RAW text, not `parsed.title`: the task grammar strips `!high`, `~30m` and
`#acme` because a task carries those as fields, but a fact is one sentence and stripping
words out of it would change what it claims. The subject is **you** — there is no record
context in a global box — and the footer says so before you commit.

### Two defects the browser caught

- **"About you" was not leading.** The rule lived only in the loader, so the component
  trusted its host — while already synthesising a self group when one was absent. Half an
  invariant. `selfFirst` is now one exported function used by both, with three tests.
- **The new Remember button clipped the placeholder** ("…try: call Sam tomorr"). Rather than
  delete the typed-grammar hint, it moved to the footer *when the field is empty* — an empty
  field does not need to be told what Enter does, it needs to be told what it accepts. The
  commit keys take over the moment there is something to commit. Measured: 142px in a 299px
  field, and the footer sits on one line.

### Verified

833 tests (+9), `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every file touched. In the browser: the home's
grouping and "About you" ordering (proved against harness data that deliberately fed it
second), the tombstoned subject group, the archived disclosure, quick capture's two buttons,
the empty-vs-typed footer swap, and the refusal path — the server action rejected, the human
sentence rendered, the text stayed.

**Not verified in the browser:** ⌘K Recall's rendered group, because `searchRecords` needs a
session and the palette has no demo-fed path. Its two moving parts are covered by tests
instead (the `recordHref`/`parseRecordHref` round trip now includes `memory`).

**Owed, still one line:** paste `supabase/migrations/0029_memories.sql`. Until then
`/memory` renders "Memory isn't switched on yet", Recall finds nothing and every action
returns cleanly — the app is correct before and after.

**Written down, not started:** a project has no memory panel, so a project is still not
offered as a subject (never record a fact somewhere it cannot be read). Quick capture cannot
pick a record subject — a fact typed there is about you. M3 is the derived detectors; M4 the
supersede/history UI, which `supersedeMemory` already supports with nothing rendering it.

## 2026-08-06 — Memory M3: the derived detectors (§7X)

**Migration 0029 is applied**, verified against the live app rather than assumed — the
`/memory` page renders real rows, and the first detector found a real pattern in this
workspace's own data on its first run.

M1 could record a fact you stated. M2 could find it again. M3 is the part no competing
product can do: the memories **nobody types**. mymind, Supermemory, Mem0 and Zep must all
be *told* things; Zenboard already holds the invoices, the time entries and the
completions.

### What shipped

- **`lib/detectors.ts`** — three pure detectors, 29 tests, no AI:
  - **payment rhythm** per client — "Meridian Studio pays about 6 days late."
  - **estimate accuracy** per project — "Work on Acme rebrand takes about 40% longer…"
  - **working hours** for you — "You finish most of your work between 11:00 and 15:00."
- **`lib/memory-suggest.ts`** — runs them over real rows, converts completions into the
  user's own hours, and suppresses anything already answered.
- **`acceptProposal` / `dismissProposal`**, and the **Noticed band** at the top of `/memory`.
- **The project overview now hosts `<MemoryPanel>`**, which is what makes `project` a legal
  subject at all.

### Silence is the default, and it is the design

Every detector returns nothing unless the pattern is real AND worth a sentence. "This
client pays on time" is not a memory — it is the absence of one. So there is a tolerance
band (±3 days), a minimum sample (3 invoices · 5 measured tasks · 20 completions), and an
**agreement test**: a median can sit past the tolerance on a split sample, and "pays 9 days
late" would then be a claim about someone who is simply erratic. §9 says that below ~50%
acceptance the detectors are noise and should be **cut, not tuned**, so they start quiet.

Two arithmetic choices worth keeping: **median, not mean** (one invoice paid a year late
must not invent a rhythm) and **totals, not averaged per-task ratios** (a 5-minute task that
took 15 would otherwise read as a 200% overrun and drown a week of accurate work).

### Nothing is written silently, and nothing nags twice

§8's never-list opens with "never write a memory silently", so a detector produces a
**proposal** and the only paths to a `memories` row are the two buttons. Suppression needed
no new table: an accepted proposal puts its key in the memory's **`anchor`** (0029's "where
did this come from" column — a detector key is exactly that), and a dismissed one goes in
**`profiles.preferences`**, because a refusal is not a fact about your work, it is a
preference about what this module may bring up.

A **superseded** derived fact is deliberately *not* suppressed: if you told us the pattern
changed, noticing the new one is the system working.

### Benchmark (rule 7)

Gmail's "Smart suggestions" and Linear's "similar issues" both surface an inference inline
and both are dismissible — but neither tells you **why**. Every row here states its evidence
("6 of 7 settled invoices, measured from the due date"), always visible, never behind a
hover. A claim about your client that you cannot check is exactly what makes this class of
feature feel like surveillance, and §9's "zero surprise" measure depends on it.

### Three defects found, one of them only by real data

- **A blank group heading on `/memory`.** Root cause was not in this sprint's code:
  `resolveSummaries` did `str(row.title) ?? 'Untitled'`, and `''` is not null — so an
  untitled row resolved to the empty string and **every mention edge and relation chip in
  the app** could render a nameless label. Fixed at the source (`?.trim() || 'Untitled'`),
  with the tombstone case kept distinct: absent from the map still means "Deleted".
- **A window that started on an empty hour.** `[09,10,11]` busy with `08` empty ties two
  four-hour windows, and the scan reported the one with a dead leading hour — padding
  presented as a habit.
- **A circular import.** `memory-suggest` → `actions/memory` → `memory-suggest`. `tsc` was
  perfectly happy. The dismissal vocabulary moved to `lib/memory.ts`, which both already
  import.

Also caught: `lib/date-vocabulary.test.ts` failed the build for a fresh `Intl.DateTimeFormat`
in the loader. That test exists because a second, differently-configured formatter is how
"18:05" and "6:05 PM" end up on the same screen. `minutesOfDayIn` already existed.

### Verified

867 tests (+34), `tsc` and `eslint` clean on every file touched. In the browser, against the
**live database**: the nav row, the Noticed band rendering a genuinely detected pattern
(56% of 36 completed tasks), its evidence line, both actions labelled for screen readers,
and the group-heading fix before/after.

**Not exercised:** accepting a proposal for real. It writes to your production database, and
that is your call rather than something to do unasked — the refusal path and the gated path
are both verified, and `acceptProposal` is a thin wrapper over `remember`, which is.

**Written down, not started:** the deferral detector ("you have moved this task nine times")
needs a change log for `scheduled_date` that no table keeps — it is the one §4.1 candidate
with no data behind it. Reply latency needs a channel the app does not yet record. Four
pre-existing unused symbols in `projects-workspace.tsx` (`useEffect`, `doneWeek`, `timeWeek`,
`PropDot`) are dead code outside this sprint's area.

## 2026-08-06 — Memory M4: the temporal spine, made visible (§7X)

The module has claimed since M1 that **facts are superseded, never overwritten**. Until
now that claim was unfalsifiable from outside: the chain existed in the data and appeared
on no screen, and confidence only ever moved down. M4 is the part that makes the temporal
model something you can check rather than something we assert.

### What shipped

- **`historyOf`** + the **"What this replaced"** disclosure on every fact.
- **`?on=YYYY-MM-DD`** — "what was true in March", built on the `asOf` predicate that has
  been tested since M1 and had no caller.
- **`confirmMemory`** and **`needsReview`**, and the **"Are these still true?"** step in the
  weekly review — §7G's question, asked of facts in the same place it is asked of goals.

### Confidence could only ever fall

`§3.1` promised derived facts "start below 1 and rise when confirmed", and nothing in three
milestones ever raised one. `confirmedConfidence` is a **step, not a jump** — one
confirmation is one observation, and it takes three separate weeks of saying "still true"
to carry a detector's guess to the top of a list. It caps at 1 in the app rather than
relying on 0029's CHECK: a value the database has to clamp is a rule the app got wrong.

`confirmMemory` also stamps `last_recalled_at` and bumps `recall_count` — the two columns
that exist to feed decay (§5.4) and had never been written. **`recall_count` is deliberately
still absent from the `Memory` type**: it is fetched in the one action that writes it, so no
surface pays to load a column none of them render.

### The as-of view is loud on purpose

A page showing March's facts that *looks* like today's is the worst thing this module could
produce, so the notice is the most prominent element on the page and leaving is one click.
Three things switch off on a past day, each for the same reason — you cannot answer a
question about now from a screen showing then:

- the **Noticed band** (accepting there would date a fact today off a screen saying March),
- **capture** in the "About you" group,
- the **synthesised** self group itself, which exists only to host capture. An empty heading
  there would imply you knew nothing about yourself that day, which is a different claim
  from "this page cannot add facts to March".

### The review step appears only when there is something to ask

Five steps when facts need review, four when they don't. A permanently-present step reading
"nothing to review" would make the weekly review longer every week in exchange for nothing,
and this ritual's whole promise is that it is short enough to actually do.

**"It changed" hands off to `/memory`** rather than forking the supersede editor into a
ritual: rewording a fact is a writing task and this step is a triage one. Keeping is the
default and costs one click, exactly as the goals step above it behaves.

### Verified against the live database

881 tests (+14), `tsc` and `eslint` clean. In the browser, signed in, on real data:

- `?on=2026-03-01` renders **"What you knew on 1 March 2026"** and correctly shows nothing —
  both existing facts were recorded in August. The temporal filter is doing real work.
- The weekly review reports **"Step 1 of 5"** and step 4 lists three facts with Still
  true / It changed / Let go.
- **The whole M1→M4 loop closes on real data:** the working-hours pattern M3 detected was
  accepted, and it now sorts FIRST in the review because it is the least certain thing
  known — which is exactly what `needsReview` promises.

Also fixed: the "About you" empty line invited capture on a page where capture is off.

**Owed:** nothing. **Written down, not started:** decay itself (§5.4) — `recall_count` is
now written on confirm but nothing yet decays a fact that is never recalled, and the
"about to fade" band waits on that. `⌘K` Recall does not bump `recall_count` either, which
is the other half of the same signal. **M5** (the clerk) is Phase 6 and unchanged.

## 2026-08-06 — Memory: decay (§5.4). The module is complete up to M5.

The last unbuilt idea in the plan. `recall_count` and `last_recalled_at` had existed since
0029 and been written exactly once (on confirm, added earlier today) and **read never** —
so every fact aged at the same rate whether you leaned on it daily or had not looked at it
since February.

### What shipped

- **`fadedConfidence` / `isFading` / `fadingFacts`** — the fade rule, pure and tested.
- **`recallMemory`** — ⌘K Recall now stamps the fact you opened.
- **The "About to fade" band** on `/memory`, and `sortMemories` now orders on the faded
  number rather than the stored one.

### Two deliberate differences from the plan, both from §9

The plan says a memory never recalled "eventually **archives itself**". It does not, and
both departures come from the same measure — **zero surprise outranks tidiness**:

**Decay is computed, never stored.** No cron, no sweep, no migration. `fadedConfidence` is
a pure function of time since the fact was last touched. A stored decay would drift from
the rule that implies it, and then two surfaces disagree about how sure we are.

**Nothing archives itself.** A fact that vanished from a client page while you were not
looking is precisely the failure §9's metric exists to catch. So fading does exactly one
thing automatically: the fact **drops in the ordering**, which stops it reaching the ambient
three on a record page (§5.3) — nothing hidden, nothing deleted, it just stops being put in
front of you. The band then *asks*. That is the plan's outcome, one confirmation later.

The rule itself: **90 days of grace, then half every 120**, and **pinned facts never fade** —
pinning is the user saying "keep this in front of me", and a rule that overrode them would
be the system arguing with its owner.

### Recall and confirm are different signals

`recallMemory` moves `last_recalled_at` and **leaves confidence exactly where it was**.
Looking something up proves you still *need* it, not that it is still *true*.
`confirmMemory` is the one that says true, and it is the one that raises. Wiring recall
needed a real change to the palette: activation was `run()` **or** navigate, so a side
effect that must accompany opening a row had nowhere to live — `Item.onSelect` now fires
alongside either, before the push, because `router.push` can unmount the tree.

### Engineering notes

- `last_recalled_at` and `recall_count` joined `Memory` and `MEMORY_COLUMNS`. The old
  comment saying they are "never rendered" was true right up until they became the reason a
  fact sorts where it does. They are still never *shown* — no counter, no "last seen" line.
- `sortMemories` now reads the clock, which quietly made an existing ordering test
  time-dependent — it passed today and would have failed at some future date. It now takes
  an explicit instant.
- `BandHeading` extracted: `/memory` has two bands that ask questions, and they must read as
  one idea in two registers rather than two features that landed separately.
- `Clock` reused rather than adding `Hourglass` to the icon seam.

### Verified

890 tests (+9), `tsc` and `eslint` clean. In the browser: the fade band renders its fact
with Still true / Let go, and the history disclosure expands to
*"Pays on net-45. Until 1 Sep 2025 · Pays on net-30, no PO needed. Until 1 Mar"* — note the
year appearing on the older entry and not the newer, which is `formatDay`'s house rule
doing its job inside a brand-new surface.

**Verified by DOM assertion rather than screenshot** for these two: the Browser pane does
not repaint on a programmatic scroll, and both surfaces sit below the fold of a long
harness page. Text, counts, button labels and the expanded chain were all asserted.

### The module is now complete up to M5

M1 spine · M2 recall · M3 derived · M4 temporal · decay. **M5 (the clerk — AI proposing
memories from docs and portal threads) is Phase 6** and deliberately not before: the plan's
rule is that the module has to be worth using before a model touches it, or we cannot tell
whether the model is helping.

**Written down, not started:** "What contradicts" — the one band never built. A
contradiction needs two live facts that disagree, and supersession means the app does not
currently produce that state; it becomes real when the clerk can propose a fact that
conflicts with one you already hold.

## 2026-08-06 — The hover preview card (§7J / SPRINT_STATUS item 1)

The other half of a working mention. A plain click has followed an internal link since
2026-08-06; this is the half that lets you decide whether you want to. It was deliberately
built **second** — a preview card layered over a link that did not navigate would have been
a fetch and a hover delay in front of a broken affordance.

### What shipped

- **`components/ds/ui/hover-card.tsx`** — the DS gained a HoverCard (Radix), because the
  constitution's rule is to extend the design system first and then build the feature.
- **`lib/shared-cache.ts`** — fetch-once-per-key, with tests.
- **`components/connected/record-preview.tsx`** — the card, wired into `staticSpans`, so
  every mention in every document has it at once.

### It answers a different question from Notion's, on purpose

Notion previews a page mention by rendering the page's **content**, which works because a
Notion mention almost always points at a page. Ours can point at **eleven** types and most
of them have no body at all — an invoice, a client, a task, a project, a form. So the card
answers **what kind of thing is this, and what state is it in**: hovering "Acme rebrand"
says *Project · Active*; hovering "INV-014" says *Invoice · Overdue*. That is precisely what
you would otherwise have navigated away to find out, which is the only thing that justifies
a preview at all. Linear's issue-id hover does the same, for the same reason.

It costs nothing until it is used: an external link is returned **untouched** (no wrapper,
no listener), and the query fires when the card **opens**, not when the link renders. A
paragraph with eight mentions makes zero requests until you hover one.

### One mechanism, not two

`use-link-meta.ts` had already written a fetch-once-per-URL cache for **external** unfurls.
Rather than write a second copy for internal records, that cache became `lib/shared-cache.ts`
and both now use it. `null` is a cached *answer* — "we asked, there is nothing" — which is
what stops a deleted record being re-queried on every hover.

### Two defects lint caught that review would not have

- **A prop named `ref`.** React treats it specially, so `<Body ref={…}>` was a real ref being
  read during render rather than an ordinary prop. Renamed to `target`.
- **`setState` in an effect** in the new harness, to read the query string. Replaced with
  `useSyncExternalStore` and a server snapshot of `null` — the house pattern here, since the
  server has no `location` and reading it during render is a hydration mismatch.

### Verified

897 tests (+7), `tsc` and `eslint` clean on every file touched — including the harness,
where the two raw `<a>` elements now carry per-line disables with the reason (they exist to
mirror exactly what `staticSpans` emits; `<Link>` would test something the editor never
renders).

In the browser, all three states, the last against the **live database**:

- **Resolved** — hovering a real project id showed **"New life · Project · Active"**.
- **Tombstone** — a fabricated id showed *"Deleted — this project no longer exists."*
- **Untouched** — the external link is not a trigger at all (`data-state` absent).

The harness gained `?ref=/projects/<uuid>`, so any real record can be previewed there rather
than only invented ones.

## 2026-08-06 — Block links (v2.3 §2 "blocks as addressable rows" — the addressable half)

**No migration**, and the reason is the finding.

### The audit came back different from the plan

`MASTER_PRODUCT_PLAN.md` v2.3 calls the JSONB `pages.content` blob **"the largest remaining
structural debt in the product"** and blames three features on it: block-level comments,
block links, and synced blocks. Only part of that survives reading the code.

**A block has carried a stable id since the editor was written.** `Block.id` is minted by
`genId()`, persisted inside the blob and round-tripped by `normalize()`. Every row already
rendered `data-block-id`, and the floating outline already scrolled to one. `duplicateIds`
already re-mints on clone, so no two blocks share an id. Nothing about *addressing* a block
was waiting on a table.

What the blob genuinely prevents is a block having an **owner other than its page** — which
is exactly what a synced block is, and what a comment thread would want a foreign key to.
Those stay migration work. So this sprint ships the addressable half today, unmigrated, and
the plan's §2 has been corrected rather than left to send the next session to build a
migration it does not need.

### What shipped

- **`lib/block-link.ts`** — the address, in one place. `blockHref` is `recordHref('doc', id)`
  plus `#block-<id>`, so the documents route is still written once.
- **`togglesHiding`** in lib/blocks.ts — the inverse of `hiddenIds`, beside it.
- **`lib/use-block-anchor.ts`** — the *request* to show a block, as a store.
- **"Copy link to block"** in the block menu, gated on a new `pageId` prop.
- **Arriving**: open the toggles the block is folded inside → scroll → flash.

### The bug that would have shipped silently

`resolveLink` normalises an internal link back through `recordHref` so a pasted absolute URL
becomes a client-side route. `recordHref` knows nothing about fragments, so every block link
would have normalised down to its page — the link would still have "worked", opening the
right document at the top, every time. `withFragment` is the one line that stops it and it
has its own test.

### Why the app has to announce it, rather than read `location.hash`

`router.push` goes out as **pushState, which deliberately does not fire `hashchange`** — so
the one case block links exist for, jumping to a block in the document you are already
reading, is exactly the case the native event misses. (`usePathname`/`useSearchParams` are
no help either: neither carries the fragment.) So the URL stays authoritative for a cold
load and for back/forward, and `zb:block-anchor` — the same custom-event seam realtime and
the focus timer use — covers every navigation the router performs.

### Three smaller decisions

- **A fragment, not a query param.** Records are search params because a record is something
  the *server* resolves; a block is a position inside an already-resolved document, which is
  what fragments are for. It also keeps the fabric honest for free: a link to a block still
  parses as a link to the doc, so one backlink per document, not one per paragraph.
- **Scan, don't select.** The id arrives from a URL, so `[data-block-id="…"]` would let a
  quote character break the selector. The rows are scanned and compared instead — verified
  with a deliberately hostile id.
- **Arriving does not select.** A real selection would mean the next Backspace deletes the
  block you were sent to look at.

### A dead DS token, found by its first caller

`--animate-flash-highlight` had existed with **zero users** and was tinted
`--color-berry-alpha-20`, which the generated palette resolves to *paper at 20%* — a
near-white wash on a near-white page. It is `--sel-block` now, the wash a swept block
already wears, so arriving reads as that block being pointed at.

Reduced motion needed its own line: the global reset collapses every animation to `0.01ms`,
which would have left those readers with **no signal at all** rather than a calmer one. They
get the same wash, held flat for the same 1200ms and cleared by the same timeout.

### Verified

977 tests (+19), `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every file touched, production build green
(and the flash rule survives it — Tailwind does not purge the plain class).

In the browser, against a fresh dev server, measured rather than eyeballed:

| case | result |
|---|---|
| cold load `#block-b-filler-20` | arrives scrolled, block in view; **no element carries that `id`**, so it was our code and not the browser |
| in-app request | scroll 0 → 2509, flash on at 40ms, off between 900 and 1400ms (1200ms timer) |
| block folded inside a collapsed toggle | not rendered before · toggle opened, row rendered, scrolled, flashed |
| id not in the document | no scroll, no flash, **no error** |
| id containing `"] , [data-block-id` | no effect, no error |
| same block twice | second request restarts the flash (the reflow) |
| menu | "Copy link to block" sits after Duplicate; typing `permalink` finds it; Enter runs it |
| copied value | `http://localhost:3007/documents?page=9f8b…#block-b-filler-6` |
| toast | "Link to block copied." |

**The dev-server trap, again.** The already-running server served a **stale CSS chunk**: the
same content hash across edits, an untouched `touch`, and `.block-anchor-flash` simply absent
while `.block-row textarea::placeholder` two lines above it was present. Next 16 refuses a
second `next dev` in one directory, so verification ran in a scratch copy with a hard-linked
`node_modules` — and there the rule compiled correctly. **Asserting the rule exists in the
served CSS is the check**; asserting that the file on disk contains it proves nothing.

**Owed:** the same-document click path is verified in parts, not end to end — `resolveLink`
keeps the fragment (tested), and the editor answers `zb:block-anchor` (measured in the
browser) — because the harness cannot host `/documents`, which needs a session.

## 2026-08-06 — Block comments (§7H). **Migration 0037 — yours to paste.**

The plan's own scoring (v2.6) says Zenboard is "furthest behind on the document substrate"
and names three blockers against Notion: blocks-as-rows, block comments, synced blocks. The
first shipped this morning. This is the second.

### It started as a feature and turned out to be a data-loss fix

A document's comments are an array inside `pages.content`, written by the document's own
autosave. Three consequences, and the third is not a limitation:

1. They are page-level only — there is no way to say "this paragraph".
2. Two tabs editing one page overwrite each other's comments; the whole blob is the unit of write.
3. **`restoreVersion` overwrites `content` wholesale, so restoring any old version silently
   reverts — or deletes — every comment on the page.** A history feature must never destroy
   something the history is not about.

This is the lesson `lib/acceptance.ts` already learned about signatures, arriving a second
time: a fact somebody asserted cannot live inside a blob the owner's autosave rewrites.

### What shipped

- **`supabase/migrations/0037_comments.sql`** — one table, anchored to `(page_id, block_id)`.
- **`lib/comments.ts`** — the rules, pure and tested: thread grouping, resolve, orphans, the
  legacy adapter.
- **`lib/actions/comments.ts`** — gated on `commentsSupported()`.
- **`components/documents/comment-thread.tsx`** — one `<Thread>`, drawn under a block and
  under the page. `<DocThreads>` replaced the forked page-level widget, which is gone.
- **`use-doc-comments.ts`** — one hook, optimistic with real rollback.
- **"Comment" in the block menu, and ⌘⇧M** — Notion's own shortcut, so the muscle memory carries.

### This is still not "blocks as rows"

`block_id` is **text with no foreign key**, for the same reason `mentions.target_id` has
none: the thing it points at is not a row. Anchoring only ever needed a stable block id, and
blocks have had one since the editor was written. What is left of the plan's structural item
is genuinely just synced blocks.

### Three decisions worth arguing with

- **A thread is a `thread_id`, not an anchor.** Two questions about the same paragraph are two
  conversations, and resolving one must not resolve the other. One uuid column buys that.
- **Inline, not a rail.** Notion opens block comments in a right-hand rail on a wide window.
  Ours is always inline under the block: the reading layout has no spare column below `xl`, so
  a rail would be the exception rather than the rule, and a comment read three inches from its
  paragraph is a footnote. The *lifecycle* is what we take from Notion — open, reply, resolve.
- **Resolved is not deleted.** A resolved thread leaves the document and stays reachable behind
  a disclosure. If those two collapse into one act, nobody ever resolves anything.

### The browser changed the design

The archived list first held resolved threads **and** orphans, so the disclosure read
**"Show 3 resolved" when one of the three was an orphan** — untrue, and worse than untrue: it
filed an *unanswered* question under a heading claiming it had been answered. An orphan now
falls back to the page as an OPEN thread (the page is the only place left that can hold it),
and `archivedThreads` is resolved-only, so the count names exactly what it holds. That was
not visible in the types or the tests; it was visible in the label.

### Verified

996 tests (+19), `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every file touched, production build green.
In the browser, against a fresh dev server, with the real components and the real rules over
an in-memory store:

| case | result |
|---|---|
| block with an open thread | drawn inline under the block, both comments, Reply · Resolve |
| block whose thread is resolved | nothing in the body |
| block with nothing to say | nothing at all |
| resolve | leaves the body; count 1 → 2; reopen puts it back |
| **delete the block under a live thread** | thread survives, labelled "On a block that has since been deleted." |
| block menu | "Comment ⌘⇧M" above Duplicate; keyword `discuss` finds it; Enter runs it |
| ⌘⇧M with the caret in a block | opens the composer |
| empty comment | Enter posts nothing, no send button |
| reply | joins the same thread — one section, three comments |
| delete one comment | the thread survives |
| ⇧Enter | new line, does not post |
| 375px | thread wraps inside the column, no sideways scroll |

**Owed, in one line: paste `supabase/migrations/0037_comments.sql`.** Until then
`commentsSupported()` is false, the "Comment" action does not appear, and the document falls
back to exactly today's page-level comments — which are still read after the migration too, so
nothing anyone has written is lost in either direction.

Also owed: the **server** path (`addComment` / `setThreadResolved` / `deleteComment`) is
covered by types and by the gate, not by a live write, because there is no session in the
harness and no table yet in the database.
