# 2026-08-06 — The morning digest (§7O channel 2): the last notification channel

**No migration.** Settings live in `profiles.preferences.digest`, jsonb.

§7O describes exactly three channels: the in-app bell, time reminders, and a morning
digest. The first two shipped (2026-07-26 and 2026-08-03/04). This is the third, and with
it §7O is closed.

## The argument the code follows

§7O opens by saying notifications are how calm products become anxious ones, then concedes
that zero signal fails too. Every rule here falls out of that one sentence:

- **Opt-in, never opt-out.** A product that starts emailing you daily because you signed up
  is the thing that section exists to argue against. `enabled` defaults false and only a
  person turns it on. `enabled: 'yes'` and `enabled: 1` are both read as **off** — a
  truthy-but-not-true value must not switch on a daily email. Asserted.
- **At most one a day, near the hour you chose, in YOUR timezone.** "Send at 08:00" means
  *their* 08:00; a worker using its own clock mails an IST user at 13:30 and calls it
  morning.
- **Late means dropped, not queued.** `DIGEST_WINDOW_MINUTES = 180`. A digest arriving at
  18:00 because a worker was down all morning is not a digest — "due today" read at six in
  the evening is an accusation. Same shape as the reminder worker's `WORKER_MAX_LATE_MS`.
- **Nothing to say means nothing is sent.** `digestEmail` returns **null** rather than
  padding. A daily email reading "nothing today" every Tuesday is unread on the Tuesday
  that matters. A capacity line alone does not qualify; neither does blocked work alone —
  three tasks stuck behind someone else is not a morning worth interrupting. A single
  client request does qualify.
- **Vacation is a DATE, not a toggle**, because a toggle is what you forget to switch back,
  and then the product is quietly broken in a way that looks like it is working. §7C and
  §7O both name vacation mode; this is its first implementation.

**The body order deliberately differs from §7O's own listing.** The plan lists "due today,
overdue, waiting-on, portal activity", which reads as an inventory. The email leads with
**today**, carrying the capacity line, then what is late, then what is stuck, then what
arrived. Leading an email with overdue work is precisely the framing §7O's first sentence
rejects. Sections cap at seven items and then count — a digest that lists forty overdue
tasks is a backlog report, and nobody acts on a backlog report before breakfast.

The capacity line from the previous sprint rides beside today's list and nowhere else: it
is a claim about today's list. That is what makes this a **plan** rather than a summary,
and it is the one thing Sunsama's daily email cannot do, because Sunsama mails the plan you
already made whereas this arrives before it.

## Two defects the live probe caught, one of them fatal

The reminders sprint established the rule: **always pair a probe with a must-fail control.**
Doing that here paid for itself twice.

**1. The must-fail control did not fail.** A deliberately bogus jsonb path —
`preferences->nosuch->>enabled=eq.true` — answered **200 with `[]`**, identical to a correct
path matching nobody. A missing key is NULL and `NULL = true` is merely false, so a typo in
the candidate filter would have meant this endpoint reported healthy forever while nobody
ever received a digest.

Fixed by **removing the query filter entirely**. `readDigestPrefs` makes the same decision,
is pure, and has tests; the query was already fetching the two columns it needed. The
response now also reports `scanned`, so `scanned: 6, considered: 6, off: 6` says "ran, and
nobody has opted in" while `scanned: 0` says the query is broken — previously the two were
the same JSON.

**2. The claim would have blocked the first digest for every account, forever.** The obvious
guard is `.neq('preferences->digest->>lastSent', today)`. But `lastSent` is absent until the
first digest ever goes out, and `NULL <> '2026-08-06'` is NULL, not true — so it matches no
row. Measured against the live database: the bare form matched **0 of 6** profiles; the
`or(is.null, neq)` form matched **6**. The same NULL exclusion reproduces on
`preferences->>timezone`, a key really set on only 3 of 6 rows — which is a far better
control than the bogus path was, because it is real data behaving the same way.

Silent, in production, on the first send. `tsc` could not see it and no unit test could
either; only asking the database could.

## Verified

930 tests (+33), `tsc` clean, lint **19 → 19** with no file worse.

Live against the running app:

| request | result |
|---|---|
| `GET` | `405` |
| `POST`, no header | `401` |
| `POST`, wrong secret | `401` |
| `POST`, correct secret | `200 {"scanned":6,"considered":6,"claimed":0,"sent":0,"empty":0,"skipped":{"off":6,…}}` |

Browser: `?section=notifications` deep-links to the pane; switching the digest off collapses
the send-time row (the pane never shows a control you cannot act on); "7 days" renders
"Silent through 12 Aug", matching `vacationThrough('2026-08-06', 7)` exactly; the harness's
"Couldn't save" confirms the error path renders too.

## Owed

**Not verified end to end: a digest actually arriving.** That needs opting a real account in
and mailing a real person, which is not something to do unasked. The projection has 33 unit
tests, the auth and skip paths are verified live, and both database expressions were probed
against the real schema.

The scheduler needs a second line (`/api/cron/digest`); `SETUP.md` has it.

**Written down, not started:** §7C also promises vacation mode pauses *rituals and habit
streaks without loss*. Only the digest half exists — the habits half belongs to §7G and is
its own sprint. `lib/digest.ts` reads a single `vacationUntil` that both halves can share.

---

# 2026-08-06 — Vacation mode, the other two thirds (§7C)

**No migration.** Same `preferences.digest.vacationUntil` the digest pane already writes.

The digest sprint shipped vacation's silencing half and recorded the rest as owed. §7C
promises more than silence: vacation "pause[s] rituals + habit streaks **without loss**".

`lib/vacation.ts` is now the one rule, and `lib/digest.ts` delegates to it — vacation was
never digest-specific, it just happened to be built there first.

## "Without loss" is the half that matters

Silencing is easy. The promise is that a week away does not cost a 90-day streak — **and
does not credit you with days you did not do**. A vacation day is neither kept nor broken:
it is not *judged*.

That is exactly what `skipped` has always meant to `lib/habit-schedule.ts`. **That parameter
has existed since habits v2 and nothing in the app has ever passed anything into it** — a
designed seam with no caller. Vacation is its first one, so this needed no new streak logic
at all, only the right set handed to the function that was already waiting for it.

Proven both ways in one test: done daily to the 1st, away the 2nd–8th, done again the 9th —
**streak 1 without vacation, 8 with it**; and seven days away with nothing done before them
is still **0**, not 7.

`vacationDaysIn` is bounded by the caller's window (habits already fetch 120 days), so a
vacation date set to 2099 cannot make the streak walk 26,000 days. The guard is the window,
never the stored value.

## Rituals

Home's plan/shutdown prompts go quiet while away. **`/rituals` stays perfectly reachable** —
someone who wants to plan a day mid-holiday is not stopped, they are simply not asked. §7C
calls rituals "skippable (we're calm, not Sunsama-strict)"; asking someone to plan a day
they told you they are not working is the product failing to hear its own setting.

## Verified

944 tests (+14), `tsc` clean, no new lint. Browser: `?h=8` shows the plan prompt,
`?h=8&vacation=1` does not, and the page otherwise renders unchanged.

Found in passing: my own test fixture hit `toISOString().slice(0, 10)` — **the fourth
appearance of that trap** — and silently described the wrong week until the assertion caught
it. Fixed to build from `addDaysISO`.

## Owed

Nothing. §7C's vacation clause is now complete across all three surfaces it names.

# 2026-08-06 — The automations doctrine page, made true (§7P)

**No migration.** `lib/automations.ts` + the Settings → Automations pane.

§7P's argument is that automation builders create haunted houses — rules someone wrote in
March firing mysteriously in November — so Zenboard ships **named, designed behaviours and
no rule builder**. That deal only holds if the written-down list of what runs behind your
back is short, fixed, and *true*.

It was not. The pane was wrong in two directions at once:

- It listed four **§7Q clerk** moments (triage, drafts, Recall, digest) under an **§7P**
  heading. Those are different doctrines; §7P is "designed behaviours, no builder", §7Q is
  the AI clerk.
- Every row read **"Planned"** — including the morning digest, which had shipped that
  morning — while **six behaviours that really do run** were not mentioned at all. The
  section heading was "What it *will* handle".

## What changed

`lib/automations.ts` is the list, next to the code it describes. Nine entries, each naming
its trigger *in the user's words*, what it deliberately does not do, and the file that
implements it. All six `on` entries were verified against the code before being claimed.

**Status is three-valued, and that is the point.** `gated` is not a synonym for planned: a
gated behaviour is fully built and starts working the moment its migration is applied.
Calling the timebox twin or reminders "Planned" would be as wrong as calling them "On" — so
they read **Ready**, with one line explaining what that means. The app already knew this
difference (it is what the capability probes are for); the doctrine page knows it now too.

The section heading is present tense — "What it does — 5 running" — and the count is
**derived**, so it cannot go stale the way "Planned" did.

## Kept honest by a test

A page that documents the product cannot be checked by a type, so `lib/automations.test.ts`
does it: every non-planned entry's `source` must be a file that exists, every `gated` entry
must name a migration that is present in `supabase/migrations`, and every trigger must be
phrased in the user's words (`When…` / `At…` / `Once…`, never `on task.updated`).

That test immediately earned itself: it rejected the first version of the data, where
`source` mixed file paths with function names (`lib/actions/portal.ts · approveRequest`)
and so could not be walked. Split into `source` (paths, checkable) and `fn` (the entry
point). A doctrine file whose references cannot be verified is the same failure as the page
it replaced, one level down.

## Verified

952 tests (+8), `tsc` clean, no new lint. Browser: the pane renders "What it does — 5
running" with On / Ready / Planned badges and the clerk listed separately.

## Owed

**§7P also promises each behaviour is "toggleable, with visible provenance"** — a switch per
behaviour and a "created by: Recurrence" line on the objects they touch. Neither exists.
That is a real gap, deliberately not started here: provenance touches every module's
activity line, and it is a larger sprint than making the page honest. Recorded rather than
half-built.

# 2026-08-15 — Published forms were crashing, and completed tasks now settle

Two reported defects, both fixed.

## 1. Every published form link returned a 500

`lib/forms.ts` incremented the view counter like this:

```ts
void (svc as unknown as { rpc: (fn, args) => Promise<unknown> })
  .rpc('increment_form_views', …)
  .catch(() => {});
```

PostgREST's `rpc()` returns a **`PostgrestFilterBuilder`** — a *thenable*, with
`.then()` and **no `.catch()`**. So the line threw `svc.rpc(...).catch is not a function`
synchronously during the server render, on **every load of every published form**. The
counter whose own comment says it "must never stop someone from filling the form" was the
only thing stopping them.

**The cast is what hid it.** `as unknown as { … Promise<unknown> }` told the compiler a
lie and the compiler believed it. The fix is one word inside the cast: the honest type is
`PromiseLike<unknown>`, which has `.then` and nothing else — so the compiler now *rejects*
`.catch()` outright and this mistake cannot be repeated here. `Promise.resolve()` adopts
the thenable to get a real promise with a real rejection path.

Verified end to end against the live database: form renders → filled → submitted →
"Thank you." page → the response row lands with status `complete`, and `view_count` goes
2 → 3, which proves the RPC now actually runs (before, it threw before reaching it).

Two of my own probes were wrong on the way and are worth recording: I read HTTP 200 as
"working" when the "this form isn't available" page is also 200, and I tested with a token
I had truncated to 14 characters when printing it. Both made the bug look like something
it was not (a production-only env problem). The dev-overlay's "script tag" warning was a
symptom of the crashed page, not a second defect.

## 2. Completed tasks now settle into a collapsed group

Ticking a task off used to remove it from the list instantly, which loses the moment of
satisfaction, makes a misclick hard to undo, and jumps the rows under a finger already
moving to the next one.

Now: the row **stays exactly where it is, struck through, for 3 seconds**, then settles
into a collapsed **Completed (n)** group. Tick it back inside those 3 seconds and nothing
ever moved. Expand the group and un-tick and it returns to the active list at once — no
beat on the way back, because you already know where it is going.

`lib/use-settling.ts` is the hook and `splitSettled` the single split, so the active and
completed sections can never disagree about who owns a row — the failure two independent
`.filter()` calls drift into. `components/tasks/completed-section.tsx` is the one
disclosure. Home had a second hand-rolled version that said "3 completed" while the
project list would have said "Completed (3)"; it now uses the shared one.

**Benchmark.** Google Tasks waits ~2s then collapses — the behaviour copied here, at the
3s asked for. Things 3 defers reordering until you leave the list, calmer but a finished
task can sit in place for minutes. Todoist removes it immediately with an undo toast,
which is the version that loses the row under your finger. No toast here, no confetti.

Collapsed by default and not persisted: what you finished is a record, not a working list,
and a list that reopens with twenty struck-through rows has undone the point. The count
rides on the summary so it answers "did I get anything done?" while shut. Reduced motion
is already honoured globally.

## Verified

1004 tests (+8), `tsc` clean, no new lint. In the browser, sampled inside one execution
because a tool round-trip is longer than the 3s beat:

| | Completed | holding | still in list |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | 1 | 0 | yes |
| +0.4s | 1 | 1 | yes |
| +1.6s | 1 | 1 | yes |
| +3.8s | 2 | 0 | no |

Un-tick inside the beat: nothing moves. Un-tick from the expanded group: back in the
active list immediately. Same on Home and on the project Tasks tab.

## Owed

The Week board and the portal task list still remove a completed task immediately — they
have no Completed group at all, so wiring them is a small follow-on rather than a change
to this behaviour. Recorded, not started.

# 2026-08-15 — Lists became real, the board became a board, Focus became a mode, and Forms grew two tabs

Five sprints against one request: make Tasks feel like Google Tasks without stopping being
Zenboard, then make Forms feel like Tally.

## 1. Lists are their own thing now (migration 0038, gated)

The Tasks rail had a section headed **List** and every row under it was a **project**. That
was a lie told by a label, and it cost something real: the only way to have a pile called
"Priority" was to invent a project, and a project shows up in the projects gallery, the
Finance rollup and the client portal. Making a bucket for your own errands polluted three
modules.

`supabase/migrations/0038_task_lists.sql` gives lists their own table plus `tasks.list_id`.
A task may be in a project, in a list, in both, or in neither — they answer different
questions ("whose work is this?" vs "which pile do I keep it in?") and neither is derived
from the other. `ON DELETE SET NULL`, so deleting a list never deletes the work in it.

**`lib/task-scopes.ts` is the one vocabulary**, and it holds three rules that are
deliberately *different from each other* — the whole reason it exists as a file:

| rule | question | answer |
|---|---|---|
| `taskScopes` | which piles is this task in? | all of them (membership) |
| `columnKey` | which board column draws it? | exactly one — the list wins over the project |
| `isHidden` | is it silenced by the sidebar? | yes if **any** pile it is in is off |

Rule 2 and rule 3 disagreeing is the point. A Life-studio task filed under Priority is drawn
in the *Priority* column, but switching **Life studio** off still has to silence it — "when
turned off, its tasks should not appear" is a statement about the task, not about its column.
23 tests, and the browser confirmed it: hiding Balluji removed both its tasks, including the
one whose column was a list.

Gated the house way. Two probes, not one — the table and the column are added by the same
migration file, but a half-applied migration is exactly the state this pattern exists to
survive, and selecting a column that isn't there fails the *whole* query. Until you paste
the DDL, the Lists section is simply absent and Tasks behaves as it did before.

## 2. Sidebar toggles: the checkbox IS the colour swatch

Every project and list row leads with a checkbox tinted in that pile's own colour, answering
two questions with one control — *which pile is this?* and *is it showing?* That is Google
Calendar's calendar list, and it is why the rail needs no separate dot beside the box.

Persisted to `profiles.preferences`, not localStorage: it follows you between machines the
way Google Tasks' checkboxes do, the route reads it server-side so the **first paint** is
already correct, and reading localStorage during render is the exact shape of hydration
mismatch this codebase has been bitten by before.

**A bug I introduced and then caught in the browser.** `hiddenScopes = []` as a default
parameter builds a *new array every render*, and `useServerState` compares with `Object.is`.
A fresh identity reads as "the server sent something new", so it set state during render,
which restarted the render, which built another new array — an infinite loop that also wiped
the toggle the user had just flipped. The symptom was that the checkbox worked and then
silently undid itself. Module-level constants fixed it; the note is in both files.

## 3. The board is a board

`?view=board` draws one column per pile — Google Tasks' layout — with a quick add at the top
of each, drag between columns to re-file, and a collapsed **Completed (n)** at each foot.
It is a *pane inside `TasksView`*, not a second page, because the rail, the header, the
filter and every mutation already live there; a parallel page would need its own copy of all
five, which is the split that broke this module once already.

Dropping onto a **project** column also clears the list. It has to: the list wins the column,
so leaving it set would spring the card straight back where it came from. Dropping onto a
**list** column leaves the project alone — quietly un-filing the client work would lose the
one fact that decides who gets billed. Both verified by dragging in the browser.

The layout switch stays two options. The week board is a *board* — the same cards in columns
cut by day instead of by pile — so it lives behind the board glyph with a **Lists · Week**
grouping control beside it, rather than being a third peer that makes you choose between
"board" and "board".

Fixed in passing, in the sprint's own area: `week-view.tsx` re-seeded from the server inside
an effect, which painted last week's columns for a frame on every navigation. It reconciles
during render now, and `orderRef` is re-pointed at drag start — where it only ever needed to
be current.

## 4. Completed tasks settle in Tasks too

The Tasks list was still filtering `!t.done` before drawing, which is precisely what made a
row vanish under the finger that ticked it. It now uses the same `useSettling` +
`CompletedSection` as Home and the project tabs. Measured in one execution: the row holds at
0.2s, 0.8s, 1.5s, 2.2s and 2.9s, and by 3.3s it is gone and the group reads
`Completed, 2 tasks`.

## 5. Focus is a mode, not a page

Focus used to change the centre and leave every piece of chrome where it was — the full
sidebar, search, the rituals link, the bell, the timer, + New. **Eleven ways to leave,
arranged around a screen whose entire premise is not leaving.** A mode that only dims the
middle is not a mode.

Now: no sidebar, no bottom tabs, no floating timer, and a header carrying one control — the
Focus toggle, because a door you cannot find is a trap rather than a focus aid. `/focus` and
below, via `lib/focus-mode.ts`, which is a function rather than `startsWith('/focus')` so the
day someone adds `/focus-settings` it doesn't strip the chrome off a page that never asked.

Focus also *shows today's tasks* now. "Up next" existed only inside a ⋮ menu, so a mode whose
whole promise is "show me what I have to do today" showed exactly one task and hid the rest
behind an unlabelled button. And finishing everything no longer says "Your task list is
empty" — that sentence is for a day with nothing on it, not for a day you cleared.

## 6. Forms: Insights and Share became places

`lib/form-insights.ts` is the one projection, and it writes down what each number honestly
means. The important one: **completion is `completed ÷ starts`, never ÷ visits.** Visits are
a coarse +1 per render — they include you testing your own link and double-count a refresh —
so dividing by them would quietly punish a form for being opened. 16 tests.

- **Insights** (new tab): Visits · Responses · Unique people · Median time, a sentence
  instead of a fifth card for the ratio, where people stop, then every answer under its
  question. Tally's shape, minus its visits-over-time chart — we store a counter, not
  per-visit timestamps, and a chart drawn from data we do not have is a lie with axes.
- **Share** (new tab): it was a modal opened from the Build tab, so the one thing you come
  back for was behind a button on a page you had finished with. Link, embed snippet, rotate
  (confirmed — it kills every link already sent), and the portal switch.
- **Responses** is now just the table, and it finally draws inside `FormChrome`. It used to
  build its own full-height page with its own back arrow, so walking to Responses made the
  form's tabs disappear.
- **The builder** now has tabs at all. It was the one tab you spend all your time on and the
  one tab with no tabs — and it carried a *second* Settings surface, a 300px rail duplicating
  the Settings tab. The rail is gone; its logic summary moved onto the page, under the
  questions it describes.

Tabs read **Responses**, not Tally's "Submissions": this app has one word for the thing
(`form_responses`, `ResponseRecord`, the hub's count) and adding a synonym for one screen is
how a glossary rots.

## Verified

1048 tests (+44), `tsc` clean, no new lint errors. Browser: the rail's two sections and their
toggles, the board's five columns and two drags, the settle timing, Focus's three states,
and all five form tabs.

## Owed

- **Paste `supabase/migrations/0038_task_lists.sql`.** Until then the Lists section is hidden
  and the board groups by project only — nothing breaks.
- **Integrations was not built.** The reference has that tab and I did not ship it, because
  the only honest contents would be a webhook (needs a table and a delivery worker) or
  auto-task/email-on-submission (needs wiring into the submit path). A tab of switches that
  do nothing is worse than no tab. It is the next Forms sprint.
- The stripped Focus **shell** is covered by `lib/focus-mode.ts`'s tests and by reading; the
  dev-preview harness cannot exercise it, because the mode is derived from the real pathname
  and the harness is not at `/focus`. It wants one signed-in look.
- The Week board and the portal task list still remove a completed task immediately.

### Correction, same day — the form tabs were in the wrong place

Shipped them in the header row and it read as a toolbar: back arrow, title, five
tab labels, status badge and the verbs, all on one 44px line. At five sections that
row has no air left, and the eye cannot separate "where am I" from "what can I do"
when both sit shoulder to shoulder at the same size.

Projects had already solved this and Forms had not: a record is a title, then a
FULL-WIDTH UNDERLINE ROW of sections, then the body. The tab strip gets its own
line and reads as navigation because it spans the page. `FormChrome` follows that
now — which is also what `DESIGN_CONSTITUTION` says in one line ("no pill tab bars
with 5+ items"), a rule Forms only started breaking when it reached five.

Two things fixed with it: the wrapper was adding a second `border-b` and a second
x-scroller on top of the ones the DS `Tabs` already brings, drawing two hairlines a
pixel apart; and the response count was glued into the tab's label string, so the
sliding underline measured the number as part of the word and ran under it. It is
the DS `count` chip now.

# 2026-08-15 — "Everything takes 6–8 seconds": measured, then cut

Not guessed. The dev server prints its own timings, and they name three separate
costs that had been added together into one complaint.

## What the log actually said

```
GET /forms/…/share    200 in 7.6s  (next.js: 4.5s, application-code: 3.2s)   ← first hit after an edit
GET /forms/…/share    200 in 573ms (next.js: 4ms,  application-code: 569ms)  ← warm
GET /forms/…/share    200 in 587ms (next.js: 22ms, application-code: 565ms)  ← warm, AGAIN
GET /projects         200 in 2.4s  (next.js: 101ms, application-code: 2.3s)
```

Three things, and only two of them are ours:

1. **`next.js: 4.5s` is Turbopack compiling the route.** It happens once per route
   after a code change, in development only. It does not exist in a production
   build, and no amount of query tuning touches it. A large part of the "6–8
   seconds" is this, which is why the same click is 573ms the second time.
2. **Every tab click was rendering the page TWICE.** Look at the pair above:
   identical route, back to back, same cost. That is a 2× multiplier on every
   navigation through a tab or a segmented control.
3. **`application-code: 2.3s` on /projects is real work** — and almost none of it
   was rendering. It was round trips, in series.

## 1. The double render

Radix's `Tabs` and `RadioGroup` — our `Tabs` and `SegmentedControl` — activate
**automatically**: `onValueChange` fires when a trigger takes focus and again
when it is clicked. Normally the second call is suppressed, because by then the
controlled value has changed. But these controls are controlled by **the URL**,
and the URL does not change until the navigation lands. So the click handler
still saw the old value, still believed it was a change, and pushed the same
route a second time.

`lib/use-nav-once.ts` remembers the one destination in flight. It is not a
debounce and has no timer: arrowing along a tab strip still navigates to each tab
in turn, and only a repeat of the *same* destination is dropped. The decision is
a pure function (`decideNav`) with 7 tests, because this repo has no React test
renderer and a guard that quietly stopped working would put the double render
back with nothing failing.

## 2. /projects — nine serial waves, and the tasks table read four times

```
tasks(…16 columns…)        ← the real read
tasks(id, status)          ← wave 3, for one column
tasks(id, section_id)      ← wave 6, for one column
tasks(id, client_visible)  ← wave 7, for one column
```

Each split had a good reason written above it — *"fetched separately so the
critical tasks fetch never depends on a column a migration might not have added
yet"* — and each cost a full ~220ms round trip, paid by every account including
the ones where all three columns exist.

**The gate is a retry now, not a split.** Ask for everything; if the database
refuses, fall back to the base columns and go and get the optional ones the old
way. A migrated account pays one query. An unmigrated one pays what it used to.
Same guarantee, one wave.

The other lever was noticing which queries only *looked* dependent:
`form_responses` was fetched with `.in('form_id', …)` after the forms came back,
but RLS already scopes that table to this user — asking for all of them is the
same answer and needs nothing to arrive first. Nine waves → two.

## 3. /tasks — the table read twice, plus a probe in front of everything

Six waves, two of which read the whole `tasks` table: once to count the rail's
three numbers, once for the list itself. **`TasksView` already computes those
counts from `tasks` in a `useMemo`** — the second full-table read was feeding a
prop the component recalculated for itself. Only the week board needs it, because
it loads a seven-day window and genuinely cannot derive them.

Two more: subtask counts were keyed on the ids of the tasks just loaded, but
"every subtask in this space" is the same answer when the parents are every task
in the space — so it stopped waiting. And the `list_id` capability probe from
this morning's sprint was a round trip sitting in front of the entire page; it is
a retry now, like the rest. Six waves → one.

## 4. Forms — 500 rows to render one integer

Every section prints the response count in its tab bar, and each was getting it
by pulling up to 500 whole response rows — answers, uploads, metadata — and
calling `.length`. On a form with real traffic that is the heaviest query on the
page, run again on every tab click. `countFormResponses` uses `head: true`, which
sends no rows at all. The routes also stopped awaiting the form and the count in
series when neither needs the other.

## Verified

1055 tests (+7), `tsc` clean, no new lint errors.

## Owed

I cannot time the signed-in routes myself — the browser pane has no session — so
the before figures above are from the running dev server's own log and the after
figures need one pass of clicking around to confirm. Watch the same log: the
pairs should be gone, and `application-code` on /projects and /tasks should fall
to roughly one round trip.

Still open, and the real ceiling: every one of these routes is `force-dynamic`,
so a navigation is always a server round trip. Notion feels instant because it
reads a local store and syncs behind you. That is an architecture change, not a
tuning pass, and it is the next thing worth planning.

---

# 2026-08-15 — Navigation stopped being data fetching (Tasks)

## What Notion actually does, since that is the target

Notion is not fast because its queries are fast. It is fast because **clicking
something is not a network operation.** The architecture, in the order it
matters:

1. **The app loads once.** One shell, one JS bundle, one authentication.
2. **Records live in a local store**, normalised and keyed by id. Every view
   reads from that store synchronously.
3. **Navigation is a change of what you are looking at**, not a request. If the
   records for the next page are already in the store, the paint is immediate.
   The server is asked only for records you do not have.
4. **Edits apply locally first** and are queued as transactions sent behind you.
   The queue survives a reload.
5. **The store is persisted** (IndexedDB), so even a cold reload paints before
   the network answers.

Zenboard is the exact inverse: every route is `force-dynamic`, so every click is
a server render. And the cruellest instance of it was on Tasks — clicking
"Today" in the rail **re-fetched every task you own, in order to draw a subset of
the tasks the browser was already holding**, then threw away the component and
remounted it, losing scroll position and any open menu with it.

That is not a tuning problem. It is a category error: a filter was implemented as
a navigation.

## What shipped: step 1 of 3

The rail (Inbox · Today · Completed · any project · any list), the Filter menu,
the label filter, and the List⇄Board switch are all questions the browser can
already answer. They now answer them.

The URL stays the single source of truth — linkable, shareable, Back and Forward
work — but it changes with `window.history.pushState`, which the Next docs
shipped in this repo describe as integrating with the router and syncing
`useSearchParams` **without a server request**. `lib/use-url-state.ts` is the one
seam; it deliberately derives from the URL rather than mirroring it into
`useState`, because two copies of the same fact drift and the drift here would be
the Back button disagreeing with the screen.

Three things had to go with it:
- **The route's `key`.** It was keyed on the rail combo, which is what forced the
  remount. The server sends the DATA; what the URL says about it is the client's
  business.
- **The `view`/`scope`/`filter` props.** The component reads them itself now.
- **`viewSwitch` passed down from the route.** A server component cannot hand
  down a control that flips state it does not own, so the layout switch and the
  board's grouping are rendered inside the view.

`?view=week` stays a real navigation, and should: the week board loads a
different seven-day window, and pretending otherwise would paint an empty board.
The rule is written on the hook — **shallow when the answer is already in memory,
real when it is not.**

## Measured

In the browser, with `fetch` counted and a `PerformanceObserver` on resources:

| action | requests before | requests now |
|---|---|---|
| Today → Priority → Inbox → Balluji (4 rail clicks) | 4 server renders | **0** |
| List → Board → List | 2 server renders | **0** |

Back after three rail clicks returns to `?scope=list:L1` with the right rows, so
history is intact. 1061 tests (+6), `tsc` clean, no new lint errors.

## What is left, honestly

This fixed Tasks' internal navigation. It did NOT fix:

- **Module to module** (Tasks → Projects → Tasks) is still a full server render
  every time, including the second time. **Step 2** is a client cache: keep what
  a route returned, paint from it instantly on return, revalidate behind the
  user. Next's Router Cache used to do some of this and no longer does for
  dynamic routes, so this wants an explicit store.
- **Edits** still round-trip through server actions and `router.refresh()`.
  **Step 3** is the mutation queue: apply locally, sync behind, survive reload.
  That is the one that makes the app feel like Notion rather than merely faster
  than it was.

Steps 2 and 3 are real projects, not tuning passes. Step 1 was the one that could
be done without changing how the whole app stores data — and it is also the one
the complaint was actually about.

# 2026-08-15 — Step 2: the browser keeps what it already fetched

Step 1 stopped Tasks from asking the server about things it already knew. Step 2
is the other half: **going to a page you were just on should not cost anything
either.**

## The finding

`experimental.staleTimes.dynamic` **defaults to 0 since Next 15** — meaning a
dynamic page is never reused. Every route here is `force-dynamic`, so Tasks →
Projects → Tasks re-rendered the whole page on the server *both* times, for data
that had not changed. The browser had the answer and threw it away.

Setting it to 30 makes the return visit paint instantly from the Client Cache.

## Why that alone would have been dishonest

A cache without a correction is just a way to be wrong quickly. Within that
30-second window, a page could show a task you finished two minutes ago as
unfinished, and nothing would ever put it right.

So the cache is half the pattern. The other half is **noticing that what you are
looking at came out of a cache, and quietly going to get the truth** — which is
exactly what Notion does, and the reason it feels instant without feeling stale.

`app/(app)/template.tsx` stamps every render with the server's clock (a template,
not a layout: a layout persists across navigations and would carry the FIRST
render's timestamp forever). The stamp is baked into the cached RSC payload, so
its AGE is a direct read of "did this come from a cache?" — no Next internals, no
guessing, nothing that breaks when the router changes. `RevalidateOnStale` reads
it and refreshes behind the user when it is old.

Two details that matter:
- **2 seconds of grace.** A network hop plus hydration on a slow connection can
  be most of a second; calling that "cached" would refetch every first visit,
  which is the double render this codebase just spent a sprint removing.
- **A future timestamp counts as fresh.** Clock skew between server and browser
  would otherwise refetch, arrive still-skewed, and refetch again.

## On naming an impure function rather than silencing the compiler

`Date.now()` written inline in the template was correctly flagged by
`react-hooks/purity`. That rule is about CLIENT re-renders needing to be
idempotent; this is a Server Component rendering once per request, where reading
the wall clock is the whole point. It moved into `lib/render-stamp.ts` as
`serverRenderedAt()`, with the reasoning written down — the difference between an
exception that has a reason and an exception that has a `eslint-disable` over it.

## Verified

**A production build succeeds** — the real check that the template and the config
change do not break anything, and it lists all 40 routes including the four new
form sections. 1067 tests (+6), `tsc` clean, no new lint errors (the 11 remaining
are all pre-existing, in files this work never touched).

From the running dev log during the session, `/tasks?view=week` settled at
**212ms · 223ms · 228ms** after the one-wave rewrite, against 400–900ms before
and a stretch of ten-second renders earlier in the day.

## Still owed

- The end-to-end feel needs one signed-in pass: I cannot drive an authenticated
  navigation from here.
- **Step 3 — the mutation queue — is not built.** Edits still round-trip through
  server actions and `router.refresh()`. Applying locally, syncing behind, and
  surviving a reload is what turns "much faster" into "instant", and it is a
  project rather than a pass.
- Unrelated but worth saying: the red **"1 Issue"** badge in the dev overlay is a
  browser EXTENSION injecting `jf-ext-*` attributes into the DOM before React
  hydrates. Every mismatch in the log is one of those. It is not the app.

# 2026-08-16 — Step 3: the mutation queue

## What this is actually for, since it is not speed

Edits in this app were already instant — every view painted an optimistic patch
before calling the server. What they were not is **durable**:

```ts
setTasks(patch)          // instant, on screen
await toggleTask(id)     // ~300ms
if (error) rollback
```

Close the tab inside that 300ms — or lose signal, or shut the laptop — and the
write is gone, *after the interface has already told you it was saved*. It said
so immediately and confidently, and it was wrong. **That is data loss dressed as
responsiveness**, and it is the honest reason to build a queue. Selling this as
a speed feature would be a lie; the instant paint was never the hard part.

## The shape

`lib/mutation-queue.ts` holds the rules as pure functions (23 tests);
`lib/mutation-store.ts` owns the three things that cannot be pure — persistence,
timers, the network. An edit that reaches `push()` is on disk before the
function returns, and from there it is delivered by this tab, by the next one
you open, or visibly undone with a reason.

Four decisions that carry the design:

**Ops are absolute, never deltas.** The queue retries and collapses, and both
are only safe for "set done to true", never "flip done". `toggleTask(id, done)`
already took the value, which is what made it queueable at all. The registry
comment says plainly that a delta-shaped action must not be added — it would
double-apply on the first retry and nothing would explain why.

**Returned error ⇒ give up. Thrown ⇒ retry.** An action that *returns* an error
has decided something (the row is gone, RLS refused) and will decide it again
forever. One that *threw* never got to decide — network, or the runtime went
away — which is exactly what a queue is for.

**Collapsing keeps its place in line.** Ticking a task and un-ticking it inside
the three-second settle beat is normal; without collapsing that is two writes
racing. The collapsed op keeps the original's position so ops on other records
cannot overtake it.

**`revert` rides on the op, not in a closure.** The queue drains in whichever
tab is open, which may not be the tab that made the edit — and a closure does
not survive a reload anyway.

## A bug I wrote and then found

The first version fed `applyPending(initialTasks, pending)` into
`useServerState` as the seed. Tidier, and wrong: the seed's identity changes on
**every queue movement** — a push, an op going in flight, an op being delivered
— and `useServerState` compares by reference. Each of those would have snapped
local state back and silently discarded optimistic edits *not* in the queue,
like a task you had just created. The overlay is applied at render instead, so
the server-backed state is left alone and only what is drawn changes.

That is the second time this sprint that `useServerState`'s reference comparison
has bitten (the first was a `= []` default parameter). It is a sharp tool.

## Verified in the browser, one full cycle

| t | queued | tries | row | Completed group |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100ms | 1 | 1 | checked | 1 task |
| 1.5s | 1 | 3 | checked | 1 task |
| 4s | 1 | 4 | settled | 2 tasks |
| 8s | **0** | — | reverted | back to 1 task |

The intent was on disk at 100ms, before the server had answered anything. The
harness has no session, so every attempt threw; it retried five times with
backoff and then gave up and put the row back — the whole loop, observed.

1090 tests (+23), `tsc` clean, **production build passes**.

## Owed

- **Only `task.toggle` is wired.** The registry also declares highlight,
  reschedule, priority, setList and setProject, but their call sites still
  `await`. Wiring them is mechanical now that the seam exists.
- **Creates and deletes are deliberately out.** A create must reconcile a
  temporary id with the one the server mints; a delete has no field patch to
  lay back over server rows. Both need more than a field map, and making field
  edits trustworthy first was worth more than covering everything at once.
- The toast on a final refusal needs the app shell, so it does not appear in the
  dev-preview harness. Worth one signed-in look.
- The end state is display = server rows + pending patches, with the views'
  hand-rolled optimistic code deleted. `applyPending` is the seam that makes
  that a later change rather than a rewrite today.

# 2026-08-16 — The task row's hover was a slab, not a row

Reported: hovering a task paints a hard-cornered rectangle inside a rounded
container, reading as an overlay dropped on top rather than the row lighting up.

The cause, once you look: the wash was painted on **the same element that
carried the divider**, at the row's full rectangle, with no radius. So its
bottom edge landed exactly on the hairline — which is what made it look applied
rather than belonging.

**Every other hover surface in the app already had the answer.** The DS
`ListRow` rounds its wash, the board's quick-add rounds its, every menu item
rounds its, the project task list rounds its. The two task rows were the only
ones that never got it.

## Why it needs two elements

A rounded wash and a full-width divider cannot share a box: the corners curve
away exactly where the line runs straight, and you see both fighting. So the
divider stays on the outer element, spanning the list, and the wash is an inner
box with a **2px vertical inset** — enough that its rounded corners never touch
the hairline. The row floats inside its slot instead of filling it.

Row height is unchanged: the padding lost to the inset is the padding the wash
gives back (`py-4` → `my-0.5 py-3.5`, `py-3` → `my-0.5 py-2.5`).

## One definition, because there are two rows

`components/tasks/task-row.tsx` (Home, project tabs) and the roomier local row
in `tasks-view.tsx` had drifted into two spellings of the same broken thing —
fixing them separately would have fixed them differently. A row's surface is one
idea, so it now has one definition in `components/tasks/row-surface.ts`.

## Verified

Measured in the browser: wash radius **8px**, margin `2px 0`, divider on the
parent, wash 77px inside an 80px row. Confirmed on both the Tasks list and Home
(the shared row). Swept the rest — the only other square-cornered rows are the
habit rows, and they have no hover wash at all, so there was nothing to fix
there. `reveal-on-hover` on the ⋮ still works: `group` moved to the outer
element, which is still an ancestor.

1090 tests, `tsc` clean, no lint errors in the files touched.

# 2026-08-16 — Agency workflow: the diagnosis, and S1 (one visibility rule)

Brief: rethink client management / project management / the portal from an
agency's point of view; make internal vs client-facing a real distinction;
single source of truth, no duplication.

`AGENCY_WORKFLOW_PLAN.md` is the deliverable. What follows is the part worth
repeating here.

## Most of what was asked for already exists

Per-project magic-link portal, drawn as a real dashboard. One gated projection
(`lib/portal.ts`) shared by the live portal and "Preview as client", so preview
cannot drift. Six share flags. Per-item `client_visible` on tasks and pages. A
full request→task lifecycle with threaded messages. Deliverable approvals.
Read-only invoices. Forms in the portal.

**So the brief is not "build a portal".** It is five structural things that make
the existing one feel like an export of a project manager.

## The five gaps, each evidenced

1. **The portal is per PROJECT, not per CLIENT** (`projects.portal_token`) — a
   client with three projects gets three links.
2. **Visibility is set somewhere other than where the work is** — per-task
   marking lives in `share-panel.tsx`, so sharing is a second pass.
3. **The four shareable things obey four different rules** — tasks ✔ per-item,
   docs ✔ per-item, files ✗ project flag only (all or nothing), updates ✗ not
   shareable at all.
4. **The owner cannot see what the client has seen** — `grep` for
   `last_seen|viewed_at|seen_at|portal_view` returns **zero results**. Of the
   five things the brief says the owner should always know, the product can
   answer two.
5. **"Updates" are inferred, not authored** — the portal derives them from
   completed task titles, which is why it reads like a changelog of your to-do
   list rather than a sentence from you.

## The find that mattered more than the plan predicted

`lib/portal.ts` read the task gates as **"bucket flag OR per-task override"** —
its own comment said so. With `share_completed_tasks` ON, **every** completed
task went to the client and `client_visible` was ignored entirely.

So the internal-vs-client-facing distinction the app appears to have was
defeated by the one switch an agency would obviously turn on. "Share what we
finished" silently meant "publish our internal task list". The timeline had the
same hole, and was commented "always safe".

That is the exact leak the brief is worried about, and it was live.

## S1 — one visibility rule

`lib/visibility.ts` is now the single answer to "can the client see this?",
covering tasks, docs, files and updates. **Two gates, both required:** the
project shares this KIND (the setup decision, made once) AND this item was
marked (the daily decision). Two rather than one because they fail differently —
turning a channel off must silence everything instantly without touching a row,
so that turning it back on restores exactly what was marked and nothing that
wasn't.

**Every function reads missing data as private.** A column that does not exist
yet, a project row that failed to load, a truthy-but-not-`true` value — all
resolve to hidden. The cost of a false negative is a client asking where
something is; the cost of a false positive cannot be undone.

`lib/portal.ts` now uses it, so the claim is true rather than aspirational.
Migration 0039 adds per-file visibility (closing gap 3) **and backfills** the
tasks the old bucket flags were already publishing — every live portal shows
exactly what it shows today, the difference being that the marks are now
explicit and new work is internal until someone says otherwise.

18 tests on the rule, 1108 total, `tsc` clean.

## Owed

- **Paste `supabase/migrations/0039_file_visibility.sql`.** It contains the
  backfill, so until it runs, portals with the bucket flags on will show fewer
  tasks than before — this is the one change in this session that is *not*
  invisible before its migration, and it is deliberate: the alternative was
  leaving the leak open.
- S1 is not finished. The rule and the portal are done; **the control still
  needs to appear where the work is** (task row, file row, doc row) rather than
  only in the share panel. That is gap 2, and it is the next thing.
- S2–S5 (authored updates · one portal per client · read state · lifecycle
  seams) are sequenced in the plan and not started.

# 2026-08-16 — A link card carries YOUR note, not just the URL

Asked for: paste any shareable link (Drive, Google Docs, Figma, anything), add a
note about it, see it as a card.

## Most of it already existed — and the missing piece was the point

There is a `bookmark` block, a `/api/unfurl` endpoint (guarded: https only, no
private hosts, signed-in only) and a card that shows favicon, site name, title,
description and the og:image.

But that description is **scraped from the page**, and for the links people
actually paste it is worthless. A Drive folder returns "Sign in to continue".
A Figma file returns "Figma". A private Notion page returns nothing.

So the card could tell you everything except the one thing that matters: *why
this link is here*. "Final logos — use these, not the old folder" had nowhere to
live.

## No schema, no migration

`block.text` has always been carried by every block — `image` already uses it as
a caption, and the editor already has a `caption` render-prop for exactly this.
The link block simply never got handed it. So the whole feature is: pass the
existing render-prop, render the existing field.

Three decisions:

**Your note replaces the scraped description**, rather than sitting beside it.
Showing both would put a real sentence next to boilerplate and make the reader
work out which to trust. It also renders in ink-800 rather than ink-600 — the
card says at a glance whose words these are.

**The note sits below the card in the editor, not inside it.** The card is an
`<a>`; a text field inside an anchor is invalid HTML that swallows its own
clicks.

**Every link-shaped block gets it** — embed, video, audio, pdf, file — not just
bookmark. One of them behaving differently is how a rule stops being a rule.

## The silent drop this would have had

`blocksToText` and `blocksToMarkdown` both returned only `b.src` for link
blocks. A note would have been invisible to search and absent from every export
and every copy-paste — the identical failure that once took a proposal's prices
out of copied text, which the code comments right next to it already warn about.
Both now carry the note (`[note](url)` in markdown).

## Verified

In the browser, on a seeded pair: the noted card renders
`drive.google.com | Final logos — use these, not the old folder | <url>` with
the note in `text-ink-800` and an editable field below it; the un-noted card is
unchanged. 6 tests cover search, export, storage round-trip and the other five
block types. 1114 total, `tsc` clean, no new lint errors.

## Note for the portal work

This lands well inside `AGENCY_WORKFLOW_PLAN.md`: a link card with a sentence of
context is how an agency hands over a Figma file or a Drive folder, and it
reaches the client through the doc's existing `client_visible` — no new sharing
path, which is the plan's whole premise.

# 2026-08-16 — Workstreams: the level already existed

Asked for: Project → Subproject/Workstream → Task → Subtask, with subprojects
optionally client-facing.

## The finding

**This level is already in the schema.** `sections` (0014) is exactly
Project → X → Task: `project_id`, name, `sort_order`, and `tasks.section_id`
already points at it. Create / rename / delete already work, and the project
Tasks tab already groups by it.

What it lacked was everything that makes it a *workstream* rather than a
heading — no status, no deadline, and no way to say "this stream is ours, that
one is the client's". It was built as a Things-style divider and named
accordingly, so it reads as formatting rather than structure.

So this is **additive**: three columns, no data migration, and every project
that already has sections becomes a project with workstreams the moment 0040
lands.

## Two rejected designs, and why

**A new `subprojects` table** would have meant two things that mean the same
thing, a migration to move rows between them, and a fork in every query that
groups tasks.

**Self-referencing `projects.parent_id`** would inherit status, deadline, files,
activity and portal flags for free — and was rejected because every existing
query reading `projects where space_id = …` (the gallery, the Finance rollup,
the client detail, the sidebar) would start returning workstreams as top-level
projects, each needing a `parent_id is null` it currently lacks. Large blast
radius to buy fields most workstreams will never set. It also invites the
question the product should not answer: can a subproject have a subproject?
Four fixed levels is the shape asked for, and a table that cannot nest cannot
drift into infinite nesting by accident.

## The name

**Workstream**, not subproject — and it matters because the client reads it.
"Subproject" tells a client their project has been split into projects. If you
prefer the other word it is one label constant.

## `lib/workstreams.ts` — the rollup rules that matter

- **Progress counts top-level tasks only.** Otherwise a stream with one fiddly
  ten-subtask task reads as more work than a stream with nine real ones.
- **An empty stream is 0%, never 100%.** "Nothing to do" and "everything done"
  are different states, and an empty stream showing a full bar is the kind of
  wrong that gets quoted back at you in a client meeting.
- **The project rolls up by task count, not by averaging stream percentages.**
  Averaging gives a 2-task stream the same weight as a 40-task one, so finishing
  the small one would move the project bar further than finishing half the big
  one. Tested with exactly that case: 2 of 42 = 5%, not 50%.
- **Hiding a stream hides everything in it**, whatever the individual tasks say.
  That is the point of "keep this stream entirely internal" — you should not
  also have to un-mark forty tasks, and forgetting one must not leak the
  stream's existence.
- **The client never sees an "Unfiled" group.** That heading exposes our filing
  rather than their project.
- **Status is derived when unset, and an explicit one always wins** — "paused"
  is a fact about intent that progress cannot know. A stream nobody has started
  gets no status at all, because a badge on every heading makes all of them
  meaningless.

Client visibility reuses `lib/visibility.ts` — a workstream is the fourth thing
that rule covers, which is the whole reason that rule exists.

19 tests, 1133 total, `tsc` clean, no lint errors.

## Owed

- **Paste `supabase/migrations/0040_workstreams.sql`.** Gated: until it runs,
  sections behave exactly as they do today.
- **The UI is not wired yet.** The projection is done and tested; the project
  Tasks tab still renders sections as plain headings. Next: stream header with
  progress + due date + status, the client-facing toggle on the stream, and the
  portal grouping by stream instead of showing a flat list.
- **Assignees are not possible today** and were deliberately not added. The app
  is single-owner — `user_id` with owner-only RLS on every table — so the column
  could only ever hold your own id. It belongs to the team-seats track with the
  policy changes that make it mean something.
- Per-workstream files and activity were also left out, with reasons written in
  the migration rather than left as a gap someone re-derives.

# Sharing where the work is — S1 finished, end to end (2026-08-17)

The remaining half of S1 from `AGENCY_WORKFLOW_PLAN.md`, plus the client-facing
half of workstreams. Scope was set by the user: *"only the client, project and
portal sharing"*, and *no SQL work*.

## The finding that unblocked all of it

**0038, 0039 and 0040 are already applied.** I had them listed as owed. A
service-role probe (paired with a must-fail control, so a 200 means the column
really exists) returned 200 for `tasks.client_visible`, `pages.client_visible`,
`attachments.client_visible`, `sections.client_visible/status/due_date`,
`task_lists` and `task_links`; a bogus column on the same table returned 42703
and a bogus table PGRST205. So nothing in this sprint needed a migration.

The same probe answered a design question for free: **zero `sections` rows
exist**, and no task with a `section_id` is marked client-visible. That made the
stream gate below a free decision rather than a change that could quietly empty
a live portal.

## The problem

Marking work client-facing was a **second pass**. Per-task visibility lived in a
share drawer you opened on purpose, docs had their own bespoke pill with
different words, and files and workstreams had nothing at all. The friction was
never the click — it was the context switch: finish the task here, then go over
there and remember to tick it.

## One control, four surfaces

`components/sharing/share-toggle.tsx` — one component, one wording, on task
rows, workstream headers, doc rows and file rows.

**Three states, not two,** because `lib/visibility.ts` has two gates and
"hidden" therefore has two different causes that need different fixes:

| state | when | how it reads |
|---|---|---|
| `shared` | both gates open | solid chip "Client", **always** visible — a thing being client-facing is a fact you need at a glance |
| `marked-off` | marked, but the project's channel is off | **dashed** chip, also always visible, tooltip naming the switch to go and find |
| `internal` | not marked | quiet chip revealed on row hover, like the highlight star |

Every state is **74px wide**, verified in the browser, so toggling never moves
the row and a column of chips stays a column.

The accessible name is the ACTION ("Share “Logo v2” with the client"), not the
state — `aria-pressed` carries the state, and a button *named* "Client" tells a
screen-reader user nothing about what pressing it does.

## The failure direction that is not allowed

`components/sharing/apply-share.ts` (4 tests). Every optimistic write in the app
reverts on a *returned* error; server actions can also **throw** —
`requireSession()` throws on an expired session — and a bare `await` leaves the
optimistic state applied. For a task toggle that is cosmetic. For a sharing mark
it is a chip reading "Client" for a row the database never marked, and you would
act on it: send the link, tell the client it is there. So any failure, returned
or thrown, reverts, and the message says the change did not stick rather than
leaking "Not authenticated" to the reader.

## Workstreams become client-facing

- A stream header carries the same chip, plus **"· n shared"** when the stream
  is client-facing but not everything in it is — a legitimate state on the way
  to sharing, and a silent one without the count.
- The stream menu gained the bulk pass: **"Share all tasks with client"** /
  **"Make all tasks internal"**, run from the header so the scope of "all" is
  the group you are looking at, with a toast because it changes rows off screen.
- The stream toggle deliberately **does not cascade**. A cascade would silently
  re-expose every task you had made internal the next time the stream was
  switched off and on.

## The portal, on the other side of the rule

- **Work is grouped by workstream** (`clientGroups`), each with its own progress
  bar, then anything ungrouped under "Everything else". A project with no
  client-facing streams renders exactly as it did before they existed.
- **A third gate:** a task inside a stream is governed entirely by that stream.
  The first version filtered on "is in a VISIBLE stream", which let every task
  in an *internal* stream fall straight through into the flat list — the exact
  leak the gate exists to close. The timeline obeys it too, for the same reason
  the timeline already obeys the task rule: a section cannot be "always safe" if
  its source is not.
- **A visible stream with nothing visible in it is dropped** (`clientGroups`,
  test added). The owner keeps empty streams — you must be able to drag the
  first task into one — but a client shown "Brand guidelines" with nothing under
  it learns only that work exists they are not allowed to see.
- **Files reach the client at last.** `attachments` had `client_visible` since
  0039 and nothing read it: the portal had no files section at all. Same channel
  as documents (`share_files`), same per-item mark, shown under Documents
  because to a client "the brief" and "the logo pack" are one errand.
  `signPortalFile` re-checks every gate itself — an id in a request is a claim,
  not a permission — and mints a 5-minute URL. The storage `path` is never
  selected into the projection.
- The share panel's "Documents" switch is now **"Documents and files"**: it was
  already the channel `lib/visibility.ts` maps both onto, so the label was
  quietly disagreeing with the rule. It also warns when an enabled portal shares
  nothing — the most embarrassing failure this feature has — and its task list
  now counts what the PORTAL will show, not what has been ticked.

## Verified

- **1138 tests** (67 files), `tsc` clean, **0 lint errors** on every touched file
  (4 pre-existing unused-var warnings in `projects-workspace.tsx` untouched).
- **Browser, `/dev-preview/projects`:** all three chip states on one screen —
  a shared open task, an internal one revealed on hover, and a *completed*
  marked task reading dashed because the completed-tasks channel is off. Chip
  widths asserted at 74px in all states; `aria-pressed` and the accessible names
  read back from the DOM. Clicking an internal chip flipped it optimistically
  and the header's "· 1 shared" disappeared, because 2 of 2 were then shared.
- **Browser, `/dev-preview/portal`:** Packaging (1 of 3 done) and Brand
  guidelines grouped with progress bars, "Everything else" holding the ungrouped
  work, and a Files group with sizes and Download buttons.
- Both dev-preview fixtures were extended to carry the new states rather than
  being read past.

## Owed

- **The file row is the one surface I could not exercise in the browser.**
  `listAttachments` requires a session and the dev-preview harness is auth-free,
  so the Files tab renders its empty state there. The control is the same
  component verified on tasks and docs, and the panel's wiring is type-checked —
  but it has not been seen with a real file in it.
- Not built, and deliberately: **authored updates (S2)** — the portal's Recent
  updates are still derived from completed task titles. `ShareChannels` already
  carries an `updates` slot that reads as off, so the rule is ready for it.
- Still open from the plan: S3 one portal per client · S4 read state
  (`portal_views`) · S5 the lifecycle seams.

# Updates become a real object — S2 (2026-08-17)

Gap 5 of `AGENCY_WORKFLOW_PLAN.md`, and the last one that could be closed under
the user's *no SQL work* constraint. It turned out that it could be closed
without any.

## The problem

The portal's "Recent updates" was derived from **completed task titles**. Safe —
and precisely why the portal read like a project manager rather than like a
studio. The client got a changelog of our to-do list instead of a sentence from
a person, and nothing in the system existed whose purpose was *"something I want
to tell the client"*.

## The finding: the object already existed

The project Overview has had an **Update composer** since §7E. It writes a
`project_activity` row of `type = 'note'` and shows the newest one as the
project's written status. That IS the update. It simply had no way to be
addressed to anybody.

So a client update is the **same row with a different type** — `client_update`.
One object, two audiences, which is this plan's own rule: *there is one thing
with a visibility, and the portal reads the visible ones.* A parallel
`client_updates` table would have meant writing your status twice and watching
the two copies drift.

**And it needs no migration.** `project_activity.type` is plain `text` with no
CHECK, and shipped code already writes `'invoiced'` and `'accepted'` — neither
of which appears in the DDL comment's list of values. Verified by reading 0003
and by the fact that those two writes work today.

### Why the type, and not a `client_visible` column

`type` is already the vocabulary of *what kind of thing happened*, and "a note I
wrote for the client" is a genuinely different kind of event from a private one
— not a flag smuggled into the wrong column. The consequence is the good one:
promoting an update is a one-column write, and the internal activity log shows
**"you told the client X"** for free, because it is the same row it was always
reading.

## Two design decisions worth keeping

**Updates ride the Timeline switch, not a new channel of their own.** That
switch already means "tell the client what has been happening", and an authored
update is a better answer to it than the derived task events it replaces. So a
project that had Timeline on gets the improvement, and one that had it off is
not opted into a new kind of publishing by a sprint it did not ask for. It also
removed a lie: `ShareChannels.updates` had been reading `projects.share_updates`,
a column that does not exist, so it was always false.

**Two buttons, not one button and a mode.** With a draft in the composer you get
**Post** and **Post to client**. A sticky "post to client" toggle would sooner
or later send a private note to a client because it was still switched on from
last time, and that is not a mistake you can take back. Enter posts the safe
one; reaching the client is always a deliberate second target.

## What shipped

- `lib/updates.ts` (8 tests) — `NOTE` / `CLIENT_UPDATE`, `typeFor`, `isUpdate`,
  `isAddressedToClient`, `clientUpdates`, `allUpdates`. The owner's list keeps
  **both audiences in one column**: "what did I last say about this project?"
  must have one answer.
- Owner, project Overview: the latest update carries the same `ShareToggle` as
  every other shareable thing, plus delete; the four before it are listed under
  it with their own chips. `setUpdateClientVisible` and `deleteUpdate` both
  constrain on `.in('type', [note, client_update])`, so an id belonging to a
  `status_change` or `accepted` row can never be retyped or deleted through them
  — the project's history cannot be edited by way of this feature.
- Portal: **"Latest update"** now leads the Overview as prose with its date, and
  the derived task list below it was renamed to the honest **"Recently
  completed"**. More than one update earns its own nav section; exactly one does
  not, because a nav item leading to the paragraph already on screen is a door
  into the room you are standing in.
- `components/ds/icons.ts` gained `Megaphone` (the seam, never a direct import)
  — something the studio *said*, as distinct from the Bell's "something happened
  to you".

## Verified

- **1146 tests** (68 files), `tsc` clean, no new lint errors (1 pre-existing
  error and 5 pre-existing warnings in the touched files, all untouched).
- **Browser, `/dev-preview/portal`:** "Updates 2" in the nav, the Overview
  leading with the update's paragraph over "Recently completed", and the Updates
  section rendering both notes with dates.
- **Browser, `/dev-preview/projects`:** the chip and delete revealed on hover of
  the status update; both **Post** and **Post to client** appearing once there
  is a draft.
- **`applyShare` proved live, not just in a unit test.** Clicking the chip in the
  auth-free harness logged `ƒ setUpdateClientVisible("a1", true)` → HTTP 500
  (no session), and the chip **went back to "Internal"** instead of staying
  flipped. That is the exact failure the helper exists for, observed end to end.

## Owed

- The harness shows no error toast because `<Toaster/>` lives in the app shell
  and the dev-preview page renders the workspace outside it. Real app only.
- **Not built:** notifying the client that an update was posted. The portal is a
  link, not an inbox — mail to a client is S5 territory and needs an address we
  do not reliably have.
- Still open from the plan: **S3** one portal per client · **S4** read state
  (`portal_views`) · **S5** the lifecycle seams. All three need a migration, so
  they wait on the no-SQL constraint being lifted.

# The week board fits the week (2026-08-17)

## The defect, measured

The board used fixed columns and set their sum as the scroller's `minWidth`:

```
COL_INBOX 320 + COL_DAY 268 × 7 = 2196px
```

Columns carried `flexShrink: 0`, so they never gave any of it back. With the
232px tasks rail beside it, seeing seven days needed roughly a **2500px
window**. Measured in the browser at 1280px: a 1050px pane holding 2196px of
board — **three of seven days**, the rest behind a horizontal scroll.

A board whose entire premise is "see your week" that cannot show a week is
failing at its one job. Benchmarked against Google Calendar rather than a
Notion/Linear board on purpose: an arbitrary-column board may scroll, but a
*week* is a fixed seven, and Calendar always shows all of them and shrinks.

## What shipped

- **`lib/week-layout.ts`** (10 tests) — the one place the rule lives. Unscheduled
  is a fixed staging column; the seven days **share what is left** via
  `flex: 1 1 0` with a `COL_DAY_MIN` floor. The layout itself is CSS, not JS:
  flexbox already solves this exactly, and a ResizeObserver recomputing widths
  per frame would be a worse answer. The numbers live in the file so the rule is
  stated once and can be tested.
- **A collapsible staging column.** Collapsed it is a 44px spine — still a
  droppable with the same id, because a column you cannot drop onto is not
  collapsed, it is gone, and dragging a task out of the week back into staging
  is the gesture the board is built around. Remembered per browser (not per
  account: it is a response to *this window's* size).
- **A container query** (`ds-theme.css`) so a card thins with its column — a
  media query cannot see a column's width. The priority label goes and its
  colour bar stays; the project name goes and its dot stays; unset "Estimate"/
  "Project" invitations go entirely rather than becoming empty boxes. Quieter,
  never less truthful.

## Two mistakes I made, and what caught them

**The floor was a column number, not a text number.** At `COL_DAY_MIN = 140` the
week fitted — and the titles read `"Revi / the / lau…"`. A 140px column is not
140px of title: column padding, card padding, the checkbox and the kebab take
~90px between them. Only the screenshot caught it. The container query now buys
that budget back at narrow widths (8px paddings, and the kebab goes
`position: absolute` so its 22px stops being the difference between two words on
a line and one). Titles now read `"Review the launch…"`.

**Exact-fit is not fit.** I sized the week to a pane I assumed was 1280; the
browser reported **1276**, so the board overflowed by four pixels and the
scrollbar came straight back. `COL_INBOX` is 288 rather than 300 to leave
headroom, and the test's pane constants are now the **measured** numbers with a
comment saying why they are not derived from the window width.

## Verified in the browser, at both real machine sizes

| viewport | pane | staging column | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1512 | 1276 | open | 7 days at ~141px — **no scroll** |
| 1280 | 1044 | open | scrolls (1268 > 1044) — the collapse is offered |
| 1280 | 1044 | collapsed | 7 days at ~143px — **no scroll** |

And the collapsed spine was verified as a real drop target by an actual pointer
drag, not by reading the code: dragging Monday's card onto it emptied Monday,
took the spine count 2 → 3, and recomputed the header from
"3 open · 2 unscheduled · 1h 30m planned" to "2 open · 3 unscheduled · 1h planned".

**1156 tests** (69 files), `tsc` clean, 0 lint errors on every touched file.

## A lint error I introduced, and why it is not disabled

Reading the collapsed flag in a `useEffect` tripped `react-hooks/set-state-in-effect`
— correctly, since it renders twice on every mount. `localStorage` **is** an
external store, so it is read through `useSyncExternalStore` with a defined
server snapshot (always open, so a collapsed board is never hydrated into markup
rendered open). The `storage` event is part of the subscription, so two windows
on the same week stay in step.

## Owed

- `components/ui/panel.tsx` is **dead code** — zero importers; the live Panel is
  `components/ds/ui/panel.tsx` re-exported through `components/ui/panels.tsx`.
  Found while auditing, left alone: it belongs to the consistency sweep below,
  not to this sprint.

# Consistency sweep #1 — "where am I?" is answerable in every hub (2026-08-17)

First sprint under the new `CONSISTENCY_PRINCIPLE.md` ("same principles, not
necessarily the same screens"). Picked by asking the principle's own test —
*would somebody who learned this gesture on another screen be right here?* —
and finding a place where the answer was no.

## The drift, evidenced

Every hub is one route holding "which record is open" and "which mode am I in".
Each answered differently, and the differences were invisible until you pressed
Back or tried to send someone a link:

| hub | record | mode (tab/view) |
|---|---|---|
| Clients | URL (`?c=`) ✔ | **`useState`** — not in the URL at all |
| Projects | route ✔ | **read from the URL, never written back** |
| Forms | route ✔ | routes ✔ |
| Tasks | URL ✔ | `useUrlState` ✔ |

Three answers to one question. The Projects one is the worst kind — asymmetric:
a notification could deep-link to `?tab=portal`, but clicking Portal yourself
changed nothing, so you could not link to where you were and Back skipped
straight out of the project.

**I got this wrong first and checked before building on it.** My initial grep
said Clients had no URL state at all; it goes through a helper (`useRecordParam`)
that the grep missed. The record *was* addressable. Only the tab was not.

## The rule, written down

`lib/hub-url.ts` (renamed from `use-record-param.ts` — the old name no longer
covered what the file does) now states it:

> **Selecting a record → `replaceState`.** Browsing. Clicking through six
> clients must not bury the page you arrived from under six Back presses.
>
> **Changing a mode → `pushState`.** A tab is a place you went on purpose, so
> Back should return you to the previous one and you should be able to send it.

That difference is a **decision**, not an accident — which is exactly what the
principle asks for: a divergence is allowed when it is named, caused by the use
case, and written where the code is. Neither costs a server round trip.

New `useModeParam(key, fallback, valid, aliases?)` beside the existing
`useRecordParam`. Two hooks in one file rather than a third file, because they
are one concept with two deliberate variants.

## What that fixed

- **Clients**: the tab is in the URL. `/clients?tab=pipeline` is a link, and
  Back returns to the tab you came from instead of leaving Clients.
- **Projects**: the tab is *written* as well as read.
- **A bug found on the way.** The project route whitelisted five tabs
  (`overview/tasks/docs/money/portal`) while the hub had six — so `?tab=files`
  was a legitimate deep link that silently landed on Overview. Two lists in two
  files; there is one list now, and a test for exactly that case.
- The legacy `?tab=forms` → `docs` alias moved out of the route and next to the
  tab list it renames, so every entry point resolves it identically.
- `initialTab` is gone from `ProjectsWorkspace` — the component reads the URL
  itself, so the prop was a lying signature, and the `useChanged(initialTab)`
  reconcile went with it (one copy of the fact, nothing to keep in step).

## Verified in the browser, by clicking

Projects: Money → `?tab=money`, **history 5 → 6**; Portal → `?tab=portal`,
history 6 → 7; Back → `?tab=money` **and the pane followed**. One history entry
per click, which matters: Radix Tabs fire on focus **and** click, so a
URL-controlled tab bar pushes twice without a guard and Back appears to do
nothing the first time. `useModeParam` ignores a write of the value it already
holds.

Clients: Pipeline → `?tab=pipeline` and the pane switched; Back → param removed
and the Clients tab returned. The default writes no param — a URL should not
carry its own default.

**1161 tests** (70 files), `tsc` clean, **0 lint errors** on every touched file.

## Recorded, not started (rule: no parallel work)

- `components/ui/panel.tsx` — dead, zero importers.
- `ViewContainer` (the one page-width primitive) is adopted by 2 of 5 hubs.
- `documents-view.tsx` renders **two** `PageHeader`s.
- `PageView` — the recorded directive that every record opens through one
  component — is adopted by task detail, project docs, database rows and version
  history, while `forms/responses-view`, `habits-board` and `share-panel` still
  open bespoke `Drawer`s.
