## Picking things out of a Collection — 2026-09-16 (COLLECTION_PLAN K10)

§15–16: "keep these hidden until needed" and "do not permanently show selection controls on every card". A
Collection should look like what it holds, and grow controls only under the hand that wants them.

**A box on hover picks an item, with nothing held down.** It sits top-left, hidden at rest, revealed with the
card's menu — and it stays showing on a card already picked, because a card that is selected must say so whether
or not a pointer is near it. Shift still takes the run between two, ⌘-click still toggles, and on a coarse
pointer the box is simply there (the `reveal-on-hover` utility already says that; no new rule).

**The card's menu now carries the whole verb list** (§15): Open · Open website · **Rename** · **Tags** ·
**Copy link** · Move left · Move right · Delete.
- **Rename happens on the card** — its name becomes a field with the text selected, Enter commits, Escape
  abandons. The same act as renaming a Collection on the Index.
- **Tags is a real submenu** of the Collection's own words, each one a checkbox that leaves the menu open, so
  three tags are three clicks rather than three trips.
- **Copy link** appears only on something that has one.

**The selection bar gained Copy links and Select all** (§16): `3 selected · Open · Tag · Copy links · Delete ·
Select all · ✕`. Copy links takes every address in the selection, one to a line, and says how many; a selection
with no addresses in it says so instead of silently copying nothing. Select all takes what is ON SCREEN — the
same meaning ⌘A has had since K8, so a filtered Collection selects what it is showing.

**Found while building, and measured:**
- **A popover opened from a menu lives 25 milliseconds.** "Tags" first opened the same `Pop` + `OptionList`
  picker the item page uses. It mounted and was dismissed 25ms later, before the menu it came from had even been
  removed (a MutationObserver in the live page said so) — a modal Radix menu tearing down dismisses the layer
  that opened underneath it, and no amount of deferring fixed it reliably. Radix nests MENUS properly, so Tags
  is a `DropdownMenuSub` with `DropdownMenuCheckboxItem`s: no race, and the roles and the keyboard come free.
- **A menu that closes takes the caret with it.** Rename's field mounted while the menu's focus trap was still
  up, so React's `autoFocus` was undone and focus landed on `<body>`. The menu now declines to hand focus back
  (`onCloseAutoFocus`) when what it opened wants it, and the field claims the caret after the next paint.
- **One way to copy, everywhere.** `copyText` (`components/ds/ui/clipboard.ts`) — a copy that fails silently is
  worse than no copy, because the person walks away with an old clipboard believing otherwise. The database's
  own `copyViewLink` was the same five lines and now calls it.

**Proved with trusted input** — `scripts/verify/verify-collection-select.mjs` (new), A–J:
- **A:** at rest the box and the menu are `opacity: 0`; a pointer over the card makes both `1`.
- **B:** a click on the box picks the item (`1 selected`), opens nothing, and the box stays showing with the
  pointer gone.
- **C:** Shift on a third box takes all three.
- **D:** Select all takes 8, and the button leaves when there is nothing left to take.
- **E:** Copy links says "7 links copied." and the clipboard, read back, holds 7 lines — the note has no address.
- **E2:** a selection of only a note says "Nothing here has a link."
- **F:** the menu reads Open · Open image · Rename · Tags · Copy link · Move left ⌥← · Move right ⌥→ · Delete.
- **G:** Rename focuses the card's name field with its text selected; typing and Enter rename the card.
- **H:** Tags opens the Collection's four words with the item's four ticked; unticking Motion leaves the menu
  open and takes the chip off the card.
- **J:** with touch emulated, the box is `opacity: 1` without hovering. No console errors.
- **Neighbours re-run:** find (A–L) · notes (A–F) · tags · item (A–M) all green.

**Guards,** watched failing first:
- `lib/collection.test.ts`: `itemLinks` is every address there is, in the order shown, and nothing for what has
  none.

`tsc` clean · **2347 tests / 156 files** · eslint clean on every file touched.

### Recorded, not started
- **Two tag pickers, on purpose.** The item's page and the selection bar open the searchable picker that can
  MAKE a tag; a card's menu offers the words the Collection already has. Quick versus deliberate — but if a
  third shape ever appears, they should become one.
- **"Move" in §16's example bar** would mean moving items to another Collection. That is a cross-Collection act
  with no home yet; it is not K10.
- **The canvas has no boxes.** It has its own selection (click, marquee) and no meta line to hang a box on.

## How a Collection shows itself — 2026-09-16 (COLLECTION_PLAN K11)

§28 asks for a Collection's own view settings. Three of them earn their place, and they belong to the
**Collection**, not to the person looking: a moodboard someone arranged as large uncropped pictures is that
board for everyone who opens it.

- **Card size** — Small · Medium · Large, which is the narrowest a column may be before the masonry drops one
  (150 · 220 · 320). In a 1074px page that is 6 · 4 · 3 columns.
- **Preview** — **Original ratio** (every card the shape of its own picture: the masonry §13 asks for) ·
  **Cover** (one shape for every picture, cropped to it) · **Fit** (one shape, the whole picture inside it).
- **Show titles** — off leaves the pictures alone. A note keeps its words, because a note is nothing else; and
  a tile keeps the two words saying what it is, because the alternative is a wall of blank rectangles.

**§28's "Layout: masonry | grid" is not a fourth setting.** "Original ratio" IS the masonry, and either uniform
preview IS the grid. One choice cannot disagree with itself. The rest of §28's list is either built (Filter,
Sort), a database idea with no Collection meaning (property visibility, conditional colour), or lives elsewhere
(the page's name; "Open pages in" is a PageView setting).

**What uniform actually means, and it is worth saying:** with Cover or Fit, every *picture* is one shape while
the words under it still vary — which is what a gallery looks like. Turn titles off as well and every *card* is
one shape: the tidy grid. Measured both ways in the check.

**Saved like the order, through `store.learn`** — how a thing is shown is not a step in what was done to it, so
⌘Z after choosing Large does not take it back. Only what is not the ordinary is written, so an untouched
Collection carries no settings at all and the control reads as unset.

**Proved with trusted input** — `scripts/verify/verify-collection-look.mjs` (new), A–G:
- **A:** the panel reads Card size · Preview · Show titles with Medium and Original ratio ticked, and the
  control is not set.
- **B:** Large → 3 columns of 350px; Small → 6 of 169px; the control now reads set.
- **C:** Cover → every picture one shape (four cards at 279px).
- **D:** Fit → one shape still, and `object-fit: contain` — the whole picture.
- **E:** titles off → no title element anywhere; the note still reads "Idea: a quieter onboarding…".
- **F:** the setting survives Canvas and back, ⌘Z does not undo it, and returning to Medium · Original ratio ·
  titles on unsets the control and gives the masonry back.
- **G:** dark, and a phone: one column, nothing overflowing sideways. No console errors.
- **Neighbours re-run:** select · find · notes · tags · item (A–M) · index, all green.

**Guards,** watched failing first (3 new): `setView` keeps only what is not the ordinary and keeps nothing when
everything is; `collectionView` answers for every Collection, set or not; the settings survive the trip into a
page and back, and junk does not.

`tsc` clean · **2350 tests / 156 files** in UTC, Asia/Kolkata and America/Los_Angeles · eslint clean.

### Recorded, not started
- **A phone is one column at any card size,** because 254px of grid cannot hold two 150px cards with words in
  them. Pictures-only could, but the size is not told whether titles are on; not worth the coupling today.
- **The canvas ignores all three.** It has its own sizes — each item's saved box — which is the point of it.
- **Image ratio (square · landscape · portrait)**, §28's "potentially add", is not built: Cover already gives
  one shape, and a second shape control would need a reason beyond the word "potentially".


## Motion has one vocabulary: exits stop easing in, and a theme flip stops smearing — 2026-09-16

The user asked to start improving the app with the Emil Kowalski design-engineering
skill. Both motion skills the project works from (emil-design-eng, better-ui) agree on
two rules the app was breaking, and both breaks lived in shared tokens rather than on
any screen.

**An exit was easing in.** `--animate-exit`, `--animate-slide-out-right`,
`--animate-slide-out-bottom` and `--animate-settle-out` all ran on `--ease-in-quiet`
(`cubic-bezier(0.40, 0, 1, 1)`), a curve that holds nearly still through its first
frames — exactly when the reader is watching a menu close, so the close read as
sticky. Each one now takes `--ease-out-quiet`, the same family its entrance uses. The
asymmetry an exit does want is duration, and that was already right: exits run at
`--duration-fast` against the `--duration-base` an entrance takes.
`components/ds/ui/accordion.tsx` had its own copy of the rule spelled inline and was
carrying the same curve.

That left `--ease-in-quiet` with no callers, and `--ease-inout` never had any, so both
are gone from `app/tokens.css` and `app/ds-theme.css`. Verified live on
`/dev-preview/shell`: `--animate-exit` resolves to `exit .1s cubic-bezier(.16, 1, .3,
1)`, and neither removed token resolves to anything.

**A theme flip smeared.** Nothing suppressed transitions while the theme changed, and
the app carries 160 colour transitions, so all of them animated together and the
switch took their duration to arrive instead of landing at once. `applyAppearance` —
the one place the theme is stamped, shared by the settings panel, the sidebar toggle
and the OS watcher — now holds transitions across the swap: inject
`*,*::before,*::after{transition:none !important}`, read `document.body.offsetHeight`
to force the style flush while the override still applies, then drop it. Only a real
flip is held; a density or accent change keeps its transitions, and the first stamp
after boot only repeats what the init script already wrote.

**The browser found a bug that review would not have.** The first version restored on
a double `requestAnimationFrame`, which is what the recipe says. Measured with the
preview pane hidden, the rAF pair never ran at all and `transition:none !important`
stayed in `<head>` — the whole app sat with motion disabled. A hidden tab is not a
corner case here: `watchSystemTheme` flips a BACKGROUND tab when the OS goes dark at
sunset. A `setTimeout(restore, 150)` now sits underneath the frames, whichever arrives
first wins, and `restore` is idempotent. Measured again in the same hidden pane: the
override goes in, a nav row reads `transition-duration: 0s` at the moment `data-theme`
becomes `dark`, and the override is gone about a second later (a hidden tab throttles
timers to roughly one a second; a visible tab restores in two frames).

**Guards.** `app/design-system.test.ts` gains "an exit starts fast", which reads the
CURVE rather than the token's name: it parses every `cubic-bezier` in the two token
files and requires the first control point above the diagonal (y1 > x1) for every
`--animate-*` exit, and for every `data-[state=closed]:animate-[…]` a component spells
by hand. Its control asserts the removed ease-in fails that same check, and the guard
was proven by putting the accordion back on the old curve: it named
`components/ds/ui/accordion.tsx:40`, and passed again once restored.
`lib/theme.test.ts` covers the hold from four sides — held across the swap and given
back two frames later, not held for an accent change, not held on the first stamp, and
still restored when no frame ever runs.

`tsc --noEmit` clean; `vitest run` clean.

### Recorded, not started

- **Two duration ladders, the same words, different values.** `--dur-*` (tokens.css:
  80 / 120 / 180 / 240 / 320ms, 76 uses) and `--duration-*` (ds-theme.css: 20 / 100 /
  150 / 200 / 200 / 700ms, 23 uses) both spell instant · fast · base · slow, so "fast"
  means 120ms in the app layer and 100ms in the DS layer, and "instant" differs by 4×.
  `--dur-mid` (180ms) repeats `--dur-base`, `--duration-slower` repeats
  `--duration-slow`, and `--duration-hold` and `--duration-slower` have no callers at
  all. Merging them retimes ~99 call sites, so it wants its own pass with a
  before/after measurement rather than a rider on this one.
- **Entrances that start slow.** `--animate-slide-in-right` and
  `--animate-slide-in-bottom` (drawers, sheets) run on `--ease-standard`
  (`cubic-bezier(0.20, 0, 0.00, 1)`), whose first control point sits below the
  diagonal — so a drawer begins slowly, the same complaint the exits had. The new
  guard deliberately covers exits only until this is decided.
- **`--ease` is a third easing vocabulary.** `globals.css` defines
  `--ease: cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1)` and around twenty hover and colour transitions
  use it, beside `--ease-out` and `--ease-out-quiet`, which are the same curve under
  two names.
- **CLAUDE.md's motion line is the stale half.** It still says "No scale, bounce, or
  entrance animations" while the app deliberately presses at 0.97/0.98 on a spring
  (measured, and the answer to "feels very laggy and boring and slow") and ships
  `zb-page-in`, `zb-modal-in` and `zb-pop-in`. The rule needs rewriting to what the
  code decided, not the other way round.


## A toast leaves the way it arrived — 2026-09-16

Row 1 of the `find-animation-opportunities` sweep. A toast ENTERED on `animate-rise`
— up 8px, scale 0.98, fade — and then vanished mid-air, because the expiry loop
filtered it straight out of the array. Enter with motion, leave with none, is the one
place the interface still teleported.

`dismissToast` is two steps now. It marks the toast `leaving`, which keeps the row
mounted running `--animate-toast-out` (`@keyframes toast-out`, the mirror of `rise`:
back down 8px, scale 0.98, fade, `--duration-fast` `--ease-out-quiet`), and `remove`
takes it out for good. The card reports its own `animationend`, so nothing in the
store restates a duration the token already owns — and a 400ms floor timer runs
underneath, because a card whose animation never runs (a hidden tab, or a reader on
reduced motion, where the global reset collapses every duration to 0.01ms) still has
to leave. First one wins; `remove` is idempotent. This is the same lesson the theme
hold paid for yesterday: never let a frame-based callback be the only way back.

Three smaller things fell out of it:
- **Expiry dismisses rather than deletes**, so a toast that runs out of time leaves
  exactly the way one closed by hand does. The clocks moved into `expiredIds(list,
  now)` — pure, so §4.41's rule (4s · 8s with an action · never for an error) is
  tested instead of eyeballed through a `setInterval`.
- **A leaving toast is not a dedupe target.** A repeat of a dying message is a new
  event, not a ×2 on a corpse.
- **A leaving card stops taking clicks** (`pointer-events-none`): an Undo pressed as
  it fades is an Undo you cannot tell whether you got.
- The store grew a proper read side, `subscribeToasts` / `getToasts`, which the
  Toaster now uses for `useSyncExternalStore` and the tests read directly.

`components/ds/ui/toast.test.ts` covers it: the card survives its own dismissal and
goes at the floor, a second dismissal does not restart the exit, a repeat of a leaving
message opens a new toast while a repeat of a live one counts up, and the clocks hold.

Measured on `/dev-preview/confirm` with a real click: the card appears running `rise`,
carries `data-leaving` with a computed `animation-name: toast-out` while still in the
DOM, then goes. An 8s Undo toast still lives its 8s. (The pane reports
`document.hidden`, which throttles both timers and the polling loop to about one a
second, so the wall-clock figures there read ~9s and ~11s; the shapes are what the
measurement is for.)

`tsc --noEmit` clean; `vitest run` 2367 tests pass.


## A dropped card flies to its slot — 2026-09-16

Row 2 of the `find-animation-opportunities` sweep, and the first one the sweep could
not settle from code alone.

**Measured before touching anything**, with a real pointer drag over the DevTools
protocol (`scripts/verify/verify-board-drag.mjs`, content board, card dragged from
x=166 and released at x=478): the card read `left: 340` on all fourteen samples across
the 420ms after release. A 138px jump with nothing in between — the one thing a drag
must never do, because the whole gesture is a claim about where the thing went.

**The instrument was wrong first, though.** That script samples the CARD, which lands
in its slot instantly BY DESIGN — dnd-kit draws two objects, and the one that is
supposed to travel is the overlay you are holding. `scripts/verify/verify-drop-settle.mjs`
(a sibling, so the original keeps answering its own question) samples the overlay's
rect and the settling card's opacity every 25ms across the release.

**`lib/drop-settle.ts` is now the one answer.** `dropSettle()` returns dnd-kit's drop
animation at `--duration-slow` on `--ease-out-quiet`, taken from the MOTION seam rather
than spelled again, with a side effect that hides the card underneath while the overlay
flies so a drop never shows the same card twice. It returns `null` under
`prefers-reduced-motion`, where the instant answer is the honest one.

Measured after, same drag: overlay top 264 → 282 → 299 → 302 → 305 → 306 over ~150ms,
holding until it hands over at ~200ms, with the card at `opacity: 0` for the whole
flight and 1 the moment the overlay goes. The decelerating step sizes (18, 17, 3, 3, 1)
are `--ease-out-quiet` doing its work.

**`NO_SETTLE` is the declared opposite**, because two overlays should NOT fly: the
document block editor and the table both hold a `DragGhost` chip that NAMES the thing
rather than being it, and their `DropLine` has already said where it lands. Flying a
chip into a paragraph would animate a claim that is not true. It is a name rather than
a bare `null` so the decision is visible to a reader and to the guard.

**The guard found two call sites the grep had missed.** `app/design-system.test.ts`
gains "a drop lands where the drag said it would": every `<DragOverlay>` either takes
`dropSettle()` or declares `NO_SETTLE`, nobody spells the bare `dropAnimation={null}`
that used to hide the decision, and a control asserts the scan finds overlays at all.
It named `components/documents/block-editor.tsx` and `components/week/week-view.tsx`,
which passed NO `dropAnimation` prop — so they had been quietly taking dnd-kit's own
default, 250ms on plain `ease`, a curve and a duration from neither of this app's
ladders. The week board settles now; the block editor declares.

`tsc --noEmit` clean; `vitest run` 2370 tests pass.


## The check arrives — 2026-09-16

Row 3, the last of the `find-animation-opportunities` sweep, and deliberately the
smallest thing in the vocabulary.

The tick appeared hard: the Radix `Indicator` carried `transition-none`, while
`globals.css` held a `@keyframes tick` (0.2 → 1.1 → 1) that **nothing referenced** —
an intention someone had years ago and never wired. A checkbox is ticked dozens of
times a day, and at that frequency the gate allows near-imperceptible motion or none
at all. So what shipped is `--animate-tick`: scale 0.8 → 1 with opacity, one
`--duration-fast` on `--ease-out-quiet`, and **no overshoot** — a bounce on a control
used this often reads as a toy, which is the same argument the board cards' layout
animation already made. The dead keyframe is deleted; ds-theme.css now holds the only
definition.

Measured on `/dev-preview/tasks` with a real click: scale 0.800 → 0.936 → 0.980 →
0.994 → 1.000 and opacity 0 → 1 across 100ms, the step sizes decelerating the way the
curve says they should.

**The measurement caught a stale build, and reading the token would not have.** The
first run reported exactly what the new token says — `animation-name: tick`, `0.1s`,
`cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)` — while the transform it actually ran was 0.2 → 1.1 →
1: the OLD keyframe. The name resolved; the keyframe behind it did not. Turbopack was
still serving the compiled global CSS from before the edit (the cache this repo has
been bitten by before), so the document held a definition the source no longer has.
`rm -rf .next` plus a dev-server restart fixed it, and the check that proves it is
reading `document.styleSheets` for the `@keyframes` the browser actually holds, not
the computed `animation-name`.

`tsc --noEmit` clean; `vitest run` clean.


## One duration ladder — 2026-09-16

The app ran two, with the same words on different numbers: `--dur-*` in `tokens.css`
(80 / 120 / 180 / 240 / 320ms) beside `--duration-*` in `ds-theme.css` (20 / 100 / 150 /
200 / 200 / 700ms). "Fast" meant 120ms or 100ms depending on which layer a component
grew up in, and "instant" differed by 4×. Nobody could see which ladder a line spoke,
which is the condition every drift in this codebase has started from.

**Counted before choosing:** 76 uses of the app ladder against 178 of the DS one (23
`var()` plus 155 Tailwind `duration-*` utilities), and `components/ds/ui/motion.tsx`
already mirrors the DS numbers in JS. So the DS ladder is the one the app actually
speaks, and the other folded into it — mapped by what each token was timing, with
every move landing inside both the motion budget and CLAUDE.md's 100–150ms hover band:

| Retired | Was | Now | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--dur-instant` | 80ms | `--duration-fast` 100ms | These timed hover washes, never the press — the press has always had its own 20ms |
| `--dur-fast` | 120ms | `--duration-fast` 100ms | 47 uses, the bulk of the sweep |
| `--dur-base`, `--dur-mid` | 180ms | `--duration-base` 150ms | `--dur-mid` was a second name for `--dur-base`'s value |
| `--dur-slow`, `--dur-collapse` | 240ms, 220ms | `--duration-slow` 200ms | |
| `--dur-slower` | 320ms | — | No callers |

**Two rungs of the surviving ladder were dead too.** `--duration-slower` was a fifth
NAME for 200ms — the same wait, said twice — and `--duration-hold` (700ms) had no
callers at all. Four rungs left, each a different number, which is what makes the scale
readable: a rung nobody can distinguish is how one ladder becomes two again.

Measured live on `/dev-preview/shell` after the rebuild: the ladder resolves to 20ms ·
.1s · .15s · .2s, every retired `--dur-*` resolves to nothing, and a sidebar nav row
animates on ONE number (0.1s) where it used to run its background at 80ms against its
colour at 120ms **inside the same rule**.

**Guard** — "one duration ladder", four assertions: it reads the rungs it guards
(control), every rung is a distinct number, no rung is unused, and nobody asks for the
retired ladder. CSS comments are stripped before scanning, so the note in `tokens.css`
that explains what was removed cannot trip it.

**One stray edit, named rather than buried:** the sweep walked `.open-next/` and
rewrote 14 `var()` uses inside a compiled CSS chunk there. That is Cloudflare build
output, regenerated wholesale by the next `opennextjs-cloudflare build`, so nothing is
lost — but a source sweep has no business there, and the exclusion list (`node_modules`,
`.next`, `.git`) needed `.open-next` added.

`tsc --noEmit` clean; `vitest run` 2374 tests pass.


## One easing vocabulary, and the hover it was hiding — 2026-09-16

**Three names, two curves.** `--ease-out` and `--ease-out-quiet` were byte-identical
(`cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.30, 1)`), and `globals.css` kept a third, `--ease`
(`.2,.8,.2,1`), on 61 hover and colour transitions. 70 uses now say one name. What
survives says what it is FOR: `--ease-out-quiet` for arrivals, departures and colour ·
`--ease-standard` for movement ON screen, which accelerates out of rest · `--ease-spring`
for the press release only, where the overshoot is the point.

**Retiring `--ease-out` removed a collision as well as a duplicate.** Tailwind v4 ships
its own `--ease-out` (`cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.2, 1)`); ours only won by cascade order,
which is not a thing to build a vocabulary on. With ours gone, `--ease-out` resolves to
Tailwind's again — visible proof the two had been fighting.

**Entrances that started slow, fixed.** `--animate-slide-in-right` and
`--animate-slide-in-bottom` (drawers, sheets) ran on `--ease-standard`, whose first
control point sits below the diagonal: a drawer that holds still for its first frames is
exactly the sluggishness both motion skills name first. They take `--ease-out-quiet` now.
The menu panel and the rich-text popover carried `zb-pop-in 120ms var(--ease-standard)` —
a hardcoded duration off the ladder AND a slow-starting curve — and now take
`var(--duration-fast) var(--ease-out-quiet)`.

### The global press was eating every button's hover

Measuring the result turned up something much larger than the sweep.

`transition` is a SHORTHAND. The rule that presses every control —
`button:not(.zb-nopress), [role="button"]:not(.zb-nopress)`, specificity 0,1,1 and late
in the file — outranks both `.zb-press` and `.zb-nav-item` (0,1,0), so when the press
went global it did not ADD a transform transition: it REPLACED their lists. Measured on
`/dev-preview/shell`:

| Element | `transition-property` before |
| --- | --- |
| `a.zb-nav-item` | `background, color` |
| `button.zb-nav-item` | `transform` |
| `button.zb-press` | `transform` |
| any plain `<button>` | `transform` |

So every hover wash in the app landed instantly on buttons — including on `.zb-press`,
the class written to carry that wash, whose careful list of box-shadow, background,
border-color and colour had not applied to a button since the press went global. Only
links kept theirs, which is why nobody caught it by eye: the sidebar looked right where
its rows are `<a>` and wrong where they are `<button>`, in the same list.

A shorthand cannot be added to, so the rule that wins has to carry the whole list. It
does now, and measured after: `transform, background-color, color, border-color,
box-shadow` — transform on the spring, the rest on the quiet curve, all at 100ms.

**Guards.** "one easing vocabulary" (reads the vocabulary · every arrival and departure
starts fast · a curve is spelled only in the token files and the motion seam · nobody
asks for a retired name) and "the global press does not eat the hover" (finds the rule ·
carries the colour properties · presses on the spring and washes on the quiet curve).
Each has its control.

Also: `.next` needed clearing again — an HMR-only rebuild kept serving a `:root` that
still declared the deleted `--ease`.

`tsc --noEmit` clean; `vitest run` 2381 tests pass.
